BALLADE OF HIS "YOUNG LADY." My lady's heart 'twere hard to touch, And sighs and vows she'd soon repel; But7,if she liked one twice as much One would not like 11Pr half as well. She careth not for sage or swell, For guardsman stout or poet lean, Who haunt Parnassus or Fall Mall: My lady-love is just thirteen. She loves a rabbit iu a hutch (A fat Aquinas in his cell), She loves an aged cat, whose clutch At breakfast-time exerts a spell, A most ungracious Florizel. In fact it's easy to be seen, Were she at all averse to tell, My lady-love is just thirteen: - Although she reads the Higher Dutch, On culture's peaks apart to dwell She feigns not; nor of things as such Does she discourse, nor parallel Dante and Dante Gab‘iel.; Yet she has 'views' advanced and keen On chocolate and caramel,— My lady-love is just thirteen. Envoy. Madam, just homage you compel, Mature, self-conscious, and serene. One heart alone you cannot quell; My lady-love is just thirteen. —Longnian's Magazine. J. B. B. NTCHOLS.

"I never contract bad habits," said Robinson to his wife. "No, dear, you generally expand them," was her reply. "What plan," said one actor to another. " shall I adopt to fill the house at my benefit?" " Invite your creditors," Was the reply. A country debating society is nerving itself up to wrestle with the question: "When a roman and a mouse meet, which is the more frightened. It is related as a singular fapt that fat men never com- mit crime. It doesn't seem so singular when you reflect that it is difficult for a fat man to stoop to anything low. The party had been harvesting, and were now returning. "Jock," said the worthy's intended, " dicl'ee kiss oi in tha tunnel?" "Non, lassie, ah didna." Short pause, and then unconcernedly—" oe, 'twas sown 'oon alse thun 1" The Due de Vivonne being indisposed, his friends sent for a physician. When the Due heard he was in attendance in the antechamber, he said: "Tell him I cannot see him, be- cause I am not well; let him call againhnother time." An old man picked up half-a-crown in the street. "Old man, that's mine," said a keen-looking little rascal, "so hand it over." "Did thine have a hole in it ?" asked the old man. " Yes " replied the other smartly. "Then it is not thine," mildly replied the old man; "thou must learn to be a little sharper next time my boy." The following story is told of a college professor, the author of an article on "Ancient Methods of Filtration." By a misprint his subject was announced in the advertise- ments as "Ancient Methods of Flirtation," much to the amusement of his friends, one of whom, at a social party, said to him: "Professor, do give us your lecture on Ah- cient Methods of Flirtation.'" The Professor, who is a bachelor and a social h4bnrite, instantly replied: "Miss X, that lecture can be delivered only to a single auditor at a One, and must be illustrated with experiments." WOMAN'S MlSSlON.—Diverse are the functions of the sweet maidenhood; for there are girls whose work is in the house—housewifely •, and these, in all generations, will be- come wives and mothers ;and there are others who love the work that lies outside the house, and these, in the next generation, will become lawyers, doctors, and priestesses. Some are born to be nurses, some to be dressmakers, some to be cooks; but these are very few. Some are born to run after the last new thing, to worship the latest apostle, and to revere the last new gospel. But some are born to be beautiful, gracious, and sympathetic. In the hands of such women, some men develop noble ambitions, some show themselves at their best, and a few recover that ancient virtue which used to be called goodness.—Good Words. UNPUNCTUALITY.—That was an awkward predicament in which poor Mr. P. found himself—namely, five minutes too late for his wedding—minutes which seemed to the mar- riage party, and especially to the bride, like hours of tor- ture. Strange that such a mischance did not cure him of unpunctual habits; yet it proved unavailing; for that gen- tleman and his wife kept the company invited to meet them at their first dinner party waiting for fully half an hour; and still, though old married people, continue in all things the same evil usage, causing thereby an amount of annoy- ance to their friends never to be sufficiently regretted, and making their enemies "chortle" malignantly. An officer, invited by an eccentric maiden aunt to wait upon her at a certain hour, forfeited a valuable gold watch, because he arrived five minutes late, the stern old dame brooking no delay, and bestowing the gift on another relative instead. We pity the condition of the struggling young doctor who, being sent for in great haste by a certain millionaire, de- layed five minutes, and found, on arriving at the house of the patient, that another M.D. had entered the house before him, thus suicidally damaging his own pros- pects at the beginning of his career. Five minutes before the hour and you have matters in your own hands; two minutes after it and you are left out in the cold, as the lady felt who drove in a cab to the last train, and, arriving two minutes late, had the pleasure of a ten-mile drive on a drill winter night, with 20e. to pay at the end of her journey, instead of 2s.—Clannbers's Jpurnal. A TURNING-POINT IN THE LIFE OF COLUMBUS.—There was a Franciscan monastery outside the town [Palos], where poor travellers used to apply for aid. One day Columbus, leading his boy by the hand, knocked at the door of this , refuge, and begged, for the love of Heaven, that a little bread and a draught of water might be given to the child. lie was desired to enter, and as he satwithin waiting for the promised alms, the prior, Juan Perez de Marchena, passed by-. Something in the appearance of Columbus arrested his attention, and he stopped to speak to him. . . . Seeing the mingled curiosity and compassion of the prior, Colum- tueunfolded something of his story, and the result was an invitation to repose himself for some days at the monastery. The acquaintance rapidly ripened, and the prior was soon . put in possession of the quenchless ambition of his strange gnest, and of all the grounds on which he rested his un- conquerable faith. The brethren of the convent were per- haps slow in sympathy; but in the town of Palos was a lively physician, whose company the prior speedily re- quested, that he might hear these visions of a world beyond chaos. The physician had intelligence enough to under- stand the reasoning of Columbus, and confirmed the faith of the prior. The latter now cast about to find some means of aiding the enterprise, and bethought him of a former *acquaintanceship with Fernando de Talavera, the confessor I of the Queen. To this ecclesiastic he wrote a letter of in- troductiori for Columbus, highly commending his genius, and beseeching Fernando to procure for him an audience at court. With a generosity that deserves immortal remem- brance, the good monk provided the poor adventurer with an outfit suitable for his appearance before the grandees of Spain, and also with a purse of money to sustain him. He offered also to take charge of the boy during his father's ab- aence ; and so with a grateful hearten! euddenly brightened prospects, Columbus set out afresh. —Good Words. THE CUCICOO.—Some years ago A lengthened correspon- dence appeared in the Daily ilretps as to the cuckoo, and the popular rhymes to which its appearance has given rise. It waa said, that the bird in cpeetion had been heard in certain neighbourhoods of London. This was in the early part of April, 1870. Be that as it may, on the assumption that the report was correct, correspondents from all parts of the country rushed into print. div.head: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

A correspondent of Nature, Mr. Oswald Fitch, records an' instance of benevolence in his cat, which was observed to tike some fish bones from the house to the garden and to place them in front of a mis-e-ably thin and evidently hungry stranger cat. Mr. Fitch's cat repeated the act, and (this is perhaps the most curious part of the story) then returned to its own dinner in the scullery and finished the remainder of the repast, its digestion being no doubt im- proved by its previous charitable forbearance. The Athenteum says that Mr. B. Quaritch has in prepara- tion a volume of transcripts in fac-simile by the photo- intaglio process, from famous and beautiful works of the Italian engravers of the fifteenth century" in the British Museum, beginning with the illustrations to "Ii Monte Sancto di Dio," Florence, 1477, which have been assigned to B. Baldini, and were executed from designs by Botticelli; to be followed by the illustrations to the " Divina Comme- dia" of Dante, attributed to the same artist, and published by Landino in Florence, 1481. M. Jules Guerin has described before the French Academy of Sciences a method of obtaining local insensibility, as distinct from general ansethesia, for employment in surgical operations, the dangers incidental to the use of chloroform being thus avoided. The method rests on the principle.that consciousness of the irritation of the nerve•fibres is subor- dinate to the integrity of the peripheral nervous zone, and the condition of insensibility to the pain of the operation is produced by the preliminary application of Vienna caustic to the part of the skin to be operated upon. MONOTYPE PRINTING.—A Boston artist, Mr. C. A. Walker, has invented an improvement in monotype print- ing. This improvement consists simply in painting the monotype in colours and in printing it on linen paper which absorbs the oil and leaves the pure pigments on the surface. Mr. Walker has made numerous experiments with this process, and has taken fifty examples of his work to be exhibited at Messrs. Kneedler and Co.'s gallery in New York. Many of his pictures resemble water colours, some- what too minutely finished but pure in tone; others have the general appearance of an oil painting. ALCOHOL FROM SMOKE.—The latest instance of the utili- sation of waste products is that effected at Elk Rapids,l Michigan, with the gaseous matter given forth by a blast- furnace in which are manufactured fifty tons of charcoal iron per day. In the case to which we refer, the vast amount of smoke from the pits, formerly lost in air, is now turned to account by being driven by suction or draught into stills surrounded by cold water, the result of the con- densation being first, acetate of lime; secondly, methyl alcohol ; third, tar; the fourth part produces gas, which is consumed under the boilers. Each cord of word produces 29,000 cubic feet of smoke; 2,900,000 feet of smoke handled in twenty-four hours, producing 12,000 pounds of acetate of lime, 200 gallons of alcohol, 25 pounds of tar.— Stearns' New Idea. An improved method of liquifying oxygen so as to obtain it in what M. Jamin spoke of as a "static" condition, dis- covered by a young Pole, M. Wroblewski4 a student in the laboratory of M. Cailletet (who, with M. Pictet, first suc- ceeded in reducing the gas to the liquid form), has been described before the French Academy of Sciences. M. Wroblewski has succeeded in producing a more intense degree of cold than any previously known by putting ethy- lene in a state of ebullition in vacua. The hydrogen th'er- mometer registered 136 degrees Centigrade below zero. At this temperature, and with a pressure of 22 atmospheres, liquid oxygen was obtained in a stable form as compared with the unstable and fugitive state in which it was ob- tained by MM. Pictet and Cailletet. The liquid is colour- less, and in this respect contrasts with the blue colour of the liquid ozone obtained by M. Chapuis. M. Wroblewski has also, by the same method, succeeded in obtaining liquid. nitrogen. AN ANCIENT CHINESE PLAY.—It is announced that Wong Chin Foo, the editor of the Chinese American, will publish his English translation of the Chinese drama, "Fan Ton; or, The Royal Slave." The translator says that it , was written twelve centuries ago, when "civilisation was at its highest point. Men and women studied at the same uni- versities and competed for the same literary li..nours. Since that time the play has steadily held its place on the Eastern stage. Fan Ton is a son of a king in the Tong dynasty. His father becomes enamoured of a beautiful and well- educated peasant girl, who for a few years lives in the royal household and becomes the favourite of the Empress and Emperor. She aspires, however, to the throne. The Em- press is put out of the way first, and then she marries the Emperor, who is also killed, and the peasant girl thus be- comes Empress. The young prince is sold as a slave. The interest centres in the Royal slave, who, by valour and the aid of the peasantry, finally regains the throne, despite the many intrigues of the Empress, who is killed in the last act of the play." PISCICIILTURE.—A TANK ON WHEELS.—It appears that one of th 3 palace cars belonging to the United States Fish Commission started recently for California with a passenger list of young fish numbering 18,040. The car in its appear- ance resembled a modern sleeping-car, having the compart- ments at each end. The central part had an aisle running through the centre, and, in place of the seats on each side, were wooden ledges about 3ft. high, on which were placed the tin fish tanks. The human passengers, as well as the fish, lived in the car. The fish were not placed in the tanks filled with water, as the motion of the train would dash the water about and destroy many lives among the young pas- sengers. But, instead, about 20 fish were placed in gallon tin pails, and these pails were put in the tanks, and then the latter filled with water. With the carp, however, the water in the pails was sufficient, and the motion of the car , tended to the circulation of air in the water, keeping it fresh. The attendants renewed the water every eight hours, and kept a careful watch to remove any fish that might have died. The percentage of fish lost by death, however, was very small. The fish did not complete their travels when they left the car. At St. Louis, the first stop made by the car, supplies of fish were left for applicants residing in Missouri and Arkansas. From this point pails of fish were sent all over the States by express at the expense of t the consignee. SNAKES.—Miss Catherine C. Hopley has written a chatty book on what many people will still, in spite of Miss Hop- ley's protests, consider a rather repulsive subject— " Snakes." She has, however, studied her subject in the spirit of a naturalist, and whoever has heard the affec- tionate tone of reproof with which the attendant in the magnificent snake-house at Amsterdam addresses the most troublesome occupant of the cages as "bad fellow" will I know that it is possible to learn to like even snakes. This Miss Hopley evidently has done, and she has therefore suc- ceeded in producing a very readable book, in which she cor- rects several common errors. The volume is not at all unlikely to develop in the reader some regard for Miss Hop- ley's pets. One of the curious things which Miss Hopley brings out is the way in which snakes seem to think with the whole of their bodies. Thus she gives a very remark- able account of how a "four-rayed" snake while engaged in devouring one bird captured another by pressure then threw a coil round it, meanwhile capturing a third, also by pressure. The last capture was likewise secured by a coil, the other coil, with the prey enclosed, being deftly slipped higher up the body, so that mere length of rope, so to speak, might be available for the second coil. This per- formance, which took place while the first of the three birds was being quietly swallowed, Miss Hopley speaks of as a display of "independent constricting powers," two or more parts of the reptile being engaged in different work at the stifle time. Miss Hopley's liking for snakes is, indeed, ob- viously to a large extent the result of her admiration for the sagacity with which these creatures employ their bodies as hands.

-WHAT NITRo-GLycERTNE rs.—Nitro-glycerine is produced by mixing nitric and sulphuric acids with glycerine at a low temperature. The important agents are the glycerine and the nitric acid. The sulphuric acid appears to do little save attract to itself any water which may be present in the glycerine or the nitric acid.' It is well known that sul- phuric acid has a strong affinity for water, and it is this characteristic which renders it useful in this connection. Nitric acid is prepared by treating nitrate of potash—salt- petre—or nitrate of soda with sulphuric acid—oil of vitriol. Glycerine is best produced pure by beating up an oil or fat with about half its weight of water into an emul- sion. This is then pumped through a coil of iron piping heated to the temperature of melting lead, the rate of pump- ing being such that the mixture of oil and water will oc- cupy about ten minutes in traversing the coil. The fluid which conies out of the worm quickly separates into two portions, glycerine lying at the bottom. The supernatant oily liquid being drawn off, the glycerine remains, nearly pure. Its formula is G 3 118 03. Nitro-glycerine is made by adding nitric and sulphuric acids to glycerine. Unfor- tunately, no skill whatever is required to produce the re- quired explosive, only a knowledge of one or two simple facts; but skill is required to produce nitro-glycerine pure enough to be comparatively safe. Nitro-glycerine is a brownish, smooth, oily liquid, and a deadly poison. Its formula is C3115N309. Its explosive force is due to the un- stable nature of the compound. We have in most explo- sives carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen to begin with; to these have been added—by treatment with nitric acid—a certain portion of nitric peroxide, N 02, that is, one atom of nitro- gen and two atoms of oxygen; but these two gases have a very feeble affinity for each other, while, on the contrary, the carbon and the hydrogen have intense affinities for oxy- gen. On the least provocation, therefore, the oxygen leaves the nitrogen, which, set free, ceases to be a liquid, and be- comes a gas, while intense heat is produced, which volatilises and breaks up the other compounds, and augments enor- mously the pressure of the escaping gases. Those who are familiar with the experiments of Pictet, on the liquefaction of gas, know how intense is the cold and how enormous the pressure required to liquefy even a small quantity of such a gas as nitrogen, but this liquefaction has been accomplished in the explosive by chemical affinity; and the moment this affinity is destroyed, the chained force is let loose—we know with what result. Now, it will be seen that nitro-glycerine ought to be a powerful explosive, for in it no less than three molecules of N 02 take the place of three atuns of hydrogen.

The splenic apoplexy called black-leg is reported to have made its appearance among the cattle in the northern parts of Texas.

A food exhibition is to be held on the Champs Elysees during the 50 days following the 6th of May. Exhibitors will be allowed to clear out their stocks provided they can replace fresh supplies of their exhibits by the following morning. Dr. Geo. B. Loring, Commissioner of Agriculture in the United States, states that he has decided to furnish land, the necessary animals, and well-equipped apparatus for a thorough experiment with, and investigation of, the differ- ent diseases of domestic animals.

There is at the present time a good demand for Irish-bred horses. At SetvelPs Repository, Dublin, last week, 46 horses were sold that realised over £lOO each, 13 realised between £2OO and £3OO, and seven between £3OO and £4OO. Of Mr. Trotter's stud 37 averaged £174 each. On the 17th instant, Grand Duchess Nancy, of the Under- ley herd, had a roan heifer calf, by Prince Saladin 4th. Mr. R. Thompson of Inglewood, Penrith, has sold to an American breeder 12 females and two bulls from the Ingle- wood herd. The price is said to be £9OO. A consignment of Aberdeen polled c-attle and Ayrshire cows has recently been made to China. The stock were shipped to Greenock on Saturday week by Messrs. Sturgeon and Son, Grey's Hall, Essex. The polled cattle, together with some other breeding stock, are intended for the Kiai- Ping breeding farm, Tin Sin, extending, it is said, to about 100,000 acres, and owned by Mr. Tong-Kin-Sing, an enter- prising merchant and cattle breeder in the north of China. The Ayrshires' together with some Dairy Shorthorns from the SouthcastFarm, Leighton Buzzard, are for the Shang- hai Dairy Company. MAJOR-GENERAL H. Y. D. SCOTT, C. 8., F.R.S., late Royal Engineers, died last week at his residence, Silverdale, Sydenham, aged 61. He was secretary to the Royal Com- missioners of the 1851 Exhibition. He had just finished superintending the construction of- the Great International Fisheries Exhibition. He leaves a wolow and fifteen chil- dren. Major-General Scott took an active interest in the possibility of turning sewage to agricultural and commercial use. He had devisee' a system of precipitation and com- bustion by which the solid matters of sewage were to be- come available as a cement, while the soluble parts should be turned on to the4and. SEWAGE CE'LTURE NEAR PARIS.—The National Agricul- tural Society of France has of late more than once discussed the effect of the cultivation of the peninsula of Gennevil- Hers by the aid of the Paris drainage. It appears that a large and growing population has'been attracted by the re- munerative value of the crops to be thus obtained; while from the dairy farmer's point of view the results are equally valuable, the cows giving a superior quality of milk, which finds a ready sale in the better quarters of the city. It is further claimed that, after filtration through the soil, the residue which enters the Seine is purer by far than that launched in the stream by the factories; and that popular prejudices against the products of the laud are entirely re- moved.

CEMENT ron CONCRETE WALL—The proportion of sand to be mixed with cement for concrete for footpaths is three of sand to one of cement. The sand is first spread evenly upon a mixing-board and the cement is spread over the sand. The two are then mixed dry by shovelling over into a heap; then dividing into two heaps and then casting it back into one again; five parts of gravel or broken shells may be added to make the concrete, as follows :—The gravel or shell is put into a heap by itself and well wetted. The mixed sand and cement are wetted and mixed to a thin mortar, a small quantity at a time; then the wet gravel is added, and the whole is worked over quickly until every particle of the gravel is covered with cement; the concrete is then spread and beaten down, and if it is too moist dry sand is sprinkled en to it and beaten down until no more will be taken up. After a short time it may be rolled or smoothed with a plank rubber and left until it is hard. INSTITUTE OF AGRICULTURE.-011 Thursday week, Prof. Tanner and a large class of members of the Institute of Agriculture met at Messrs. Welford's dairies at St. Peter's Park, Paddington. The proceedings consisted of the ex- amination of the very handsome and well-equipped build- ings—including a cowshed, with walls of china tiles—and the witnessing of butter-making by the latest and most modern appliances. In all, nearly 100 gallons of milk were passed through two of Laval's separators. The cream from this was made into butter in an eccentric churn, driven by steam-power, and the butter kneaded, and the buttermilk expressed on revolving butter-workers. The internal work- ing of the separator was explained by Prof. Tanner. In the cowshed a short address on the constituents of milk, and their variations from different breeds, by Prof. A. H. Stokes, F.C.S. The class were evidently very delighted with their visit, and many members took away with them rolls of the butter which they had seen less than an hour before as milk.

MEAT FROM RUSSIA.—A cargo of fresh meat has been landed in London from Libau, a Russian port in the Baltic. The meat consists of beef and mutton sent over in dry air refrigerating chambers, such as are used in the case of meat from the United States. This is a very significant circum- stance at this particular time. It is thought that very little dead meat would come from the Continent of Europe if the cattle traffic was stopped permanently, but who can tell what may result from this small beginning? Russian cattle and sheep have been prohibited for some years, be- cause in Russia they have always Rinderpest with them; consequently Russia has gone into the dead meat trade. Why should not France, Germany, Denmark, and the Penin- sula do the same thing? Because they dont wan't to ; and, as Lord Carlingford points out, they are not likely to make a commencement until thecattle traffic is permanently stopped. For some months past Russia has been sending frozen poul- tu from Black Sea ports, and very excellent it is. Now she is making a start with a trade of greater importance, and one which may grow into dimensions which have never been dreamed of here. It is never wise to despise the day of small things, and this cargo of fresh meat from the Baltic may be literally the first drop of a coming deluge. It would be strange if Russia should become a rival to the United States in respect to her exports of fresh meat after checkmaking that country last year with her exports of grain. Stranger things than that have happened, and may happen again. It has been stated that this Russian fresh meat—not frozen meat—can be laid down in London at 30. per lb._

THE ORIGIN OF CULTIVATED PLANT;.--7A work on this subject, from the pen of M. de Candolle, has recently ap- peared. It treats of 247 species. The author has utilised evidence from Swiss lake dwellings, from ancient Egyptian monuments, and from Chinese works (better interpreted by Dr. Bretschneider than by his predecessors). He has ex- amined many herbaria, consulted travellers, drc. Of all the 247 species, except three, he has been able to say whether they come from the old or the new world, and to specify with certainty or high probability the country of their origin. The exceptions are two species of the genus Oucurbita and the ordinary kidney bean (Phaseolus vvlgaris). There are many species, however, that have not yet been certainly found in a wild state. Where the country of origin has been little visited by botanists, this is not sur- prising ; but the case is sometimes otherwise. Certain species very long cultivated seem to be in course of extinc- tion or extinct; they have not been found wild or have bcen met with only once, perhaps, in a single locality in their native region, though the latter has been well ex- plored. Probably, too, their ancient home has been more or less of wide extent, considering the extension of their cultivation among people that had little connection with each other. M. de Candolle counts 44 species of the old world which appear to have been cultivated more than 4,000 years, and five of the new, probably cultivated as long. Of these 49, six or seven seem to be extinct or in course of extinction. Maize has never been found in the wild state. The bean and tobacco (Nicotiana Tobacum) have been found only once; the chick pea, the lentil (Errum lens and Ervum Ervillia), and wheat, have only been found very rarely and under conditions doubtful as to the spontaneous quality. Most of these species present the character of seeds filled with starch, without any protection against rodents and in- sects, who seek them eagerly; and it is not wonderful that they should perish in the struggle for existence. With to- bacco (which had been found with certainty in the wild state only at one point of the Republic of Ecuador by M. Andre) the case is different. Since the natives smoked or chewed tobacco from Peru to the United States, it is prob- able that the habitat of the plant was once much wider.— Times.

Life is made up not of great sacrifices or duties, but of little things, of which smiles and kindness and small obli- gations, given habitually, are what win and preserve the heart.—Sir Humphrey Dam WESTERN INFLUENCES IN THE CENTRAL ASIAN DESERT. —Cards I met only once in the desert, and they had then the curious name of "Urns Kitabi," i.e., the Koran of the Muscovite, whilst drink was confined to those outlaws who, by their frequent inroads into Persia, had become ac- quainted with wine or with brandy. Now there are two large brandy distilleries in close proximity to the Akhal country, whilst the Yomuts can procure that poison from the numerous shops opened in Krasnowodsk and in Tchiki- shlar, an opportunity of which they seem to make ample use. Ido not doubt that there will be other drawbacks caused by the introduction of Western culture through Russian channels, but in spite of all these inconveniences, which appear wherever Europeans come in contact with uncivilised races, we are bound to say that the change is for the better, and that, considering what life in the desert was twenty years ago, Russia's advance in that part of Central Asia, if judged from a humanitarian and not a political point of view, must be taken as beneficial to the cause of humanity.—Professor Vambery,in Good Words.

When a young and struggling actor, Grassot hit on an ingenious plan to save himself the walk from the theatre after rehearsal to his lodgings, which were situated near Montmartre Cemetery. He dressed in black, and if he espied a funeral procession with a vacant seat in any of the coaches promptly pulled out a handkerchief, and hid his face in it while hailing the vehicle. Under the impression that he was one of the mourners arrived late, he was, of course, immediately installed in the vacant seat. This went on for some time, till one unlucky day Grassot attempted to talk to his companions. "Poor thing, I weep for her," he said from the folds of his handkerchief. "H. is dead, not she," replied his opposite neighbour. "I know, I know; but so young." "Our good friend was sixty-eight last birthday," objected another. "I alluded to his children, monsieur," said the unhappy Grassot. "But he had none," said the mourners in chorus, and Grassot was thankful that the coach halted at this moment at the cemetery, thus enabling him to escape. In the future he resolved that his rule of sympathy should be, " Peu de parolles et beaucoup de mou- choir."

The rain which was descending as we were concluding our remarks for the press last week has been most welcome, and has had a marked effect on turnips, onions, peas, and beans, amongst the sown things, and their progress has been almost magical. We have no recollection of seeing onions come up so rapidly, which we account for in this way. The ground was turned over two or three times on warm days; in this way we husbanded the heat, so that the temperature was several degrees higher than if it had been left in its normal condition.

PEAS.—Those who have not aspired for an early lot of these should sow now such kinds as Harrison's Glory, Ad- vancer, and William the Ist. The latter, though one of the earliest, will hold its own amongst the 2nd earlies. We usually draw drills not less than 3in. wide at the bottom, first stretching a line to guide us, and with the draw hoe we open the drills. If not sufficiently wide by doing one side we more the line and draw some towards us on the other side. This affords an opportunity to spread the seeds over a greater space. Peas are not partial to too much fresh manure, but succeed best on ground which has been well supplied for a previous crop, such as celery or onions. Mice have a great liking for peas, judging from the per- sistency with which they burrow into the ground after them, and an entire crop has been destroyed in this way. Happily we have a preventive in paraffin oil applied thus: —Place the peas in a vessel and pour two or three table- spoonfuls to every pint of seeds. This will be found enough to moisten them, if well shaken up. Another deterrent is to wet the seeds with water, drain the water off, and sprinkle a small handful of red lead and shake all up until every seed is of the colour of the lead. Whichever plan is selected, either is a perfect safeguard against the inroads of mice. BROAD BEANS.—The Green Windsor may be sown in drills similar in depth to peas, rather deeper than otherwise, and if there is a spot in the garden more moist than another let it be used for these. In such a situation they will con- tinue bearing much longer. The distance between the seeds in the drill may be from two to four inches, according to the richness of the soil, and where very poor the row may be set double.

SCARLET RUNNEES may be sown in rows or in patches in convenient places for training them. We pointed out in a previous issue what we considered the most suitable arrange- ment for these in a small garden. The seeds should be covered over four inches deep, and it is advisable not to sow the whole even now, but reserve some for a week later. The Scarlet Runner is q tender plant, and if in the early part of May the weather icvpry warm, the seeds soon germinate and the plants make tileir appearance above ground ta be destroyed by the first frost. If, on the other hand, the first seed deposited are subject to much moisture and cold, they decompose instead of germinating, and under the most favourable conditions they are frequently irregular. Slugs also seem to find them out, almost before they are out of the ground, and devour the centre, rendering the plant worthless and causing the rows to have a gappy appearance. To meet the emergencies we devote a space at the ends of the rows, in which we place the seeds thick or only an inch or two distant, covering them over as in the rows. These are easier protected from slugs by encircling them with ashes, over which the slug does not care to travel, especially if dry, and if traps are laid near too they maybe destroyed. From these thickly-sown patches we get a sufficient number of plants to make up defects. FRENCH BEANS or drop Kidney Bean are sown about two inches deep and two to four inch between the seeds in the rows. On good soil a single plant will grow nearly a foot in diameter, whilst on others three or four would not attain that dimension. Where the land is cold and tenacious the drills should be drawn somewhat deeper, to admit of a layer of fine ashes over the bottom. The seeds might be covered with the same material.

MUSTARD AND CRESS, which is frequently sown in patches, is preferable in rows, being more convenient for cutting. The seeds are also, in many instances, sown too thick and covered over too deep. All the covering required is only as much as will hide the seed from view. Mustard seed will germinate if left uncovered, providing the light is excluded.

RIDGE CIICDMBERS.—This is the time to make prepara- tion for these, either by excavating a trench 18in. wide and about 2ft. deep for any kind of fermenting material, or the material may be partly below and above ground. The more there is the longer it will retain the heat. It is best to pur- chase a plant or two, which costs little more than the packet of seed.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—THE LILY OF THE VALLEY.— Few are aware how freely this innocent and beautiful-look- ing flower thrives in most soils. It does not make much progress the first year after its removal, but, after, it spreads like couch grass. Though it has now made some growth, it is the best time to plant it. Bulbous plants, such as snowdrops, daffodils, and crocuses, as they go out of flower should have a stick inserted in the centre of each to indicate their position when the tops die. We use pieces of wire a foot long; they are, of course, more durable. When digging and manuring has not been practical amongst the plants in this department, in consequence of their prox- imity to each other, they may be highly stimulated by sur- facing the ground round them with horse droppings. The rain will wash the nutriment out of it down to the roots, and in time the roots will come up and take possession of the manure.

THE WINDOW.—We showed in a former paper how the green tie-, so troublesome at this time of the year, may be asphyxiated with the fumes of tobacco. As that mode of destroying them may be as objectionable to anti-smokers as it is to the unfortunate insect, we will add another. To every quart of warm water (rain is the best) squeeze the juice out of a quarter of an ounce of tobacco by placing it in a piece of rag or muslin; afterwards dissolve a piece of soft soap, the size of a walnut; when cool it may be applied with a soft brush, or the plant may be held over one vessel and the liquid poured on to it. In this way the same will do several plants, and that which is left can be put in a bottle for a future time. Balsams should be sown in the smallest pots made, two or three seeds in a pot, and as soon as they come up pull all out but one, which should be left as near the centre as can be. This plan is much preferable to that of sowing a quantity in a pot, which necessitates the destruction of many roots in the operation of parting them for potting. Our remarks on potting must be deferred for another paper.
Mere sensibility is not true taste, but sensibility to real excellence is.

To live long it is necessary to live slowly; to live happily, to live wisely. Talking and eloquence are not the same; to speak, and to speak well, are two things. The happiness or unhappiness of old age is often nothing but the extract of a past life. In character, in manners, in style, in all things, the su- preme excellence is simplicity. "Boots blacked inside" is posted on a doorway. But who wants his boots blacked inside?

Anybody can tell you what to put in a newspaper; but the real problem is what to leave out. A lawyer who climbs upon a chair after a law-book gets a little higher in order that he may get a little lore. When Mr. Fish had his ctildren's portraits painted, they were spoken of as sardines—little Fishes done up in oil.

Don't live a single hour of your life without doing exactly what is to be done in it, and going straight through it from beginning to end. Work, pay, study, whatever it is, take hold at once and finish it up squarely and clearly, then do the other thing, without letting any moments drop between. Nature seems to exist for the excellent. The world is up- held by the veracity of good men. They make the earth wholesome. Life is sweet and tolerable in our belief in such society, and, actually or ideally, we manage to live without superiors. _ _

What if you fail in business? You *still have life and , health. Don't sit down and cry about mishaps, for that will , never get you out of debt, nor buy your children frocks. ' Go to work, eat sparingly, dress moderately, drink nothing exciting, keep a merry heart, and you'll rise again. Lady Bloomfield, in her "Reminiscences of Court and Diplomatic Life," tells a curious anecdote about her own father, who isolated himself from the younger members of his family on account of his dislike to the noise of children. "It is said," she writes, "that one day my father was walking in Portland-place, when he met a nurse carrying a baby in her arms ;. and, being struck by the beauty of the infant, he inquired whose it was. The nurse, much as- tonished, answered, Your own, Sir Thomas!'" Mdme. Nilsson was recently the guest of the President of the United States. Just'as she was finishing her first song, says the 2tretc York World, little Nellie Arthur, the Presi- dent's daughter, came tripping into the room, and was introduced to Madame Nilsson,--who stooped to kiss her. "What shall I sing for you ?" Mdme. Nilsson asked, hold- ing little Nellie by both hands. "Oh, sing 'Please give me a penny," she answered; "I think that is a very pretty song." Mime. Nilsson turned again to the piano, and sang most charmingly the little French ballad " Un petit sous s'il roue plait." As she rose from the piano and turned to little Nellie Arthur, who stood as if entranced, the great artist asked, with outstretched hands, "Don't you think that is worth a penny ?" ELIJAH'S MANTLE.—In the May number of the Fort- nightly Review an article is contributed by Lord Randolph Churchill, entitled "Elijah's Mantle," in which the member for Woodstock delivered himself of certain reflections on the unveiling of the Beaconsfield statue by Sir Stafford North- cote ten or eleven days ago. The noble Lord, himself assum- ing the prophetic rae, says that as time goes on Tory suc- cesses will be fewer and separated from each other by inter- vals of growing length, unless indeed the policy and the principles of the Tory party should undergo a surprising development; unless the secret of Lord Beaconsfield's theory of government is appreciated, understood, believed in, sown broadcast amongst the people; unless the mantle of Elijah should fall upon someone who is capable enough and fortunate enough to carry with him a united party, to bring to perfection those schemes of,simperial rule and social reform which Lord Beaconsfield had only time to dream of, to hint at, and to sketch. The expression "Tory democracy," says Lord Randolph, has excited the wonder of some, the alarm of others, and great and bitter ridicule from the R idical party. But the "Tory democracy." may yet exist; the elements for its composition only require to be collected, and the labour may some day be effected by that man, whoever he may be, upon whom the mantle of Elijah has descended.

FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

It is stated that the English Gov ,rnment have been officially informed that the coronation of the Czar at Moscow will take place on the 27th of May. There were serious disturbances on Sunday at Port Said between the Greek and the Arab population, and the Euro- peans only escaped a general massacre by the prompt land- inr, of men from the Iris and the Falcon. At the request of the Governor and the Consuls the crews and marines from the British vessels occupieol the town, and the Greek Consul took refuge on board the Falcon. Two men are said to have been killed and thirty wounded. A Cairo telegram says :—A despatch from Colonel Hicks announces that on April 29th he gave battle to a body of 5,000 insurgents. The engagement lasted half-an-hour, and resulted in the defeat of the latter, with hemy loss, 500 men being killed, including the False Prophet's lieutenant- general, and many wounded. The loss on the side of the Egyptians was only slight. Colonel Hicks praises the gal- lantry displayed by the troops under his command. The, representative of the Daily News at Alexandria tele- graphs that the possibility of a second Suez Canal under English direction is exciting much interest in Egypt. It is believed that there exists two schemes for a canal from Alexandria to Suez, both combining navigation for ships of the iargest class and irrigation of the lands. One, promoted by Mr. Pender, passes Cairo. The other, promoted by Sir George Elliott, crosses the Nile nearer the sea, avoiding Cairo. The correspondent adds that either canal would greatly enrich Egypt and benefit the world. PROBABLE WAR BETWEEN FRANCE AND CRINA.—The Paris Soleil discusses the contingency of a war between France and China, which, it says, it may be expected that the Tonquita expedition vill sooner or later bring about. China, it points out, is a country of four hundred millions of inhabitants, possessing an army of fire hundred thousand men, armed with Winchester rides. Estimating that one European soldier is equal to ten Chinese soldiers, the Soleil urges that it would, nevertheless, be no agreeable prospect for France to find herself engaged in a war necessitating the despatch of an army of 50,000 men to the extreme East.

THE PIIILA.DELPHIA CONVENTION.—The "platform" of the Irish Convention at Philadelphia was arranged on Fri- day. The new organisation is to band together the citizens of America and Canada, Irish and of Irish descent, as "The Irish National League of America." Air. Alexander Sullivan, a lawyer, of Chicago, lies been elected president ; Major Byrne, of- Cincinatti, vice-president ; and Mr. J. J. Hynes, secretary. The Central Council is to consist of one member from each State, these to be named by the State delegations. The governing body to be an executive com- mittee of seven centrally located, and every Irish- American society may become a branch of the League. Every member is to pay oae dollar annually as dues, and this sum is to be paid to the League in quarterly payments. The resolutions of the Irish-American people open with a denunciation of English government in Ireland, which, " never having acquired the consent of the governed, has no moral right whatever to exist in Ireland ;" support is pledged to Irishmen in their efforts to recover national self-government; the "noble setiment of Bishop Butler" is endorsed, that "every stroke of Forster's savage lash was for Irishmen a new proof of Parnell's worth ; " sympathy is expressed for the Irish labourers; a demand is made that the farmers allow the labourers a fair day's wages for a fair day's work; the Irish are counselled to buy noth- ing in England which they can produce in Ireland or pro- cure from America or France ; pledges are given to promote Irish manufacturers by encouraging their import into America, and to persuade American tradesmen from keeping English goods on sale; contempt and detestation is ex- pressed for the English Ministry; the policy of the English Govlrnmsnt is declared to be unnatural and inhuman; and a protest on the subject is ordered to be made to the Presi- dent of the United States; and finally the Convention wel- comes the "sturdy undaunted patriot and prudent custodian Patrick Egan." THE STATE OF IRELAND.

MORE ASTOUNDING REVELATIONS. At the Dublin Police Court, the ot!Aer day, Sylvester Kingston, the man who was recently arrested at Bootle, Thomas Gibney, and Thomas Healey, were charged with conspiring to murder Joe Poole, a tailor and Fenian centre, in Dublin. The principal ;witness was Thomas Devine, who was arrested in connection with the murder of Constable Cox, and has turned informer. His evidence was of a very astounding character. He showed that there was a Stephen. its Party, a Council Party,and a Vigilance Committee in the Fenian organisation; and that the business of the Vigilance Committee, like that of the Invincibles, was to remove all obnoxious people. He said that William Lamie, now an informer, was a sub-centre; John Sullivan, a Dublin actioneer, was a centre, as was also Joe Poole and James O'Connor. Joe Dowling was the centre of the Vigilance Circle. Delegates attended from England, and one of these was James Boland, of Man- chester. To watch and murder doubtful members of the society seems to have been a distinguishing feature of the organisation. Bailey was murdered for informing about the Fenian arsenal in Cross Kevin-street. Poole and Sullivan were tried by ten members of the society, and when they were sentenced to death Kingston observed that Poole deserved it and was sworn to carry out the sentence. On the night Constable Cox was shot, Poole had to be killed, and it was the unexpected presence of the police that saved him. After Delaney failed to shoot Judge Lawson a meeting was held, and it was resolved that the judge should die next time, no matter what party of protection he bad. Thomas Gibney had to assist Kingston in the murder of Poole; and Kenny's murder was carried out by the Vigilance Committee of the Stephenite Party because he gave information. Devine's evideve is certainly the most astouuding that has ever yet been published in connection with the Fenian war in Dublin, and shows how jealously members of secret societies have watched each other.

The Lord Lieutenant has awas.led compensation amount- ing to £11,550 to the relatives of persons murdered during the past two or three years in the counties of Mayo, Gal- way, and Limerick, but chiefly in Mayo. A return published en Monday of the evictions through- out Ireland in the quarter ended 31st March shows that the number of families turned out was 793, consisting of 3,859 persons. There were readmitted as tenants 29 families, and as caretakers 324 families.

Timothy Keeffe was executed on Monday, at Cork, for tbe murder of his uncle, John Keeffe, 12 months since. The farm of the culprit's family had been sold under an execu- tion at the suit of the murdered man, who purchased it from the Sheriff, and this was the motive alleged for the crime. We (Freeman's Journal) are now in a position to state that altogether the benefits of the Arrears Act will extend to about 138,000 holdings, each valued, for poor law pur- poses, under £3O. The sum which the State contributes is a little over £160,000, which wit wipe out, it is estimated, arrears to the amount of at least two and a half millions sterling..

Conderable interest is being attracted to the Dublin Trinity Ward municipal election petition owing to a doubt as to whether Jas. Carey the notorious informer, was legally expelled from the Corporation. It is stated that the Irish law adviser and the Town Clerk are of opinion that by law Carey is still the representative of the Trinity Ward in the Dublin Town Council.

An action for assault commenced by Mr. O'Kelly, M.P., against Mr. Harvey resident magistrate, has been dismissed by the Irish Court of Exchequer "for want of prosecution." Mr. Harvey had, while in the attitude of dispersing a Land League meeting, put his hand on Mr. O'Kelly's shoulder, thus committing that legal "assault and battery" which has always been so cherished an idea to aggrieved Irishmen both in real life and in native fiction.

ALARMING RIOTS AT LIMERICK : :_'ONFLICT BETWEEN THE POLICE AND THE MILITARY.—A Limerick correspon- dent says considerable disturbance was caused in the city on Sunday night owing to the conduct of some members of the Royal Irish Fusiliers who assaulted the pot ce and obstruc- ted them in the discharge of their duty. When the accused were about to be arrested they resisted, and struck the con- stables with their belts. Subsequently a large crowd assem- bled, who groaned and stoned the police, who by this time had drawn their swords for protection. The arrest of the military had to be abandoned until an extra police force came up, when several men were arrested.

The Parliamentary Committee of the Liberty and Pro- perty Defence League have issued a report in which they state that "out of over a hundred public bills now before Parliament no fewer than forty are altogether or in part a contravention of principles for the defence of which this League was established, viz freedom of contract and indi- vidual liberty versus State interference. A hope is expressed that members of Parliament may be induced to arrest "the present tendency to substitute State help for self-help in the business and other transactions of national life, bearing in mind that although for children and lunatics paternal solici- tude is required, the similar treatment of sane grown per- sons only tends to deteriorate the race in the long run by diminishing self-reliance on the one hand and self-control on the other."

CONFESSION OF TILE CAVAN MURDER. - A young man named Philip Gallaghan gave himself into the custody of the police at Eccles, near Manchester, on Saturday, in con- nection with the murder at Cavan last Wednesday week. He has mane a statement to the effect that, seeing his cousin struggling with the deceased man Harte, he kicked the latter several times in the breast ad left him apparently deal—At the Manchester County Police Court, on Monday, Philip Gall.4ghan, described as a labourer, of Dean, county Cavan, Ireland, was charged on his own confession with murder. Information telegraphed from Cavan agrees with Gallaghan's statement, and he was remanded, pending the arrival of police to convey him thither.—The prisoner was again placed in the dock on Wednesday. Inspector Bourke stated to the bench that an escort had arrived from Ireland and ashed that the prisoner might he handed over in their custody. The application was granted and the prisoner was accordingly removed

When the Liverpool Assizes grand jury closed their labours on Saturday, they handed in a presentment express- ing regret that so much- of the time of the judges should now be taken up by cases which have hitherto been perfectly well disposed of at sessions. A few days ago the Rev. C. Williams, vicar of Coalville. Leicestershire, announced that he purposed addressing a parochial meeting in favour of the Affirmation Bill. This step provoked the indignation of his congregation, and on Sunday morning, when he ascended the pulpit, there was A hostile demonstration, led by one of the churchwardens. Mr. Williams has consequently abandoned the proposed meeting. and will content himself by stating his views in a pamphlet.
THE DYNAIOTE CONSPIRACY.
THE ST, HELENS AND LiVERPOOL PRISONERS.

At the Liverpool AssiZei, on .P.Ciday afternoon, a sudden change was effected in the proceedinjs. connected with the prosecution of the two prisoners, t.iS peasey (31), rail- way porter, apprehended at Liverpool,. and Patrick Flanni- gan (27), railway breaksman, apprehended at Bt. Helens, who stand committed for trial in connection with what is known as the Liverpool conspiracy to blow up public build- ings. The two prisoners were specially brought from Walton Gaol on the order of the judge (Mr. Justice Day), and placed in the dock during an application for th 3 postponement of their trial until next assizes. Mr. Aspinall, Q.C., with whom was the Hon. A. D. Elliott, appeared for the Crown; Dr. O'Feely appeared for both prisoners. The specific charges against them were : Unlawfully or knowingly having in their possession, at Liverpool, on the 28th March, 1883, certain explosive substances, witn intent thereby, or by means thereef, to commit a fe!ony, contrary to the statute 24 and 25 Vic., c 27 ; conspiring, confederating, and agreeing, at the same time and place, together and with certain other persons un- known to commit felonies—to wit, to feloniously, unlaw- fully, and maliciously place near certain buildings certain explosive substances with intent to destroy the same. Mr. Aspinall based his application for postponement on the ground that Timothy Featherstone and Daniel O'Herlihy, who were arrested at Cork, were involved in the same con- spiracy and were to be prosecuted along with Deasy and Flanagan. Dr. O'Feely, on behalf of the prisoners, opposed the application.—The Judge consented to the postpone- ment.

Before Mr. Raffles and Admiral Gough, at the Liverpool I Police Court, Dale-street, on Friday, Timothy Featherstone and Daniel O'Herlilay were charged under warrant—the first with knowingly having had in his possession certain exillosive substances with intent by means thereof to com- mit felony, and the other with aiding and abetting him in his purpose. Bath are supposed to have been acting with Deasey and Flannigan, now in custody in Liverpool, and others, whose names are unknown' for the purpose of felony. There was great animation in the Police Buildings, from tbe Detective Office upwards, over the matter, and among those present in the court were many well-known police officials, not only representing the Liverpool force but the Irish con- stabulary. The prisoners had been brought to Liverpool by Inspector Marsh, accompanied by Irish const ibles. The men were well-dressed and in the prime of life. O'Herlihy is a stern-featured, determined looking man, with a full dark beard, moustache, and a broad, capacious forehead. The other man is meaner of feature, and, therefore, less determined of look, with slight beard and moustache. Patrick Welch, a constable in the Royal Irish Constabulary stationed at Cork, said he was present with Sub,lns.pector Starkie when Featherstone was arrested at a boarding-house in Cork. He found several articles in his possession, amongst others a letter addressed to Montgomery and Co., manufacturing chemists, 4, Dundas-street, Glasgow, with an unused stamp ready for posting. The letter was as fol- lows :—" After using your last consignments and being satisfied with the results, I now give another order and en- close a post-office order, for which you will send me four carboys of sulphuric acid. I have also to return the empty carboys. (Signed), DANIEL O'HERLIHY, 10, Great George- street West, Cork." He had received foal the gaol a letter written by Featherstone, and he had compared it with the handwriting of the letter to G!asgow, and they were both in the same handwriting, and also in the same ' handwriting as the documents in the possession of Deasy.—Mr. Quelch, who appeared for the defendant, asked some questions of the witness as to the handwriting, but Mr. Raffles said he had better not go into that case just now as there would be experts called with respect to that point.—Mr. Marks said he could, if neces3ary, prove that the nitric acid sent to O'Herlihy from Glasgow was taken from the quay by Deasy,-Mr. Raffles said the case had , better not be further proceeded with that day, as there was quite enough to justify a remand, and he accordingly re- manded both the prisoners until to-day (Saturday). THE PRP:iONERS AT BOW-STRhET.

I Thomas Gallagher, Dalton, Ausburg, Whitehe id, and Cu tin, charged with treason-felony, were again brought before Sir JZ.re3 bgb3mt at the Bow-street Police Court; London, on Thursday MUing. Tile reading (Wei Of tho evidence given before the prisoners was proceeded with, and having been concluded, the prisoners were remanded till Thursday next. During the reading none of the prisoners asked any questions, and only a few formal and unimportant questions were put to the witnesses by counsel. A DYNAMITE ALARM AT THE CREWE WORKS. A Crewe correspondent says that considerable excitement was causes in Crewe, on Thursday night by the reported discovery of a quantity of dynamite in the steel works of the London and North-Western Railway Company. It ap- pears that Mr. Roebuck, foreman of one of the departments, had his attention called to two bottles which were found among a quantity of scrap iron abont to be melted in a large new foundry. Both were capped and had a fuse at- tached. They were examined by a competent person, who said they had contained nitro-glycerine or dynamite, but they were now empty. It is not known how the bottles got there. The matter is being investigated.

One of the several mysterious strangers who visited Can- terbury shortly before the enthronisation ceremony, has been identified by the local police as the prisoner arrested in London in connection with the dynamite conspiracy. On Tuesday, at Holywell, Mr. Superintendent Hughes directed the attention of the magistrates to the material made use of in the recent alleged attempt to blow up the County Hall, and which consisted of a large copper tube tilled with gunpowder and furnace dust. The superintendent stated that he had traced the origin of the affair to a young man named Aaron Thomas, employed at tbe se,t. Winefrede Brew- ery. The magistrates were of opinion that the circum- stances were not sufficient strong to found a charge upon. A Woolwich correspondent says a large quantity of car- tridges charged with dynamite, and weigbiug in all 80 to 100 pounds, was destroyed on Tuesday in the meadow sur- rounding the Home Office magazine, below Woolwich Royal Arsenal. The cartridges, which appeared to have been manufactured and sold in the ordinary course of trade by a well-known English firm, had been seized at Fulham by the Metropolitan Baard of Works, hut no particulars were given except that the owner of the cartridges was unknown. By Colonel Majendie's direction the dynamite was destroyed by burning, in presence of Lieutenant-Colonel Barlow, R.A., assistant superintendent of the Royal Laboratory, and In- spector Cavil!, of the Woolwich Dockyard police. A Leiceeter correspondent states that a seizure of nitro- glycerine has been made in that town. The police for some days had been secretly prosecuting inquiries, having be- come suspicious that illegal explosives were stored in the town, and on Sunday, Mr. Dunn, chief constable, went to a summer house in Ayleston Road, and seized 35 packages of explosives. Dr. Meadows, borough analyst, examined the material, and certified it to b 3 gelatinized nitro-glycerine, containing 90 per cent of nitro-glycerine. Altogether about 311 b were seized. The Chief Constable made a private ap- plication to the Mayor, who granted a warrant for the ap- prehensTon of the occupier of the premises. The man was arrested, and on Tuesday morning was brought before the Mayor and other magistrates, at the Town Hall. His name is William Mitchell, and by occu- pation he is a " steeple-jack." He was charged under the new Act with having explosives in his possession under a reasonable enspicion that he intended to use them for an unlawful obj ,ct. The facts having been stated, the prisoner said the fiubstance was in ounc3 cart- ridges, wllich he bought for the purpose of firing a royal salute on the occasion of the visit of the Prince and Prin- cess of Wales to Leicester last Whitsuntide. He was re- manded for a week and bail refused.

div.head: THREATENING A MAGISTRATE AND
div.p: THREATENING A MAGISTRATE AND
HIS GARDENER AT ROBY. A CASE OF CONSCIENCE.

An elderly and rather decrepid-looking man named Jos. Bellion was charged at Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr. Willis and Mr. W. L. Evans, with threatening Richard Davies.—Mr. J. O. Swift appeared on behalf of the complainant, who, he stated, was until a few days ago head gardener for Mr. F. W. Earle, Edenhuret, Roby. Fourteen months ago, when Mr. Earle was abroad, Davies engaged defendant as an extra hand for a few weeks. He stayed on till the end of March, when somehow or other he scalded himself—at least that was his excuse br not ap- pearing at his work; and during his absence Mr. Earle good-naturedly paid him his wages. Some changes were then being made. Davies was leaving, feeling be was toe old for his work, a new bead gardener was coming, and de- fendant's services were dispensed with. Mr. Earle gave him a good character, and he went away apparently satisfied and on friendly terms with Mr. Davies, who, on parting, gave him some money to get a drink with. Davies was therefore considerably surprised when on the following Tues- day he received a letter from the defendant, dated Bibby- street, Old Swan, April 23rd, demanding more wages, and stating that "to bring matters to a climax," the writer (defendant) would put his claim in the hands of his legal adviser. The letter continued "If the affair should by any means go against me, I shall take other means to enforce my rights, which will eimply appall you, and make you and your employer regret the day when you abused and insulted the workingman in the person of yours truly, JOSF.PH BELLION." In a fcrtnight defendant added .the further threat—" If you will serve me 80 your time is not far off." These threats had to some extent made Davies feel nervous, and he therefore asked by way of pro- tection that defendant should be bound over to keep the peace.—Defendant said there were no threats in the letter. He was only asking for his legitimate rights; and all he meant was that if Davies did not see justice done to him his conscience wou'd prick him, and he would suffer through his conscience.—Mr. Willis: You say a little more than that. You threaten hini.—Defendant : That is all the meaning of my words. I never had any intention of making any threats, and he knows I never had a wrong word with him while I was working there.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in .£lO and two sureties of £5 each, or 14 days' imprisonment.

The Birmingham police have Captured a number of sharpers practising the latest race- course fraud. The trick takes the form of a lottery, all the Zrtiz's, of course, falling to the rogues. The stock consists a monkey, a table, a number of small pieces of tin, and of aBe3all wooden balls. Twelve people each pay sixpence, and r,e given two pieces of tin each, the numbers corresponding *nth those on the balls. The sharper explains that the lot- tery will be conducted by the learned money, and the mon- ey, after a few capers, draws a ball from the box and hands it to his master. The latter takes care that no one sees tbe Leal number on the ball, but calls out a figure he knows to e,in Possession of a confederate, who receives the prize of half-a-crown. A brisk trade was being done when the police ined the lot. The monkey Was confiscated, and sent to a tthlic menagerie. Monkeys and paraphernalia are supplied swindlers by members of the fraternity in London. ekunnEn OF A SUPPOSED Rivee —An extraordinary Charge of murder was heard at Taunton Assizes on Monday. Josepht Wedlake, a young farmer, of Winton, was indicted 48aer the wilful murder of Mark Cox, ironstone miner, of the „„111,8 Place. The prisoner was in love with a niece of his ;7"cte's wife, who lived on the same farm with him. This I°ang woman was engaged to a farmer named Fletcher. :ter they came from church on Sunday, January the 7th, t Prisoner told his brother that he intended to kill Pletcher. Next morning the body of Mark Cox, frightfully !nutilated about the head, was discovered lying en the road In the direction Fletcher would have to take on his way erne. it appeared that the prisoner had broken his skull 11; With an axe under the impression that he was attacking _ etcher. The prisoner's brother was taken into custody fullsuspicion of the murder, and the prisoner then made a confession of the crime.—He was found guilty and sen- enced to death. The action brought by Mr. Newdegate was as much zit Proceeding in aid of public rights as an indictment for eI•3OY, and the Chief Justice lays down distinctly that " the d ,eerrine of maintenance is not confined to civil actions." nnerefore, if a farmer is robbed of a sheep, and his neigh- Deur contributes £5 towards the cest of the prosecution, the _ ef who has been sentenced to five years' penal servitude :en recover from the subscriber the cost of defending him- :elf, and damages for the five years' inconvenience he has Qttffered in detention. In other words, the law punishes a 'l an in one court and compensates him for his punishment another.
