ASFITON. THE SUDDEN DEATH OF AN ASHTON PUnLICAN,—Mr. Rowbotton, of Wigan, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Colliers' Arms, Seneley Green, on Friday afternoon last, on the body of Jonathan Cunliffe, 41 years of age, a pub- lican, who was found dead in bed on the previous Wednes- day morning under the circumstances reported in our last issue. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from excessive drinking. AN UNFORTUNATE ACCIDENT AT ASHTON : MORE LIGHT WANTED.—A gentleman reehling in Brook Aide Terrace, Stoneycroft, Ashton, met with an unfortunate accident about ten o'clock on Sunday night last—the accident being due to the want of adequate gas-light in the neighbourhood were the accident occurred. The gentleman in question was passing along the narrow passage leading from opposite Warrington-road to Stoneycroft or the Old Wigan-road, and along the side of the ground belonging to the Recreation Saciety, when, owing to the "pitchy darkness" and the total absence of any artificial light, he missed the small bridge at the bottom and walked straight into the brook. At the time there was a great flush of water, and the unfortunate gentleman was thoroughly drenched. If, as we are informed, this by-way is much used by the public the authorities should take means to secure the safety of pedestrians. I CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT ASHTON. —At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday last, Peter Percy, a carter in the employ of Mr. Daulton, pottery manufacturer, St. Helens, was charged with cruelty to a horse by beating and kicking it.—Police-constable Barker stated that about half- past six on the night of the sth April defendant was in charge of a horse and cart on the highway at Park-lane, and witness's attention was called to him beating the horse. He struck it several times across the head and caused it to swerve on one side and nearly upset the cart. Defendant I backed it and then kicked it four or five times in the ab- dotnen. The horse groaned and the sound of the kicks could be heard for a considerable distance. Witness asked him his reason for kicking it, and he said it would turn into every gateway.—ln answer to the charge defendant said he was very sorry and handed in certificates of good character.—A tine of 5s and costs was inflicted. ANNUAL CHURCH PARADE OF THE ASHTON YEOMANRY TROOP--The annual church parade of the "A " (Ashton- in-Makerfield) and "B " (Moss-bank) troops of the Lanca- shire Hussars Yeomanry Cavalry took place on Sunday last. In the forenoon rain fell very heavily, and it was at one time doubtful whether the parade would take place. But about noon the weather conaiderably improved, and as a consequence a large number of persons assembled in the principal thoroughfares to witness the parade. The men mustered at Garswood Hall about half-past two, and 37 men from Ashton and 24 from Moss-bank put in an appearance. Headed by the capital band of the regiment, conducted by Mr. Batley, of Manchester, the men, under the command of Captain Moreland, adjutant, marched to St. Thomas's Church, Ashton. Among the other officers present were —Dr. Beaman, surgeon; Sergeants Shaw, Glover, and Pilling; and Quartermaster-Sergeant Livesley, of Ashton. On arriving at the church divine service was held. The prayers and lessons were read by the vicar, the Rev. H. Siddall, and an eloquent address was given by the Rev. J. F. Hocter, of Liverpool. At the conclusion of tile service the men returned to Garswood Hall, and after they had been served with refreshments were dismissed. CONJURING ENTERTAINMENT AT ASIITON.—Last Mon- day evening, an excellent conjuring and magical entertain- ment was given before a large audience in St. Thornaa's schools, Ashton, by Mr. Marcus Leighton, of Wigan. The proceeds were in aid of the day school funds, and Mr, Leighton very kindly gave his services. He introduced some striking novelties, and some old tricks, which were remarkably well accomplished. The performance opened with a few capital card tricks, and tricks with coins fol- lowed. Next a series of "‘ magical surprises" were given, and were well received, judging from the frequent out- bursts of applause. The concluding part of the entertain- ment consisted of a "complete exposure of Spiritualism." His explanation of the various devices used by mediums and lelievers in Spiritualism were given with much ability. Next followed the Chinese sack trick, another form of the Indian sack trick, and last and most important were the "Cabinet manifestations," as recently given by Irving Bishop, Esq., at Manchester and Liverpool. They con- sisted of so-called spirit writing, nailing two pieces of wood, ringing bells, playing mnsical instruments, &ea while he was securely bound to a pillar in the cabinet. The Vicar (the Rev. H. Siddall) briefly thanked Mr. Leighton for his kindness in giving the entertainment. COLLIERS' MEETING AT Asnrore.—A well-attended meeting of the colliers of Ashton and district was held in the Cave-Browne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, on Tues- day evening last. Mr. J. Partington presided, and Mr. Samuel Woods, of Park-lane, millers' agent, was also present.—The Chairman pointed out the good that had been done by the agitation of great and popular ques- tions, and strongly urged upon all present the necessity of joining the Miners' Association, and so doing their share towards the improvement of their position.—Mr. Samuel Woods, in commencing, said they were deeply indebted to the committee and officers of the school for having so kindly placed that beautiful and convenient room at their disposal. (Applause.) In comparing their present position with what it was six months ago, they had cause for thankfulness and gratitude. Their organization at present numbered some thousand members, and they could much better deal with the numerous difficulties that stood in their path. He pointed out that it was their intention to hold a great demonstration in July next, and Dr. Beaman had kindly granted them the use of Haydock Park. One or two members of Parliament were expected to be present to address the men, and various amusements would be provided. He cautioned them against being deceived by sophistic tl documents contrary to their interests, and maintained that the deplorable strike of 1881 was causal by the action of the employers in forcing the men to contract themselves out of the benefits of the Employers' Liability Act. He said he would warn the masters as to how they dealt with an old sore, for he knew that a great proportion of the men felt very keenly upon the point, and Ile was afraid another dispute would bring about disastrous results. The following resolutions were subsequently passed :—" That this meeting is of opinion that a strong and powerful organization is the only instrument that can improve our position morally, financially, and politically, and pledges itself to do all in its power to bring such a state of things about as early as possible." "That this meeting desires to express its sincere thanks to the trustees, officers, and friends of this school for their kindness in placing the school at the disposal of the miners of Ashton for their meetings."

TRANSFER OF LICENSES AT GOLBORNE.—The license of the Legit Arms Hotel was, on Saturday last, at the Newton Town Hall, transferred from William Walinsley to John Nicholls.—he license of the New Inn, Golborne, was also tranferred ff William Wahnsley. CAUTION TO COLLIERS: A GOLBORNE COLLIER FINED row UNRAAIIIING A SIIOT.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, William Morris, a collier, was summoned on a charge which was to the effect that being employed in a certain coal mine, known as the Wigan Mine, he contravened one of the general rules established and there in force, by un- ramming a charge of powder which had missed tire.—The de- fendant's brother-in-law appeared on his behalf, and Mr. Swift, solicitor, of St. Helens, represented Messrs. Rd. Evans and Co., the prosecutors.—Mr. Swift stated that on the 11th April defendant had been working, and at night left his place in the usual way. The shot-lighter afterwards went round and found that three holes had been drilled for the purpose of being tired. He accordingly tilled them and two of the shots went off properly, but the third misfired. In the morning the spot was examined, and as it was found that powder was still in the hole, the defendant was told that the shot was not to be unrammed. Instead of carrying this in- timation out, however, defendant did unram the shot. General rule 8, section 2, of the Coal Mines' Regulation Act stated that 'a charge of powder which has misfired shall not be unrammed," and the magistrates had power to inflict a pecuniary penalty of 40s and costs, but if they thought life was endangered they had power to impose im- prisonment for a period not exceeding three months. It scorned to be a very serious and bad case, inasmuch as the defendant was warned and told what he must not do, and he knew perfectly well that he bad no right to attempt to unram the shot.—John West, the shot-lighter, was then called, and proved that a shot was fired on the 11th April. On examining the hole the next day he found that it had been unrammed. To unram it a drill tipped with steel must have been used. The mine was a fiery one, and in his opinion it was exceedingly dangerous to do such a thing.—llenry Wilcock, foreman, deposed that he told the defendant not to unram the shot, but drill clear of the hole. He, however, did not drill a fresh place, but unram- med the shot.—Henry Cook, certificated manager, said the defendant had told him that he did not unram the shot until be thought there was no harm in doing so.—The Chairman said the Bench considered the else proved, and as it was the first offence brought before them they would inflict a penalty of LI and costs. In future cases the fine would be higher.

div.head: KING-SLEY.
div.p: KING-SLEY.

ASSAULT.—On Monday, at the Eddisbury petty sessions, Samuel Baker was summoned for assaulting James Dykes at Kingsley on the 15th of April.—Complainant said that on the evening in question, as he was crossing some fields, the defendant accused him of having said something against I him. He denied doing anything of the kind, but Baker, I assuming a fighting attitude, knocked him down and beat I him very severely. He didn't know what it was about, and asked the defendant to reason with him as they had always been very good friends, but he declined, and continued to beat him.—Mrs. Ann Millington gave corroborate evidence as to the assault.—Mr. Fletcher, who appeared for the de- fence, said be was instructed that both these men had been at the Horse Shoe publichouse, where they had been having a few words. Baker challenged Dykes to fight, and the re- sult was that when they fought in the fields Dykes got the worst of it.—There was a second charge of assault, arising out of a continuation of the same affair, on the 16th of April. The defendant having been summoned for this assault fell upon Dykes a second time, and beat him so that be went into a fit. Both assaults were practically admitted, and Mr. Fletcher urged, in extenuation, that his client had previously done the complainant many kindnesses and was incensed at the treatment he had received from him.—De- fendant was fined 10s. and costs in each case. LEIGH.

How SWINE FEVER Is SPREAD—The magistrates at the Leigh Petty Sessions had before them on Monday two men, named Joseph and John Battersby, father and son, charged under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act with selling pigs that had not been fourteen days on the premises. This prohibition was made by an Order in Council on the 22nd of March last. On the 19th April Battersby received a con- signment of pigs from Liverpool, which ought not to have been disposed of until fourteen days had elapsed. On the following day he sold two of the animals, and the day after swine fever broke out among what remained, and one of the pigs had to be destroyed. Where the pigs bad gone to was not known, and probably disease might have been carried elsewhere—The Bench imposed a tine of 50s. on each of the defendants, and costs. SINGULAR SCENE IN A WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—After morn- ing service at Leigh Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday, the par- ents of a child presented themselves before the minister to have the b tby baptised. As the ceremony proceeded to that portion where the child is handed over to the rev, gentle- man the mother stepped forward with it, but the minister requested that the father should enact that part of the event. This he stoutly refused to do. being undesirous of introducing a custom in Wesleyan chapels which had been extinct for many years. A scene of some minutes' duration ensued, both parties being obstinate, the minister demanding to know if the man was ashamed of his own child,and finally taking the little one from the mother's arms and finish- ing the ceremony. The greatest excitement was pro- duced in the chapel owing to these extraordinary proceed- ings.

div.head: CRONTON.
div.p: CRONTON.

ROBBERY BY A DOMESTIC SERVANT.—Before Mr. F. A. Gossage and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Mary Kilinarton, a young girl, was charged with stealing a number of articles of clothing, the property of Elizabeth Beesley. The prosecutrix keeps a, laundry in Mill-lane, Crouton, and the prisonex was a ser- vant in her employ. On the 14th ult. a number of articles were received at the laundry, and on the 21st several of them were missed. The prisoner was afterwards found in poEtession Of two infants dresses, and various other property concealed limier a inattress.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and the chairman having anniented on her sAd position, com- mitted her to gaol for a month. FRODSHAM.

THE REV. LEWIS KENNEDY KINDER, B.A. (Clare Col- lege, Cambridge), late curate of tbe Parish Church, Frod- sham, Cheshire, has been licensed to the curacy of St. Mark's Church, Camberwell, London. THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WRIST CHESHIRE.-011" Tuesday an important meeting was held at Norley, near Frodsham, at which Mr. Duncan, of Gayton Hall, Neston, was introduced to a largely representative meeting of farmers as the new Liberal candidate for West Cheshire. He was accompanied by Mr. James Tomkinson, the senior candi- date, and both gentlemen met with a most cordial reception at the Temperance Hall. Mr. Tomkinson, in the course of a vigorous address, drew a sharp contest between the finances of the present and preceding Government.—Mr. Duncan, who was very warmly received, said he had noticed that the Tory papers were censuriug the Liberal party for going to Parliament to obtain a policy. For his own part, he thought that that was exactly what the Liberal Government ought to do. They were accepting the opinions of the representa- tives of the people, and that was what the Liberals under- stood by governing through the popular voice. Mr. Duncan then proceeded to refer to the Affirmation Bill, remarking that the great speech which Mr. Gladstone de- iivered on Friday night would constitute one of the brightest pages in the history of this country. The present oath was a stumbling block to some, and a matter for trifling to others, and Mr. Gladstone was going to remove it in the interests of civil and retigious liberty. (Applause). Very strong opinions were held on this im- portant subject, and he thought it was a great mistake to introduce the name of the Deity so prominently as it had been introduced recently in public assemblies, and even in courts of justice. He hoped that the results of these debates would be that the Government would cbtain a large majority in favour of affirmation. He then went on to speak of the equalisation of the county franchise, and said that this question was intimately connected with the temperance question, which, he was glad to find, was warmly supported in that neighbourhood. It would he necessary for them to give their strongest support to the proposal for the tqualisa- of the franchise, because it would be largely through the County Boards Bill that they would obtain local option in dealing with public-house, licenses, and, in fact, that popular con' rol of the liquor traffic which they all desired. For the same reason the Tories opposed the equalisation of the franchise, because they found it would put the power into the hands of the people. (Applause.) GARSTON.

GAIISTON SESSIONS.—At the Garston sessions, on Thurs- day, before Messrs. G. W. MOBS and G. G. Macrae, Archi- bald Bathgate was fined 5s and costs for allowing his cart to be used on the highway at G-arston, Several persons were fined for drunkenness and disorderly conduct. ALLEGED TIIEFT BY A DOMESTIC—At the Liverpool County Magistrates Court, on Monday, a middle-aged woman, named Margaret King, who until lately was in the employ of Mr. A. F. Holder, of Grassendale Park, Garston, as cook, was charged on remand with stealing a quantity of wine, the property of her late master.—The prosecutor stated that the prisoner had been in his employ for about a month. Some time ago he put a quantity of wine and champagne into his cellar, and on the 22nd ultimo, in consequence of prisoner being intoxicated, he went into the kitchen and found a cup belonging to the defendant containing some fresh charnpagne.—lnspector Baxendale said that the priso- ner was also seen to pour some wine out of a bottle similar

div.p: WINSFORD.

LEcTLTRE.—On Monday evening Miss McLatchie gave another of her highly popular lectures, entitled Oliver Cromwell and the English martyrs," in the High-street Free Methodist Chapel. Mr. Robert Verdin presided.

CONCERT.—Sorne of the friends connected with the United Free Methodist Mission-room, Over, being &sirens of having an American organ, a concert was got up for the purpose of furnishing funds on Friday last, in the Board schools, High-street. Altogether a very pleasant evening was spent, but the audience being small the funds were not so much benefited as was expected. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS,

THE DO—UBI7E—MURDER AT SMALLWOOD.—Patrick Carey, alias John White, who was sentenced to death by Mr. Jus- tice Hawkins for the double murder at Smallwood, has again been visited by his wife, who was accompanied by two of their children. The execution takes place at eight o'clock on Tuesday morning, and it is not thought probable that representatives of Ora press will be admitted. BOILER EXPLOSION AT CHESTER.—EarIy on Tuesday morning a terrible boiler explosion occurred on the premises of Mr. F. Lyle, aerated water manufacturer, Victoria-road, Chester. The boiler was used with a five horse-power engine, and it appeared that throughout Monday night Mr. Lyle had been working his factory for the purpose of supplying his customers with an extra quantity of aerated waters. The process of bottling was in full operation when the explosion occurred, and Mr. Lyle and one of his work- men sustained serious injuries. BICYCLE AND TRICYCLE TOURNAMENT AT SALE. On Saturd ty afternoon a bicycle and tricycle tournament took place at the Sale Moor Gardens. There was only a meagre attendance of spectators—perhaps on account of the stormy weather in the early part of the day. The two mile bicycle race was won by the limit man, J. C. Berger, of Manches- ter, with 300 yards start; J. T. Ward, of Sale, being second; and J. M‘Kay, Sale, third. The time occupied was 7m. 13 secs. The three mile tricycle race occupied 13m. 55secs., and was won by J. W. Morley, Manchester, 100 yards start; H. M. Oxley, Manchester (540), second ; and M. Ruddle, Manchester, third. M. J. Loundes, Congleton, was scratched in both races; he did not put in an appearance. THE PREMIER AND THE CHESHIRE FARMERS—Through Mr. Tollemache, M.P., the Wirral Farmers' Club recently forwarded to Mr. Gladstone an important series of resolu- tions passed by the club in favour of agricultural legisla- tion. The resolutions relate to compensation for improve- ments, unrestricted liberty of cultivation, subject to the landlord's right to recover damages for injury committed by the tenant; that notice to quit an agricultural holding should not be less than twelve months; that the law of dis- tress should be abolished; and that the Ground Game Act shOuld be so amended as to confer on tenants the same right as landlords to kill hares and rabbits. The Premier replied through Mr. Tollemache acknowledging the receipt of the resolutions, and stating that he has not failed to take notice of their representations. As regards the question of com- pensating tenants for improvements, he would beg to refer to the announcement in the Queen's Speech, and subsequent statements bearing on the subject which have been made in I Parliament. _ _ _

..... CHARGE OF MANSLAUGHTER IN CHESIIIRE.—At Eddes- bury, on Monday, John Knowles, agricultural labourer, was charged with the manslaughter of John Thomas Smith, aged 11 years. On the 6th April the prisoner was driving his master's son, named Cheers, and the deceased, home in a cart. The deceased and Cheers rode in front, and prisoner ,at the back. There were no reins attached to the ' horse. While in a narrow lane the horse took fright at a boy's driving hoop, and bolting up the hedge bank turned the cart up. The cart fell on Cheers, breaking his arm, and killing Smith instantaneously. The coroner's jury, notwithstanding the strong summing up of the coroner, had refused to bring in a verdict of manslaughter, and the police now took the matter up, on the assumption that the prisoner caused Smith's death by negligence in driving without reins. It was urged that the prisoner was not driv- ing on the highway, but really on Masken's premises, and the magistrates considering the occurrence purely accidental, discharged the prisoner. WIGAN.

MINERS' CONFERENCE. - On Tuesday, a miners' pit set conference, representing Lancashire, Cheshire, and North Staffordshire, was held at the Miners' Hall, Millgate,Wigan. The various districts were well represented. After consider- ing the general question of restricting the output of coal, it was unanimously resolved that from Monday next the whole of the districts should commence to work at the rate of 45 hours per week.

THE RURAL DEANERY OF WINWICK.—The Rev. Canon Whitley, rector of Newton-in-Makerfield, has been appointed by the Bishop of Liverpool rural dean to the dunery of Winwick, vacant by the resignation of the Rev. Canon Hopwood.

LY HR. "ONLY PULLING HER JACKET DOWN." Thomas Hinton, Lymm, was charged at Aitrincham Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. J. Allen, with having stolen half a sovereign from the pocket of Ann Harrison, a domestic, in the service of Miss Smith, Church Green, Lymm.—lt ap• peered that prosecutrix, on the previous day, was watching the funeral of the late sexton of Lymm Church, when she had her attention drawn to the prisoner by Mrs. Moston. who told her that " Yaffer " had had his hand in her pocket. Prosecutrix then went home, a short distance from the place, and examined the contents of her pocket, and found that half a sovereign was missing. Information was immediately conveyed to Sergeant Harrington, who apprehended prisoner, but on a search being made no half sovereign was found upon him—Samuel Ancock, manager of the Lymm Cocoa-room, was called, and said he was in the churchyard during the funeral, and saw prisoner apparently with his hand in prosecutrix's pocket, but he thought he was only trying to get the young woman's handkerchief "for fun," and he made a made a remark to that effect to the church clerk, who was in his company.—Prisoner now said he was "only pulling her jacket down."—Mr. Allen thought there was some doubt about the case, and he would give prisoner the benefit of it, and discharge him. THE PROJECTED SHIP CANAL.—A meeting of the rate- payers and others was held on Monday evening in the Plough Hotel, Lymm' for the purpose of passing resolutions in favour of the Ship Canal, and asking the support of the district to the fund now being raised to carry the bill through Parliament. Mr. A. W. Callender occupied the chair, and there was a fair attendance. The Chairman, in opening the proceedinv, said that although Manchester was to be the principal recipient of the benefits anticipated, Lymm would also be benefited if the scheme was successful. They would hear no more of thoserdisastrous floods to which they bad been subjected, and they would also have another contributor to their local rates, and that would, at all events give them some slight relief.—On the motion of Mr. T. A. El ul me, seconded by Mr. Cameron, and supported by Mr. B.T. Leach, the following resolution was unanimously adopted— " That to secure the future welfare of the various trades of Manchester and the surrounding districts it is absolutely necessary to adopt cheaper means than at present exist for the transport of merchandise and other commodities be- tween those places, the sea coast, and foreign ports, and that in the opinion of this meeting the proposed Ship Canal is best calculated to carry out this object."—Mr. N. C. Schou, jun , proposed the second resolution, which was as follows: —"That as the proposed canal will do away with the dis- astrous flooding to which Lymm and its surroundings are annually subjected, it is to our interest, as residents, to do all in our power to aid the promoters in every possible way to obtain Parliamentary sanction to the project, and we hereby pledge ourselves to do so."—This resolution, which was seconded by Mr. J. Marsh, was also carried unanimously; and after a vote of thanks had been accorded to the chair- man, the meeting terminated. MOORE. THE LATE Mn. In brilliant "Queen's weather" the marriage of Mr. Frank Wilson Jolley, file manufacturer, Warrington, son of the late Mr. John Jolley, to Miss Carrie Elizabeth Light. burn, eldest daughter of Mr. J. W. Lightburn, of Rockfieid, Higher Runcorn, was • solemnised in Runcorn Parish Church, on Tuesday morning. The public position of Mr. Lightburn, who is a member of the Board of Commissioners, and the bride's amiable character, which has gained her a wide circle of acquaintances, caused great interest to be taken in the happy event, and a good congregation occupied the pews of the sacred edifice some time before 11 o'olos,k, the period fixed for the ceremony. At that hour the bride, accompanied by her father and the bridesmaids, Miss Nellie Lightburn (sister of the bride), Miss Potter, and Miss White, entered the church, Mr. Johnson, the organist, pltsy. ing an interlude on the organ as the party walked up the centre aisle. The bride was attired in a dress of electro. Ottoman silk and moire, with a sailor bonnet trimmed with pale blue velvet, and electro feathers to match, The bridesmaids wore dresses of ruby satin, with crushed 'strawberry check silk tops, their head dresses being white Dunstable bats trimmed with tea roses. The bridegroom, who was attended by Mr. Frank Lightburn (best man), Mr. John Jolley, and Mr. L. Greening met the bride in the chancel. The wedding party had previously taken their seats there, and the ceremony was proceeded with, the Rev. Canon Barclay, vicar, officia- ting. At its conclusion the bells sent forth a merry peal, and the important formality of signing the register tools place in the vestry. As the happy pair left the church Use "Wedding march" was played on the organ, and well- wishers outside showered rice upon them in abundance. The party was driven to Rockfield, where breakfast was pro- vided, and during the afternoon the newly married couple departed to London, where they intend to spend the honey- moon. aunt, where she stayed for two or three days. On proceed- ing to Cooper's house, Mrs. Cooper flatly denied the asser- tion that she had eloped wth the young an Addison, de. claring that she simply had a quarrel with her husband its the presence of Addison, and that since that moment she had never spoken to nor seen him. On being questioned ae to which Addison it was, she declared it wan not the " runner Addison," but "his brother Joo." She was told that the report stated that her husband " determined that if she resolved to go she should at least not carry with her the token of the vows she had made at tic hymeneal altar, and endeavoured to take the ring from her finger," whereupon she amusingly and derisively asked how that could be when she had no ring and had not had one ion her finger for some years. Of her subsequent movements, she stated that on the Friday, after her husband had beaten her, she went to the house of an aunt, a grocer in St. John's. road, Liverpool, and staved there until her husband came for her on the Tuesday, when she returned home with hive and had since been living, with him. Questions were asked at both houses with the object of testing the reliability ot the statements made, and though there was a slight die- crepancy on one or two immaterial pointa there was au entire agreement as to there not haying been any elope- ment.

div.head: -WARRINGTON CHURCH LECTURES.
div.p: -WARRINGTON CHURCH LECTURES.

An intermediate lecture on "The principles of the Eng- lish Reformation was given in the Workmen's Club, Market- place, on Wednesday evening, by the 11. v. E. C. E. Carle- ton. Alderman Webster preside& there was only a sparse attendance. The having remarked upon the importance of t 'no subject, introduced the LECTURER, who -dwelt for a short time on the imme- diate causes which led to the Reformation. He said that by

the providence of God the Reformation was commenced in the reign of Henry VIII., but the action of the king vita certainly not actuated by any desire for reformation, and he (the lecturer) attributed the authorship and honour of the Reformation to God, and to Him the praise was due. TEe Reformation had left its mark in the country in many ways, but he desired that evening to contemplate it solely on its religious side. There were many religious communi- ties in the country; they had the various sects of Noncon- formists and the Church, and most of these bodies appealed

to the Reformation; but to anyone who knew the real facts of it this was a little strange, and, indeed, not a little amus- ing. If there was one thing more certain than another in this country it was that the Nonconformists had little to do with the Reformation; their principles were not its prin- ciples. The Reformation movement was entirely a Church movement; it was in no sense a Dissenting movement. It was begun in the Church and carried on in the Church ; and when the Dissenters talked about the Reformation they should remember bow little a part they had in the movement. One was at a loss to know why the Dissenters sing the praises of the Reformation and still refuse to profess it! principles. There was a tendency, they knew, in many of them to follow the Church in many things, and among other things in illustration of this he instanced the recent opening of a church in Warrington, at which several Dis- sentinv ministers took part. The lecturer reminded his hearers that the Church of England did not spring into ex- istence at the Reformation, and said it should be borne in mind that the reformers disclaimed all idea of forming a. new Church. The Church of England disorganised, abused, and corrupted before the Reformation, became the Church of England purified and renovated after the Reformation.; The Reformation was no attempt to set up a new Church; it was the restoration of the ancient Church of Christendom. What the lecturer wished to impress upon the minds of his hearers was that the Reformation was a Church movement, and that the Church of England did not at that time spring into existence,but simply under- went a purifying process.—The CHAIRMAN said there could be RO doubt in any mind—he had no doubt himself—that the Reformation was essentially a Church movement, ace? that the Dissenters really had no part in it. Speaking of the Church Lectures, he said it was desirable that Church- mea should meet together as they had done that eveoing and hear such lectures as they had just heard. They should prepare themselves for the attacks of the enemies of the Church for they seemed to be concentrating their forces, and he believed that before long they would give an attack. —The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON said they contemplated having a further series of lectures during the year. They ' had got several promises, and intended to ask Sir Richard Cross to speak on a subject relating to Church matters, and he thought if they had meetings countenanced by such

gentlemen they could secure others to follow in their wake. —Mr. John WHITE said he thought with the Chairman that sooner or later the Church would be subject to some severe attack not only from what was known as the Liberia- tion Society but from the wave of Atheism which was sweeping over the country, and which seemed to be increas. ing more day by day. It was very desirable that they ac Churchmen should prepare for these attacks by getting tc know more about the history of their Church. He thought some association should be formed for this purpose, and he proposed a resolution to the effect that a society be formed with the object of circulating sound information or. ques- tions affecting Church interests; that the society be worked by means of a committee consisting of the clergy in the town and neighbourhood and such laymen as shall feel dis- posed to join from time to time; and that Mr. Carleton be requested to act as secretary pro. tem.—The Rev. J. CAA- sos, Winwick, seconded the resolution, and it was carried unanimonsly.—A. vOte of thanks was then accorded to the Chairman, and the meeting separated.

Of the twenty- and-a-half millions of national debt paid off during the last three years, Ireland, as near as can be calculated, has contributed one- ninth, that is upwards of two millions-and-a- quarter ; and this, too; at a time when there has been misery, famine, and disorder almost unparalleled in the country. In reply to the question of the Government "Where is the money to come from to make Irish rail- ways " the member for Galway says,— "The answer is plain. From the Irish themselves, but it cannot come if at the same time you force it from them to pay off the national debt in amounts which no one ever dreamed of before." Mr. HENRY concludes—" Here, I venture to say, are some materials fitted to be considered by those who hold the destinies of our common country in their hands, and who must well know that if force is sometimes a remedy, it is never a permanent remedy.' If the consideration of the Irish question were always approached in the spirit Manifested in Mr. HENRY'S letter by all the Irish members, or if their opinions, however extreme, were urged in St. Stephen's in the same respectful and firm tone, we veliture to predict that greater good would result to Ireland. As it is, we hope Mr. HENRY'S letter will re- ceive that consideration which it deserves, for we are convinced that the social aspect of the Irish question is one which has been too long left entirely out of view.

TRIENNIAL CONFERENCE OF THE LIBERATION SOCIETY. —Mr. James Handley was a delegate from Runcorn district at the conference held at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, on Wednesday. RUNCORN AND THE NATIONAL LIBERAL CLUB.—AI the inaugural banquet of the National Liberal Club, on Wednes- day evening, there were present from Runcorn Messrs. R. Shaw, Charles Reynolds, James Handley, and T. Handley. MATTHEWS' MINSTRELS AT RIINCORN.—This admirable troupe of minstrels, accompanied by the great American team, will give an entertainment at Runcorn Public Hall, on Thursday evening nest. The performance is announced under distinguished patronage, and a pleasant evening may be anticipated.

FARNWORTII TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. The members of the Widnes branch of the Church of England Temperance Society journeyed to Farnworth on Tuesday evening, when they gave a successful entertainment in the girls' school of that place. The Rev. G. Bond presided, and aiapital pro- gramme was gone through. THE WATCH RODEERY AT WIDNES.—Thomas Desmond, barber, and Letitia Desmond, his wife, were charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, yesterday, with stealing, on the 25th ult., a gold watch, value £5, the property of Charles Etches, watchmaker and barber, late of Waterloo-road, Widnes. The case was before the Bench on Friday last week, and the circumstances of tha robbery have already ap- peared in The Examiner.—The prisoners were committed for trial.

BETHESDA CHAPEL, RIINCORN.—rO-11101TONV (Sunday) is the anniversary of an interesting occasion to the congrega- tion of Bethesda Chapel, Runcorn. It is four years since the Rev. J. D. Thomas took charge of the pastorate, which has been an eminently satisfactory and successful one. To empbaszie the event, Mr. Thomas will to-morrow preach special sermons. In the morning the subject of his discourse will be "These four years," and in the evening "Mistakes about Christ."

SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—At the West Bank Hotel, on Wednesday, Mr. T. W. Barker, coroner, held an inquest touching the death of an infant four months old, whose father is named Henry Rimmer, a chemical labourer at Wid- nes. On the 29th ult., the father rose from bed about eight o'clock, and whilst having his breakfast his wife called him into the bedroom. On entering he found the child lying dead in her arms. He thought deceased had the appearance of having died in a fit. Evidence to this effect having been given by several witnesses, the jury returned a verdict of 'Natural causes."

PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN The anniversary sermons were preached in Greenway-road Chapel, on Sunday, by the Rev. Frederick Smith. In the afternoon a service of song, entitled "John Wesley," was rendered by the children and choir. There were good con- gregations on each occasion, and the collections amounted to £22. On Monday evening an entertainment was given in Regent-street schoolroom, under the presidency of Mr. John Ashley. A varied programme was gone through by the children. Addresses were delivered by the chairman, the Rev. J. Pickwell and Mr. T. Stringfellow. A DESTITUTE HOME AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Rose Ann Coleman was charged with having deserted her family on the sth*March. Mr. Hartley appeared on behalf of the Guardians.—Mr. Scannel, relieving officer, said the prisoner's three children were now inmates of the Workhouse, where they were admitted on the sth March. On that day he visited the house from which the prisoner had absconded, and found the children in a state of utter destitution and suffering from cold and hunger. He had known the prisoner for some time, and she bore a bad character. She had previously received 2s 6d in parish re- lief.—The prisoner was committed to gaol for two months' hard labour.

JUVENILE TEDIPLARY AT RUNCORN. The members of the Path of Safety Juvenile Temple, which is a branch of the Hope of Runcorn Good Templar lodge, gave an enter- tainment in Bethesda schools on Tuesday in aid of their funds. There was a large audience, and Mr. T. Norman, who presided, opened the proceedings with a neat speech. The juveniles went through a lengthy programme of songs, recitations, itc., in good style, while a special feature was the "lightning sketches" of Mr. Jas. S. Patin, who, though young,drew in crayons likenesses of several local celebrities. A "waxwork exhibition," managed by Master C..liniveton and Master W. Nield, was a source of much amusement. During the evening Brother Richard Anders, D.S.J.T., of Liverpool, delivered an address on juvenile templary, re- marking that in the district of South-west Lancashire, in which Runcorn was included, 2,500 members had pledged not to smoke, swear, drink, or gamble. He alluded to the self-sacrificing labours of Brother K. Evans, superintendent of the Path of Safety Temple, which was inaugurated by him a few months ago. Mrs. Heal, we may state, accom- panied the vocalists. A. WinxEs LAW CASE.—In the High Court of Justice (Chancery Division), on Thursday, before Vice-Chancellor Bacon, the hearing of the action Teebay v. the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway and others was resumed. It will be remembered that it is brought by the represen- tatives of the late Mr. Richard Teebay, who was the survi- ving trustee of Smith's estates at Widnes, against the Widnes Local Board, the Cheshire Lines Committee, and the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, to restrain them from making certain alterations in a road called Birchfield-road, which alterations consisted in raising the level of the road in certain places, and in building b2tween the plaintiff's land and the road, a high wall, thus shutting off the access from the property, which is alleged to be good building land, and the road. By an agreement, made the 18th of June, 1870, between Mr. Teebay and the defendants, among other things, it was provided that free access should be left to the plaintiff from his property to the road, and it was now claimed that, by the raising of the road and the building of a wall at the bottom of the slopes from it, the access had been cut off, and that the land had in conse- quence deteriorated very greatly in value. Mr. Hemming, Q.C., and Mr. Badcock represented the plaintiffs ; Mr. Mar- tin, Q.C., and Mr. Phepson Beale, the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee; and Mr. Harton Smith, Q C., and Mr. Medd, the Widnes Local Board.—Evidence on behalf of the plaintiff occupied the entire hearing, and had not concluded when the court adjourned.

THE VICAR OF HALTON'S BIRTHDAY. - Monday being the anniversary of the birth of the Rev. John Lockwood, vicar of Halton. that gentleman, following out a custom of several years' standing, invited a party to his house for sup- per and an evening's enjoyment. The invitation was ex- tended to the wardens, ex-wardens, sidesmen, teachers, and members of the choir, and the Vicar received very gratify- ing tokens of their esteem and regard. The teachers and elder scholars of the school offered for the acceptance of the Vicar a beautiful photographic album, which was in- scribed as follows :—" Presented to the Rev. J. Lockwood, by the teachers and elder scholars of Halton Parochial Sun- day School, as a slight token of respect and esteem; Wish- ing him many happy returns of his birthday. April 30th, 1833." The presentation was made by Mr. A. Povey, who said : "Rev, and dear Sir. It is with unfeigned pleasure that I, on behalf of the teachers and elder scholars of the Halton Parochial Sunday School, approach you with this address. We look back upon the few years gone by, spent by you in anxious, affectionate care for our success in life, as years of pleasure rendered us by your kindly considera- tion and watchful regard for our spiritual and temporal welfare. We humbly and heartily thank you, and beg your acceptance of this accompanying album as a small birthday token of .our gratitude and esteem.

Nay God your prospects ever bless. And crown your life with sweet 811CCeSs, May CCM& and darkness and dismay Before your presence fly away. May you long be spared to minister to our spiritual neces- sities, and finally receive that heavenly reward which fadeth not away, is the earnest prayer of your Sunday school teachers and elder scholars." On behalf of the choir, Mr. Jeacock, organist, presented the Vicar with an inkstand of Mount Carmel wood, and after some very kind and appropriate remarks by Mr. Joseph Stokes, ex-warden. Mr. Lockwood expressed the pleasure he felt in receiving these tributes of affection from his parishioners. The rest of the evening was spent in a very enjoyable manner.

div.head: TIIE tXAMINIIrt,SAPs",URDAY, MAY 5, 1883
div.p: TIIE tXAMINIIrt,SAPs",URDAY, MAY 5, 1883

NEW RATES FOR HALTON.—Before Mr. Charles and Mr. James Reynolds at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Mr. Woodier, assistant overseer for Halton, asked the Bench to grant a poor rate of is. in the 1, to realise £316 2a. 51. The rate was laid. The Bench also granted a highway rate of 4d. in the £ to realise £lOl is. ld. Tile RECENT CATROLIC MISSION AT RUNCORN.—The Rev. Father Marcellus Wright, who recently conducted a mission in Runcorn, along with the Rev. Father Robert, left on Monday for Paris to join the community of his order established in 60 Avenue Hoche, close to the Arc de Triomphe. It may be mentioned that this religious es- tablishment was secured from expulsion by The intei vention of her Majesty's Ambassador in Paris, the meinbers being nearly all English. FOUND DEAD AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Ridgway, the coroner, held an inquest at the Cemetery on Monday afternoon, touching the death of Thomas Calligan, who was found in the Duke's Canal on Sunday morning. The deceased, who was 52 years of age, was last seen alive on Saturday night the 14th ult, when he was apparently walking to- wards his home in Windmill-street. He was then in a state of intoxication, and he was never seen again until a boy, Edward Hill, found the body as stated. A verdict of "Found Dead' was returned.
in using their instrument; but to remedy this Mr. Dutton will in future provide a raised platform fcr the bindsmen. _ _ .

The Parish Church Band will Perform probably on Wednes- day evening next. RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. HISTORICAL SOCIETY.—ORO Of the most successful meetings of the society was held on Thurs- day evening, when about 30 members assembled,in.the news room to hear Mr. P. Linaker read a paper on "Local Legendary Lore." Mr. W. Handley presioled. Mr. Linaker, who is well versed in local history, related in eloquent terms the legend of the Griffin of Farnvvorth, which elothed in the 'web of fancy "made a most interesting story. The " Childe of Hale," of abnormal growth and mighty powers, who is said to have existed at Hale about the beginning of the 17th century, was described, and his exploits recorded, whilst the tradition of St. Christopher of Norton was told in picturesque and poetical language. At the close of the lecture a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Linaker, on the motion of Mr. F. A. Lake, seconded by Mr. Randle. ILLICIT BEER SELLING AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Margaret Kennedy, a married woman, living apart from her husband in Cromwell-street, was charged with selling beer without a licence on the 21st ult. P.C. Griffiths went with a stranger to the prisoner's house, and called for a pint of beer, which was supplied him. He gave her 2s' and she returned him is 61. The beer was drawn from a 18 gallon beer barrel.—Mr. Lewin (clerk) re- marked that the prisoner was liable to a penalty of £so. The prisoner begged the Bench to deal leniently witu her, as she had a large family; but the Chairman said the case was so serious that they could not possibly overlook it, and she would have to pay a fine of £lO and costs, 9s 61, or in default one month's hard labour. On the application of Superintendent Barker the beer was ordered to be for- feited.

VOLUNTEER PARADE AT RUNCORN.—The Rev. W. C. Safford, M.A., rector of Attleborough, preached a sermon at Runcorn Parish Church, on Sunday morning, in behalf of the Curates' Aid Fund. The F and -G companies of the 2nd C.R.V. attended, under the command of Captain Hazle- burst, their parade through the town being watched by hundreds of people, although rain was falling heavily. The officers present were Colonel Ashton, Captain Kerr (adju- tant), Captain Ashton, Captain JoWife, Lieutenants Tim- mins, Rhodes, and Joule. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—Mr. J. Ashton presided at the meeting held on Tuesday, when there were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Highfield, J. Derbyshire, T. Andrews,J. Challoner, C. Rigby, J. Weir, J. G. Hamilton, R. Ashton, H. Lowe, A. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). The Authority went into committee to consider the Frodsham water supply scheme, and certain matters submitted by Mr. Bancroft, the engineer. The Authority appointed a committee to further confer with Mr. Bancroft on his proposals. There was no other business.

POACHING AT NORTON.—Wm. Bent and Win Moores, boatmen, were charged with having, on the 15th ult., in the township of Norton, unlawfully used two lurcher dogs for the purpose of searching for game without a license to do so; and also with trespassing upon land in the occupation of Wm. Kinsey.—Bent did not appear.—Evidence having been given by John Chadwick, assistant keeper to Sir Richard Brooke Henry Clifford Gardener, and George Mil- ler " Usher," the Bench fined the defendant 103. and costs lie. 6d. in the first case, and is. and costs us. 6d. in the second case, or in default, 21 days' imprisonment.

THE TROUBLES OF THE SALVATION ARMY AT WIDNES.-- At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Michael Tobin and William Grace were brought up on remand charged with committing a breach of the peace by assaulting certain members of the Salvation Army. The prisoners pleaded guilty. From the evidence, it appeared that while the army was proceeding quietly down Waterloo-road on Sunday, 'robin burst into the ranks and struck one of the Salvation- ists. He was taken into custody, when Grace conaucted himself in a like manner, and was also arrested. Grace stated that a Salvationist seized Tobin by the neck,and thus caused the disturbance. Inspector Barnett said assaults of this description were becoming too frequent. A Sunday or two ago a woman had her lip cut open, and he asked the Bench to require the prisoners to find substantial bail. The prisoners were bonnd over to keep the peace for three months, each in £2O, and two sureties of £lO each, or in default a month's imprisonment.

A MISSING THIEF CAPTURED -AT WIDNES.—Sarah Ann Coleman was charged on remand at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with stealing a woman's dress, the property of Bridget Hanlon. The robbery was committed on the 21st November last, when Hanlon, who now resides in York- street, Manchester, was living with Dr. O'Keeffe, at Brendon House. The dress was placed on a clothes line placed on a piece of vacant land off Widnes-road. It was afterwards missed and found to have been pawned with Mr. Neil by the prisoner, who was apprehended on Saturday at Flint by P.C. Pitt.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. ENTERTAINMENT AT RUNCORN.—With the object of pro- viding funds for establishing Kindergarten classes in con- nection with Holy Trinity Schools, an entertainment was given on Monday evening by the children attending the infant school. The performances of the juveniles were greatly enjoyed by the large audience which had assembled. Songs, recitations, and dialogues were given in a most creditable manner, which testified to the careful training they had gone undergone. In the "May song," given by eight girls, each girl carried a basket Of flowers, and ac- quitted themselves with much satisfaction to the audience. The Rev. W. Preston, in a short address, paid a high com- pliment to Miss Williams and her assistants, Miss Edwards and Miss Fitton, for the painstaking manner in which they had taught the children. The whole credit of the entertain- ment was due to Miss Williams, with whom the idea had originated, and he was pleased to bear testimony to her care and efficiency.

VIOLENT ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.-At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, a man, named Henry Brindrick, who was only released from gaol on the 26th ultimo, after serving five years' penal servitude, was charged with assaulting Hy. Hancock, who lives in Blantyre-street. When near Runcorn Bridge on his way home, on Saturday night, Hancock was met by a woman, named Catherine Bowden, and the priso- ner. He was knocked down and violently handled, and in the struggle which took place his Albert guard was snatched from him. John Forster, his companion, was also ill- treated, and sustained injuries so serious that he was un- conscious for some time. The stolen chain was offered in pledge at the shop of Mr. Dodd, Princess-street, Runcorn, on Monday, by Bowden, who was apprehended.—She was before the Bench on Tuesday, and remanded for a week. Brindrick was also remanded.

SERIOUS OFFENCE BY A WIDNES MAN.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Day, Archibald Hugh Little (29). described in the calendar as a hawker, was indicted for a criminal offence, upon Martha Jane Hulme, 14 years of age, at Widnes, on the 4th March.—Dr O'Feely prosecuted, and Mr. M'Connell defended the pri- soner.—Although the prisoner was described as a" hawker, well educated," he had represented himself at Widnes as a medical man, and in that capacity visited at the house of the parents of prosecutrix, in Luton-street, to attend a baby that was ill of the measles. About eleven o'clock on the 4th March he went to the house the worse for drink, and, on leaving, asked the prosecntris to go with him to show him his own door. She accompanied him to his own house, but the door was locked, and after knocking some time he went away. When he was going, he took hold of prosecutrix and criminally assaulted her.—The jury found him guilty.— Prisoner, in reply to the usual question, denied the accu- sation which prosecntrix made against him.—His lordship commented en the enormity of the offence. The chidr.m of the poor were exposed to great perils, and they must be protected. Prisoner was then sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude.

MISSIONARY MEETING AT FARNWORTH. The annual meeting, in connection with the Church Missionary Society, was held in the Girls' School, Farnworth, on Saturday evening. The Rev. George Bond, M.A., vicar, presided, and there were also present—the Revs. W. Clayton, J. Holden, and S. A. Spooner. The Chairman delivered an earnest address in which he impressed upon the audience their duty towards the Missionary Society. He alluded to the perilous labours of the missionaries on foreign shores, observing that they left home and kindred, and many of them suffered disease and death among the people of whose good they laboured. The missionaries were doing all they could for the heathen in foreign lands, and if they at home did all they could in the alleys and streets, then might they claim to be doing their utmost to advance Christ's cause.—The Rev. W. Clayton, missionary of Masilupatam, narrated Some of his experiences on the mission field in an interesting way, and the Rev. J. Holden made a financial statement. The amount contributed last year by the Farn- worth Branch to the parent society was £23 las 20, and be was hopeful that the collections this year would realise an equal sum. He proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Clayton for his speech. The Rev. S. A. Spooner seconded the motion, which was carried, and the proceedings closed.

ASSAULTING AN OLD WOMAN AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Wm. Bate, a young man, was summoned on a charge of assaulting an old woman named Sarah Roach.—The complainant stated that on the 21st ult. she went to defendant's house to ask him for some money which he ewed her. She knocked at the door, and his mother opened it, and said her son did not want her. Complainant said, " Well, whether he wants me or not, I Want my money," and she entered the house. Defendant then threw her out of the house, and if she had not seized some railings she would have fallen down a flight of steps He used threatening language towards her, and she want into a neighbour's house out of his way, but he followed her there, and struck her twice.—Alice Bowden alleged that the defendant shook the complainant in her house, and would have struck her had she not interfered.—Defendant stated that be lived with his father, who was over 75 years of age, and his mother who was 72.—The complainant was very provoking and he put her out of the house gently.—Joseph Bate, the father, said the complainant was continually teas- ing his son, and on the day in question she walked into the i kitchen accompanied by a dog,which bit his son on the calf of the leg. Defendant said he would kill her dog and pushed the complainant from the house.—Margaret Conway cor- roborated.—Mr. Reynolds said if the defendant had confined himself to putting the woman from the house he would have been within his rights, but there was no doubt he had assaulted her in a neighbour's house, and he must pay a fine of 2s 6d and costs 17s 6d, or in default 7 days hard labour. RUNCORN LODGING DENS.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. James Reynolds, William Hill, an old man, living in back Penketh- lane, was charged with keeping an unregistered lodging- house. Mr. W. H. Linaker, prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners.—lnspector Dutton said about half- past two on the morning of the 22nd ult. he visited the de- fendant's house, where he found two prostitutes and two men in separate beds. lie snake to the defendant with regard to having thes:, people in his house. Defendant replied that they were there and he could not help it. .The house was not registered. Defendant bad made an applica- tion some time ago, but the Inspecter told him he did not register brothels, but if he would promise to keep a respectable house, and could get three ratepayers to be hound with him, he should have no objection to register the house. It seemed that the defendant had been previously twice fined for a similar offence, the last penalty , he suffered being £3 and costs. The Bench considered this a bad case, and fined the defendant £5 and costs, 103 6d, or in default two months' imprisonment.—Hannah Tomkinson, of Back Peuketh-lane, was also charged with keeping an unregistered lodging-house, and she pleaded guilty. In- spector Dutton said he visited the defendant's house at three o'clock on the morning of the 22nd ult. In one room up- stairs was a man, and in another was a woman and two small children. Downstairs were two men, two women, and one child. There were five lodgers. He had had several complaints with regard to the defendant's house, which was not suitable for registration. He believed it was a house of ill-fame. Defendant said one of the lodgers was an old woman from the Workhouse, who had been benighted, and two men went to their flat immediately after the inspector had been. She denied that her house was of a bad char- acter. She was fined £2 and costs, 103 61, or in default a month.

OPEN-AIR CONCERT AT RETNEDRN.—The first open-air,preley,,- was a farmer who lived near Widnes with his wife or promenade, concert of the season took place on Ttrzsday margard, ,:::1 son Wiliam, and a domestic serva.nt. That this effort that he intended Palling ugOri a friend. About 11 o'ciOck, to provide music for the people is appreciated was shown by he returned,- and as ho approached the outer door his son and the large numbers who assembled on the market ground, the servant, who were in the kitchen, beard him muttering where the concert was held. At times the crush upon the as if he were hi a violei2t temper., His wife was at instrumentalists was so heavy that they found a difficulty that time alone in the parlour. The prisoner entered the _ _ . . . . __ _ . . _ _
kitchen. havina in his hard a heavy walking stick, which he usually carried, and commenced abusing is.son, saying,

"I'll be !Cling for you to-morrow." He aiintl.ti a blow at him, but missed him, and he then went into the par/our, where his wife was sitting, and with his stick sma&bed a sugar basin that was on the table. Deceased asked hi:l7 what he had done that for, and he replied, "I have been lost for about two hours, and you have none of you come to look for me," or words to that effect. The night was foggy, and it might be true that the man had been lost. His wife told him that his son had been looking for him, and before as-, further words pissed he struck her a violent blow with the stick over the left temple,causing her to fail back in her chair. The son and the servant, who bad followed him into the room, saw the blow given, and they tried to protect the deceased. In the parlour was a loaded and capped double- barrelled gun, which the prisoner managed to get hold of, and he told the son that if he did not go he would shoot him. The servant rushed ou:, of the house, and the son bicked into the yard, followed by his father, still in posses- sion of the gun. The prisoner closed the back door and locked it. Whilst the son was backing out of the parlour, he called to his mother to come out, and she attempted to do so, but the prisoner pushed her back. The , son and the servant heard a scuffle and heard the deceased I cry out for help two or three times, but were unable to I get in to her assistance. The noise went on for about twenty minutes and then ail became quiet. The son then made another attempt to get into the house, whereupon the prisoner half opened the door, having a bar of iron in his hand, and said he would kill his son if he did not go away. About half an hour later the son again tried to enter, but the prisoner appeared at the parlour win- dow with the gun in his hand, and threatened to shoot him. At last, the son and the servant went away and did not go . . .

near the place again until seven o'clock in the morning, when they saw the prisoner coming out of the door to get some coals. They entered the house and found Mrs. Percy lying on her back on the kitchen floor quite unconscious. They placed her on a bed, observing that she had a wound on the left temple, her right eye was very much discoloured, and there were bruises on the right side of her face. She never recovered consciousness, and was unable to give any account of what occurred after her son and the servant were shut out. Whilst she was being placed on the bed, the prisoner went into another room without having given any assistance, or manifested any concern. As soon as the circumstances were made known to the police he was arrested, and, his wife being then still alive, he was charged with inflicting grevi- ousbAily harm upon her. He replied: "When I came into the house last night she commenced calling me, and threw a chair at me. I either hit her or pushed her away, and whether she fell over a chair or not I could not say, as had had rather too many glasses of drink. She had a very bad tem- per, and many a one would have killed her many a year ago." Mrs. Percy died on the Ist February. The son William had made different statements with regard to what occurred, but his explanation was that he had been threa- tened by members of the family.—William Percy, aged 27, was examined, and bore out in the main the counsel's open- ing statement. He stated, however, that he did not see the prisoner strike the deceased in the parlour. In cross - examination, he said his father and mother had been married 42 years and had had 14 children, of whom 13 had reached full age. On the night in question his father was in drink. He had-ob- jected to witness living in the house and although the ser- vant had not charged witness with being the father of her illegitimate child, he would not deny that he was. He did not know that for some weeks previously the deceased had been complaining of being bad in her head —Margaret Roche, the servant, said that she saw the prisoner strike the deceased on the temple with his stick. She was coeer- tempered as regarded work, but never showed her temper to her husband, and the prisoner, though very passionate whea in drink, was usually good tempered.—Dr. M'Clellan de- posed that death resulted from inflammation of the brain, caused by two wounds on the head such as the stick produced might have caused. The skull was not fractured, and in five cases out of six death might not have resulted from such blows. Inspector Bar- nett stated that when he apprehended the prisoner and charged him with wounding his wife with his stick, he said, "That stick never hit her since it was a stick."—Mr. Swift addressed the jury for the defence, contending that there was no evidence of malice aforethought such as was neces- sary to support the charge of murder. Had the prisoner wished to commit murder, he had more deadly weapons at hand; and the medical evidence was that the injuries de- ceased had sustained were not such as would ordinarily cause death. The prisoner should not have been indicted even for inflicting grievous bodily harm, but simply for unlawfully wounding or for common assault.—Several wit- nesses were called who gave the prisoner a good character. —His Lordship, in summing up, said that if the jury con- sidered that the grievous bodily harm was intended, and death resulted, their verdict must be one of wilful murder, and, if not, then of manslaughter.—The jury found a verdict of manslaughter, and his Lordship sentenced the prisoner to 20 years' penal servitude. '

div.head: WIDNES AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: WIDNES AND THE SHIP CANAL.

The Ship Canal Committee of the Widnes Local Board journeyed to London this week in order to protect the in- terests of the township against the Manchester Ship Canal. Without opposing the Bill in Parliament they have suc- ceeded in obtaining all that they wished. A•clause has been inserted in the Bill to the effect that should the access to Widnes Dock and the St. Helens Canal at Widnes, and the free navigation of the River Mersey to and from the docks and canal become obstructed, the company should at their own cost, upon being required by the Local Board, remove all such obstructions, and use all means for keeping the navigation open. Should the company neglect to do this, it was provided that the Local Board, or any person pre- judicially affected thereby, may, as occasion should re- Squire, cause all necessary work to be done for keeping open and fit for use such access and navigation, and may re- cover the expenses of so doing with all costs of action from the company in any court of competent jurisdiction. The committee will doubtless present a report on the subject at the Board meeting on Tuesday.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
TlJEspAy.7-Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge.

There were 26 judgment summonses and. 115 original plaints set down for hearing, and the court &VI not rise until six o'clock. AN ADJOURNED • CASE—Thomas Edwards and wife claimed £3l 17s 5d from John Dutton and John Wright, executors of Thomas Co per, for value of goods detained, damages for detention, money lent, and money had and re- ceived.—ln this case, which had been adjcurned from March 6th, Mr. Hitchen appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Lake for the defendants.—After hearing the evidence for the defence, His Honour observed that this was a case where onus of proof rested with the plaintiffs. The prin- cipal witness was Mrs. Edwards, and as her evidence had not been corroborated to his satisfaction he must give judg- ment for the defendants.

CLAIM FOR PERSONAL INJURIES: A FRODSIIAM CASF. —Hannah Foster, of Newtown, Frodsham, claimed from Wm. Bebbington, innkeeper, Frodsham Bridge, the sum of £5O, damages for personal injuries sustained through the careless driving of the defendant at Frodsharn Bridge.—Mr. Burton appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendant was re- presented by Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich. A jury, with Mr. J. Lunt, as foreman, had been empannelled to hear the case.— Mr. Burton, in opening the case for the plaintiff, said that on the 26th day of July, 1881, the plaintiff was walking on the road to Frodsham from Runcorn, where she had been working, when near Frodsham Bridge the defendant, who was driving a horse and trap, came up and without any warning knocked the plaintiff down. He did not stop, but drove to his house and put the horse in the stable. The neighbours came and took the plaintiff into a house, and a doctor was sent for. It was found that the plaintiff's leg was broken and Dr. Weaver's assistant attended to her injuries. Next morning the defendant saw the plaintiff and procured some brandy for her. He also obtained for her parish relief.--Tfannah Foster, the plaintiff was then called and bore out the opening statement of her solicitor. In cross-examination by Mr. Fletcher, who appeared for de- fendant, the plaintiff denied being the worse for drink.—Dr. Weaver gave evidence as to the nature of the plaintiffs injuries.—Joshua Midwood,Alfred Midwood, Ernma Darling- ton, and William Miller confirmed the plaintiff's evidence.—Mr. Fletcher elected to call his witnesses before addressing the jury, and called William Bebbington, the defendant, who said on the day in question he was driving towlrds Frodsham, and as he was turning to go down to his house, the plaintiff was getting off the parapet. Before he could iraw the horse up the plaintiff was knocked down and injured. He did not consider he was to blame in the matter. No claim had been against him until he was put in the County Court. In cross-examination by Mr. Burton defendant said he had never been in a collision before. He had been run into by the post cart, and they had paid damages. He as sure that it was impossible to avoid the accident.—George Spruce, Wm. Worrell, Sarah Hancock, and Hannah Unsworth were called in support af the defendant's case.—Mr. Fletcher, for the defendant, contended that the plaintiff alone was to blame for the accident, and was not, therefore, entitled to recover anything from the defendant.—His Honour in sum- ming up eaid the question the jury bad to decide was as, to which oi the parties were guilty- of negligence. If the plaintiff through her negligence caused the accident, then she would not be entitled to recover; but if, on the other hand, the accident resulted through the negligence of the defendant, the the plaintiff would be entitled to recover damages. His Honour then reviewed the evidence at length, and left the case to the jury, who returned a verdict for plaintiff, £5, with costs.
