div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon at Dutton Workhouse. Mr. John Ashton pre- sided, and there were present the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. W. Handley, T. Norman, F. Fairhurst, R. Ashton, J. Challoner, H. Lowe, J. Higbfield, J. G. Hamilton, J. Camp- kin, T. Andrews, E. A. Wallington, C. Rigby, J. Knowles, J. Darbyshire, J.Weir, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: ALLEGED TAMPERING WITH VOTING PAPERS.
div.p: THE ALLEGED TAMPERING WITH VOTING PAPERS.

The CLERK said he had caused personal enquiries to be made in the six cases of alleged fraudulent interference with vetting papers in the recent election at Runcorn, but he had found nothing which would justify him in advising the Guardians to institute proceedings before the jusfices in any of the cases.—Mr. CHALLONER remarked that as the inquiry had been made at his suggestion, he desired to make a re- mark or two. He wished it to go from that meeting that if such a thing occurred again at Runcorn the Board would certainly take a firm stand and prosecute. Runcorn was guilty of the habit—(laughter)—and in future, if he were a Guardian, he should see that there was a prosecution. If " Runcorn did not learn sense the Board would try to make them do so."—Mr. H. LOWE said Mr. Ghalloner was entirely out of order; and the CHAIRMAN ruled that as the matter was not before the Board it could not be dis- cussed.

div.head: COST OF RELIEF.
div.p: COST OF RELIEF.

The DEPUTY CLERIC presented a return, showing that the ainount expeeded in food and clothing in-maintenance far the half-ye ir ended Lady Day ,was £672, while the amount expended in out-door relief during the same period was £722.—0n the motion of Mr. HANDLEY the return was ordered to be sent to the Relief Supervision Committee to be reported upon.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £43 12s 61, and the recommenda- tion was adopted on the motion of the Rev. J. LOCKWOOD, seconded by Mr. Pounta.N.

div.head: TETE TRAMP NUISANCE.
div.p: TETE TRAMP NUISANCE.

Mr. NoRmAN stated that the Visiting Committee had had under consideration that afternoon a letter written by Inspector Hollingworth, with reference to the increase in the number of tramps applying for relief and lodgings at Runcorn, and with a view to reducing the number and the cost of their maintenance the committee recommended that a notice be posted in Runcorn warning tramps that no tickets for lodging would be given after a certain hour in the evening, and informing them that they would have to go to the Workhouse to be lodged there. In extreme cases Mr. Hollingworth, who is the assistant relieving officer, would have discretionary plwer, and his experience would enable him to discriminate between cases o( real need and professional tramps.—Mr. RIGBY thought the best plan would be to give notice that the Workhouse would be shut up for twelve months. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. NORMAN suggested that the clerk should draw up a notice.—Mr. RIGBY: Will Mr. Norman explain how it is to be done? (Laughter.)—The Clerk was in- structed to draw up a notice, and submit it to the com- mittee.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMXIITEE,
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMXIITEE,
This committee reported that the expenditure for the past quarter was £5l 65., and the estimated expenditure for the current quarter was £64 7s. 6d.

RUNCORN ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE. A meeting of this committee was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday morning. There were present :—Messrs. E. A:Wright, J.P.. A. Thomas, J.P., H. Neild, J.Koowles, R. Ashton, W. Handley, T. Norman, J. Challoner, J. Weir, and H. Linaker (clerk).—The CLERK stated that as this was the first meeting of the committee it would be neces- sary to appoint a chairman before business was commenced. —Mr. R. AsirroN thereupon proposed that Mr. Wright be the chairman for thq ensuing year.—Mr. WRIGHT declined the honour, and moved that Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., occupy the positihn. He had noticed that Mr. Reynolds during the time he was chairman bad shown marked ability, and he was able and quite willing to devote his time to the service of the public in that capacity. He (Mr. Wright) knew of no one more qualified to fulfil the duties.—Mr. CHALLONER seconded the motion, which was carried unani- monsly.—As Mr. Reynolds was absent in London Mr. Neild was voted to the chair. The committee issued in- structions to the overseers of the various townships respect- ing new valuation lists. Letters giving notice of intention to appeal were read from Messrs. R. Davies and Co., solici- tors, Warrington, on behalf of the Wilderspool Brewery Co., and from Mr. J. R. Frith, on behalf of the Runcorn Gas Company. The appeal in the latter case was made on the ground that the works were unequally rated compared with the other works in the town. The hearing of appeals was fixed for the 19th June.

div.head: LATEST NEWS. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: LATEST NEWS. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

The- Select Committee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill resumed their enqulry yesterday morning. Mr. Leader Williams, engineer to the undertaking, wan' cross- examined by Mr. Saunders, QC., on behalf of the Bridge- water Canal Navigation Company. He sated that the esti- mated cost of the works to be constricted under the bill was £5,633;551 18s. 51, and the amounts provided by the bill to meet this estimate, as well as for improving the es- tuary of the river and for any contingencies that might arise, were six millions and one million and a quarter. Nothing was included in the estimate for estuary works, no plans having been deposited, as the estuary changed every year, and nothing was included for the purchase of the Bridgewater navigation or for compensation to those whose interests might be affected by construction of the canal. If the operations of the promoters had the effect of damaging the works of • the Bridgewater Navigation Company they would have to pay compensation, just as a railway company had to compensate for any injury they caused to the interests of private individuals. In further cross-examination by Mr. Bidder on behalf of the Mersey Docks Company, witness stated that he would form the new channel through the estuary in the first instance by scour, and would deepen it and widen it by dredging. It was true that in principle there would be less water to go over the banks than at present, when the new channel was completed, but in practice there would be no appreciable difference. In cross-examination by other counsel, Mr. Williams said he did not think that the effect of the scour from the new channel pouring into the wide channel opposite Garston would be to lessen the depth of the latter. He proposed to raise his retaining walls near Weston Point only to the height of the existing sand- banks, and it was not the case that the channel from Elles- mere Port would be turned into a sort of estuary. There was a bank in the estuary between Birkenhead and Liver- pool, and this had increased so much of late that Liverpool Corporation had had to use sluicing apparatus, arid the ferry had been to some extent interfered with. He did not helieve that if the bank still farther extended any-danger would result to navigation, it would only neces- sitate further sluicing. The new channel would not bring down more water than the existing channel except as far as the sea water, which had been carried up by the preceding tide, was concerned. He expected to use one million and a quarter cubic yards in the construction of !training walls, and two and a half million cubic yards would still remain at his disposal in case required. On conclusion of cross- examination the committee adjourned till Monday, when witness will be re-examined.

div.head: DUBLIN TRIALS. HANLON'S SENTENCE.
div.p: THE DUBLIN TRIALS. HANLON'S SENTENCE.

The trial of Lawrence Hanlon, on the charge of attempt- ing to murder Mr. Field, was resumed on Friday morning. James Egan, labourer, proved picking up a hat on the night of the murder. He beard the cries of "Police," and saw some men driving off on a car. A police constable proved taking the hat produced from Tim Kelly. This closed the case for the Crown. Mr. Bodkin, for the defence, said be would not set up an alibi; he relied on the improbability of the Crown case. The jury retired at 11-47, and returned into court at 11-56 with a verdict of guilty. The prisoner was sentenced to penal servitude for life.

div.head: "SKIN TLIE GOAT'S" SECOND TRIAL.
div.p: "SKIN TLIE GOAT'S" SECOND TRIAL.

Fitzharris, alias "Skin the Goat," was next arraigned for being an accessory after the fact in the Phenix Park murders. He pleaded not guilty, and was put back, and the court then adjourned until Monday.

div.head: ARREST OF WALSH AND SHERIDAN.
div.p: ARREST OF WALSH AND SHERIDAN.

A Dublin correspondent, telegraphing yesterday morning, says :—'l understand that a telegram has reached Dublin Castle announcing the arrest of Walsh and Sheridan in New York for the murder of Mr. Burke and Lord F. Cavendish." The intelligence is confirmed in a later telegram, and has caused great sensation in Dublin. THE CASE AGAINST GEORGE SMITH.
George Smith, against whom the Grand Jury found a true bill on Thursday for conspiracy to murder, was dis- charged the same night on his own recognizances, he under- taking to emigrate.

Mr. Gladstone has written to the secretary of the National Liberal Club congratulating him upon the success of the inaugural banquet last Wednesday. The Rev. Dr. Parker of the City Temple, London, will probably be elected by a large majority as chairman of the Congregational Union of England and %Vales.

div.head: THIRLMERE LAKE ARBITRATION.
div.p: THE THIRLMERE LAKE ARBITRATION.

The Manchester Examiner and Times announces the further litigation in the matter of Thirimere arbitration award has been avoided by a 2ompromise between the Man- chester Corporation and the Countess of Ossalinskey, owner of a portion of the Thirlmere Lake estate required for the new water supply scheme for Manchester. The Corporation on Wednesday resolved to carry the case to the Court of Appeal, but a meeting of representatives of the countess and the Corporation has since been held, and an agreement as to the sum to be paid to the countess has been arrived at.

div.head: DYNAMITE SCARE AT CREWE.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE SCARE AT CREWE.

The London and North - Western Railway officials at Crewe do not associate the discovery of the dynamite c misters in the company's steel works on Thursday with any malicious de- sign on the works. The canisters were found in a railway truck among a quantity of wood, and may have been thrown there through carelessness or with wanton intention to create alarm among the employ6i. They had contained explosive material, but were quite empty. FOUNDERING OF A STEAMER : FORTY LIVES LOST.

A Lloyd's telegram received yesterday morning states that the Italian ship Schiafilno, from Middlesborough, has arrived at Philadelphia, md reports that she picked up in the North Atlantic a large boat in a wrecked condition with name on stern Mangerton, London. The fine iron steamer Mangerton, 2,005 tons, sailed from the Mersey on the 27th January last fer Havana with a full cargo, and has not since been heard of. There is no aouht but that she has foundered in tho North Atlantic, and the whole of her crew, 40 in number, perished with the vessel. She is two months over- due, and all hopes of her safety have been abandoned.

div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

' HOUSE. OF COMMONS. MR. BRADLAUGH AT THE BAR. The SPEAKER informed the House that he had received a letter from Mr. Bradlaugh stating that he should attend at the proper time and ask to take the oath. He also asked to be heard at the Bar. Bearing in mind the surroundings of the case, he (the Speaker) desired direction from the House before he called Mr. Bradlaugh. Loud cries of "Gladstone." The right hon. gentleman did not rise. Sir S. NOETITCOTE, amid great cheering, rose and said as the Prime Minister did not rise to give advice to the House, he (Sir S. Northcote) intimated that he should again move the resolution moved on several occasions, that Mr. Bradlaugh ha not allowed to take the oath, but he had no objection to his being heard at the bar. The SPEAKER read the resalxtion referred to. Mr. GLADSTONE said he was under the impression that Mr. Labouchere would move Mr. Bradlaugh be heard. (Laughter and cheers.) Mr. LADOUCIIHRE then, amid great excitement, moved that Mr. Bradlaugh be heard at the bar.—Motion agreed ta. Mr. BRADLAUGE then appeared at the bar, and claimed , his seat. He said he had three times been elected for Northampton, and even if he was as vile as it was sought to make him out that vileness gave the House no right to guestiola his return. The attempt to keep him from per- forming his duty was treason to the constitution. The House might use force to keep hioi out, but that! was _

lagainst the law. He denied that he had written many of the statements made against him, and it was unjust to con- demn him for things he had !laver done. If the House de- prived him of his civil rights, he must submit; but while he had those rights he would claim them. He urged Parlia- ment not to trample on the law in order to crush him. .Ihe 1 i House ought to declare the seat vacant, or bring n a 1:111 to disqualify him. The law gave him that seat, and while be i had that right on his side he would claim the seat n the name of the law. [ The SPEAKER then ' read the resolution that had been ;:b 0 ' passed on iimer occasions excluding Mr. Bradlaogh front the House, and pat ii, !Tom the chair. Mr. LABOUCHERE mov-6.1 tne revious uestlon. Mr. GLADSTONE said his opinion remained unchanged on the legal right of Mr. Bradlauo.'b, therefore he should support Mr. Laboucbere's motion. ' Sir S. NORTHCOTE said if the previous qii3Ofirion was car- ried that would not settle anything. Mr. Bradiangh would come to the table, and then the Speaker would ask fordirec- tiGns from the House. Voting for the previous question would therefore be tantamount to negativing the resolution. Mr. RITCHIE and Mr. NEWDEGATE defended the observa- tions they had made during the late debate. Sir H. GIFFARD asked if the previous question was carried whether Mr. Bradlaugh could come to the table and take the oath.

I The SPEAKER replied in the affirmative. Mr. O'DotorELL condemned the course proposed on the Government side as an unworthy Inanceuvre, and unworthy of the party putting it forward. Last night's decision was now sought to be overturned by a plot, and he asked the House to vindicate ite honour. The House divided with the following result For Sir Stafford Northcote's motion 271 Against .
Majority for. IThcr resolution emeluding Mr. Bradlacgh was re-affirmed- amid laud cheering.

RAILWAY RATES—On the motion to go into Committee of Supply, Mr. SAMUELSON called attention to the report of the Select Committee on railway rates and fares, and moved that it was expedient that the railway commissionlhould be made permanent and a court of record, that in general con- formity with the recommendations of the powers of the com- mission be extended, and that on application by a railway undertaking for Parliamentary powers, locus standi should- be afforded to chambers of commerce and agriculture, and similar bodies, and to persons injuriously affected by the rates and fares sought or already authorised in case of such undertakings. He thought that great advantage would re- sult if his resolution was carried, and the Commission. made permanent, as it would give them powers-to deal more efficiently with many matters, more particularly- the rates for carrying agricultural produce., and it would also enable the Commission to deal summarily with regard to fares.— Mr. GREGORY seconded the resolution, and believed public advantage would follow its adoption. The Commissioners had now no powers to prevent overcharges. [LEFF SITTING.]

div.head: ALLEGED HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT
div.p: ALLEGED HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT
HALE.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Lad- den, labourer, Hale, was charged on remand with commit- ting a highway robbery with violence upon Alexander Ber- tram Allridge, engineer, residing in West-street, off Fair- dough-lane, Liverpoul.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, ap- peared for the defendant.—The prosecutor, who is a well. dressed young man, stated that on Sunday be was at Hale, in company with his wife and a friend. They stayed at the Wellington Hotel. They left Hale at ten minutes past ten. There was a little dispute between himself and his friend, who refused to allow him to drive. His friend insisted upon driving himself, and in consequence witness and his wife alighted from the vehicle, and proceeded to walk towards Liverpool. The umbrella produced was his. It was in the trap when he got out but his friend handed it to his wife. They walked into the schoolhouse, which was outside Hale, when he was suddenly seized by a man, and his umbrella wrenched from his hand. He could not see who it was that seized him, but he gave chase to somebody who ran away. The thief entered a yard and witness followed, and found the prisoner behind a gate. The prisoner seized him and a struggle ensued. His wife broke a window of the house in order to attract the attention of the inmates. Whilst she was doing this the struggle continued, and the prisoner tried to- choke him. When assistance arrived the prisoner was secured and detained until P.C. Roberts arrived.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Swift, the witness said a person in the wanted to fight, but the incident passed off quietly.— Mr. Swift: Did not your friend refuse to allow you to drive, saying he would not risk his life with you? No.—ln the public-house didn't you state you wonld walk to Liverpool?' Yes, and I did walk there.—Was it not because you were drunk that your friend objected to your driving? r had very little to drink—ln answer to further questions, witness said when in the lane he asked his wife to give him "that revolver," using that expression to frighten anybody that was there.—The prisoner was again remanded for a week.

to-day to this latter measure. THE AFFIRMATION BILL DEBATE.—The debate on the Par- liamentary Oaths Bill was resumed by Lord R. CHURCHILL, whosaid the bill had been brought in in deference to violence and-clamour, and that those who were opposed to it were the religious and the law-abiding, and those who supported it the residuum, the rabble, and the scum of the population, men to whom all restraint was odious. He denied that the present measure had anything in common with former legislation for the removal of Parliamentary disabilities. This was a bill for the admission of avowed atheists into Parliament, and was a fundamental change in the constitution of such vital im- portance that the opinion of the country ought to be ascer- tained before it was made. The bill flew in the face both of the common law and the statute law of the country. If it was passed the Christian constitntion of the country would have received a moral stab at the hand 3 of a man whom the people had armed in its defence and had promoted to the highest honours; and it was the bounden duty of the Tory party to oppose this legislation stage by stage, and to rouse the alarm of the nation.—Mr. LABOUCHERE followed with a speech in support of the bill. He said the petitions against it had been got up by paid agents, and did not re- present public opinion. This was not a bill to admit atheists, for atheists could sit now provided they only held their tongues. If the Opposition were consistent they would bring in a bill absolutely to exclude all atheists.—Mr. Hun- BARD opposed the bill, and Mr. W. H. LEATTIAM supported it.—Mr. WHITLEY recommended the Government to allow this to be treated as an open question.—Mr. L. STANLEY spoke in favour of the bill, as did also Mr. E. A. LEATHAM. —The debate was continued by Mr. Sergeant Simon, Sir W. Hart-Dyke, and other hon. members. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TuEsDAT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. THE EGYPTIAN HEROES ANNUITY BILL.—MT. GLAD- STONE announced that the Government had decided to alter the basis of the Alcester and Wolseley Annuity Bills, and to adopt the principle of a lump sum, the particulars of which the right hon, gentleman undertook to ex,)lain at an early day. PRECEDENCE FOR THE AFFIRMATION BILL.—The proposal to give precedence to the Affirmation Bill over the notices of motion and orders of the day was viewed with disappoint- ment by Mr. HOPWOOD, as his motion against enforced vaccination stood first on the paper. He appealed to the Government to secure for him a fair opportunity of discuss- ing the question on a future day.—Mr. LEWIS, who had a motion on the paper in reference to the New Guinea and other annexations proposed or accomplished, said he would divide the House against the action of the Government.— Mr. RYLANDS did not desire to stand in the way of Govern- ment business, but he viewed with great dislike the proposed infringement of the rights of private members.—Sir. S. Normicarn pointed out that it would be for the general con- venience of the House that the debate on the Affirmation Bill should close in the course of this week; he therefore thought it not unnatural that the Government should sug- gest the immediate resumption of the debate.—After a lively debate, in which the Irish members took a promi- nent part, the Prime Minister's motion was carried by 157 to 105. Twit DEBATE ON THE AFFIRMATION BlLL—When the DEPUTY SPEIEBR called upon Mr. Walter to resume the debate on the Oaths'Bill it was found that the hon. gentle- man was not present, and in the difficulty Mr. B. Hope undertook to speak in opposition to the bill. Such orators as Dr. Lyons, Mr. Akers-Douglas, Mr. Bellingham, and Lord Lymington took part in the listless debate which fol- lowed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. Mr. ARNOLD gave notice that on the motion of Sir Richard Cross respecting the Cuban Refugees, he should move the previous question.—Mr. GLADSTONE moved that committees should not sit on Thursday, being Ascension Day, until two o'clock, and have leave to sit until six o'clock, notwithstanding the sitting of the House.—Mr. ARNOLD hoped the motion would not be assented to, as it would interfere with the business of the committees, and as members could if they desired go to church early in the morning.—The House divided, when there voted for the motion, 69; against it, 20.—Mr. MONK moved the second reading of the Limited Partnerships Bill. The object of the bill was to extend the principle of limited liability adopted in 1865 to private partnership in a fuller and more complete manner than the present law allowed.—Mr. RYLANDS moved the rejection of the bill.—Mr. NORWOOD ridiculed Mr. Rylands's opposition to the bill as arising from feeling that he had too much competition in his own business.—After some further discussion, the second reading was negatived by 150 against 49 votes. I THE AFFIRMATION : DIVISION AND DEFEAT OF THE GOVERNMENT.—Mr. NEWTOEGATE, on resuming the debate , on the motion for the second reading of the Affirmation Bill, I entered into a long account of his lawsuits against Mr. Bradlangh. He appealed to the House to be true to its traditions by refusing to pass the bill.—The SOLICITOR- GENERAL pointed out that some of these who opposed the bill would tolerate every form of belief, but would reject unbelief regardless of the fact that there were forms of religious belief just as appalling as un- belief.—Mr. Cuermer contended that the bill was intro- duced to get Mr. Bradlaugh into the House "by hook or by crook," and he insisted that it ought not to be passed without an appeal to the country.—Mr. H. FOWLER supported the bill, as he believed a religious test was in- tolerable when it came from men who pro- feseed belief, for it admitted all forms of infidelity but one, and history had proved the futility of these tests.— Amongst the speakers who followed, Sir MASSEY LOPES pro- tested against a religious principle being decided by political partisanship, forgetting that the House of Commons is a political, and not a religions arena, and at a later hour Mr. O'Shaughnessy and Mr. Walter surprised the Opposition by vigorously supporting the Bill. Mr. GOSCHEN wished it were possible on this occasion to discard party spirit, and said he believed religion would suffer if the Conservative party were successful in their opposition to the Bill. "You have dressed religion in party livery," he-said, "and pinned a party badge upon her sleeve, and placed her, in the front of the fight, but the cause is flours. not hers." He repudiated the idea that the admission of Mr. Brad- laugh to that -House would involve any peril to religion. The peril would, be much greater in the event of his exclu- sion. It was the.opposition offered to him that had given him so extended a-notoriety as he had of late enjoyed. He (Mr. Goschen) regarded that oath as no bar toinfidelity, and he warned the Hniese against doing that which would have the effect of driving Lerge masses of people into the camp of the infidel. The throwing out of the Bill would not close the question, it would rather stimulate an agitation in which ' the holiest sentiments of religion would he bandied about in political .discussions as had never been the case before. The cheers which might greet a close division would be simply an indi- cation of party triumph, and one for which the country would probably have to pay very dearly hereafter.—Sir S. lioneereecrrE accused Mr. Goachen of adding fuel to the fire, , His speech was that of a man ighting a losing battle. 'The charge-brought against the Opposition was that he (Sir S. ' Northeate) had recommended legislation, and had since then changed his opinion on the subject. What he had really , said was.that the Government were evading the point at issue, sad if the Government were to attain their end M. should be by legi.slation. The Op- position had been thoroughly justified in that , . . iopinion, which merely meant that the other method of Government was wrong. It was untrue, as alleged by Mr. Labouchere, that he had changed his course under the influence of Lord Beaconsfield. He believed there was as much party spirit on one side as on the other. Tee question, however, WAS of such grave magnitude that hither- to some Liberals had voted on it independently of party spirit. It was true that the oath erwiy ec as enxoptittneti poatheedreaswaouli , re- ligious teat, because nobody for be .any .doubt as te the charaPNr of the oath. The new i

proposal was to do 'away v.;rth the oath. Would the affirmation proposed instel'A 01 It have the same effect on an Atheist as on a Si:Aker or Moravian? If not, what Was the use of it ? was a serious thing for Parliament to produce the effect that it was known that the passing of this Bill would produce, and its effect would not be con- fined to this country. He admitted that a constituency had a right to elect a man not disqualified, but, on the other hand, Parliament had a right to disqualify a man, and if it did so a constituency had no right to complain of the interference or injustice. Was one 1 constituency to override all the constituencies in England? 1 He thought the instinct of the people of the country against this bill was right. As to religious freedom being imperilled, he maintained that religious freedom did not mean freedom from religion. Let them look at the abolition of religion in other countries. It was one remarkable feature of the bill that if it were passed it would be a personal triumph to Mr. Bradlaugh, and the effect of that must be very seriously discouraging to the religious mujority and encouraging to the atheistic minority. The measure was one that would do no good, and would certainly produce an impres- sion of a most fatal and dangerous character. (Cheers.) —Lord lIARTINGTON charged Sir S. Northcote with having promised to do what be could to bring this question to a settlement, and after all opposing every effort of the Government to settle it. He asked what contribution Sir S. Northcote was prepared now to make for the settlement of this question? He repudiated any sympathy with the 1 teaching of Mr. Bradlaugh, and denied that Mr. Adam had anything to do with inviting Mr. Bradlaugh to contest Northampton. In India the presence of any religious opinion or the absence of any religious opinion was no dis- qualification for the civil service, and he did not think, therefore, that the passing of the bill would ex- cite so much surprise there as the Opposition represented. It was, however, a serious thing that a man duly elected to sit in that House, and willing to do all that was by law required of him, should be prevented from doing so by a vote of the House. The principle on which it was maintained that avowed atheists were now to be excluded was the same on which Roman Catholics and Jews were ex- cluded. That principle was dangerous to the State and the Protestant Constitution. It was not because Parliament held less strongly the cardinal doctrines of Christianity that the Jews were admitted, and it was not because they now held the doctrine on which religion was founded less strongly that they were in favour of admitting atheists. He was of ' opinion that the present application of the oath was unrea- sonable, as it did not exclude the most avowed atheist so long as he did not advocate atheism in the House. When it was said that it was dishonpuring to Almighty God to relieve such a man from taking the oath, it appeared to him that they were guilty of something worse than incon- sistency. By proposing this Bill the Government were doing something to preserve the oath from profanity, and to preserve those principles of freedom that the Liberal party had in times past contended fer. MAY-DAY CELEBRATIONS. WARRINGTON. From the earliest times there has been a disposition en the part of the English people to celebrate the advent of May. It is the month in which nature breaks out afresh, covering the meadows with a beauteous carpet, spangled with the daisy and the buttercup, clothing the trees and hedgerows with sweet-scented blossom and eye-refreshing foliage, and causing the feathered songsters to fill the air all day lung with their charming melodies. Coming, as it does, after the cold dreary months of winter, and boisterous and rainy months of spring, this awakening of nature has ob- tained for May the appellation of the "merry month," and to it people have always paid some sort of homage. Thus arose such practices as Maying, crowning the May queen, lady of the May, Jack-in-the-green, lisc., which were widely obeerved in England until they were suppressed by the aus- tere Puritans, who could tolerate nothing in the way of jollity. However, in the gayer days following the Restora- tion, the observances were revived, and the custom of cele- brating the advent of May continued until, with the advances of progress and enlightenment, it almost died out. Indeed, it was asserted that the practices had 'lithely ceased, but pageants obtain such a hold on the public mind that they are invariably revived after a time, though shorn of most of their objection- able features. Thus of late years the ceremony of crowning the May Queen has been again observed in various parts of Lancashire and Cheshire, and the celebrations become more numerous each succeeding year. But these pageants are confined to country places as they cannot be held in towns, but the dwellers in towns are not behind their neighbours in their festivities though the displays of the townspeople are of a more useful character. In most large towns there are on May Day processions and shows of horses, and for several years the carters of Warrington followed the prevailing cus- tom, but until last year there was no organised procession. Mr. F. Wall then arranged and carried out almost single- handed, a united procession and show of horses, which pro- ved an undoubted success. This year the matter has been taken in hand by a large committee, and on Tuesday the second annual Warrington May Day procession and show of horses took place under the most favourable auspices. All \ through the day the sun lent its cheering countenance to the festivities, which commenced at an early hour, when the bands of the Blue Coat and Workhouse schools com- menced ta pay their annual visits. The young musicians enlivened the thoroughfares until the morning was far advanced, and the number of people then in the streets was augmented by large numbers of persons who begun to take up positions for obtaining a view of the proceseion of horses. By noon Sankey-street was crowded with pedestrians, and remained so for over two hours; while crowds assembled at various points along the route. The show ground was the 1 field opposite the Town Hall, and the procession was organ- ised in the streets adjoining, which were also filled with spectators. At one o'clock a start was made, and the pro- cession proceeded along Museum, Bold, Wilson-Patten, Parker,Sankey, Bridge, Mersey, Church,lrlam,Buttermarket, Horsemarket, Bewsey, Edgeworth, Legb, and Sankey streets to the show field. In the procession were some 70 vehicles, including 9 lurries and drays drawn by pair horses, 31 lorries and 11 carts drawn by single horses, 16 traps, vans, etc., drawn by cobs and pcnies, and 3 carts drawn by donkeys. The best display was made by the contractors, the brewers ranking second in point of numbers, and the coal agents third; while the grocers, bakers, and fishmongers made a capital / show. Mr. R. bearer, and crown bearer, we were led up to the Queen. Her Majesty was in great state in a carriage drawn by four greys, and had about her all the necessary complement of maids of honour, beef-eaters, and other official people. She looked very pretty in the midst of it all, this Queen of only 14 summers, with fair hair, round sweet face, and blue eyes. No cheer greeted iho young Queen as she rode forth, the sudden spectacle of royalty having, no noubt, for the moment taken the breath out of the onlookers. The procession made a long detour round the village on its way to the common, the bulk of the spectators in 01,0 meantime getting by shorter routes to the Mal; -pole, which had a great circle made round, it with substantial railings. The back of tto throne was towatds the wind (now setting more int,;, the east), which was an arrangement comfortable to a holiday-clad majesty. The procession made its appearance, after long hearing of drums in the distance, and slowly tiled into the enclosure. The Queen descended from her carriage and made the cir- cuit of her kingdom on foot, with the due tendance of maids of honour, whose office was no sinecure with the manage- ment of the royal train, and beef-eaters, duly splendid and terrible. Her Majesty then proceeded to the throne, and took possession in the manner, no doubt, of a long-descended daughter of kings, all loyal subjects in the meanwhile sing- ing the song of " The Queen of May." The maids of honour accommodated themselves on the steps of the throne. A miniature "John Brown" (who is apparently not yet so dead as Queen Anne) in kilt and plaid of Rob Roy tartan, advanced and placed the Crown on the Royal head. Whereupon the whole kingdom (disposed in picturesque circles near the throne) burst into cheers. Then the sceptre-bearer approached and made her majesty's equipment complete. The army, the navy, the foresters, and other interesting bodies of faithful subjects advanced in turn to the throne steps and did the necessary homage. The Queen—now a complete majesty in every way, and in full undisputed possession of her do- main—leaned back in her gilt chair with some satisfaction, and witnessed with approving eye the sports provided by her loyal people. What these were it would be too much to say in detail, but with the whole kingdom engaged in them, army and navy included, they were not wanting in spirit and variety. The sun was well into the west before the end was reached, and with a sharper edge getting on the east wind every half-hour, a much gratified but gradually stiffening majesty was perhaps not sorry to hear the Na- tional Anthem.

div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

The "menie month" was ushered in with brilliant sun- shine and genial breezes, under which even smoke-begrimed , and dirty Widnes looked bright. May flowers are foreign to its arid soil, but that the inhabitants might welcome the ad- vent of summer in a somewhat formal manner, the May-day Association, following its custom for three years past, or- ganised a procession of horses and turnouts, for which prizes were offered. The chairman of the Association is Mr. Thomas Edwardson, the treasurer Mr. James Hulme, and the hon. secretary Mr. J. B. Foulkes; while the com- mittee consists of Messrs. W. Higginson, D. Farrall, R. Smithson, T. D. Matthews, Henry Edgerley, and Robert Moore. In the various classes were 19 entries, a slight fal- ling off on last year, and the competitors drew up on a piece of vacant land off Waterloo-road, for judging, which was announced to commence at 1 o'clock. By about three o'clock the judges, who were Mr. John Johnson (Cuerdley), Mr. H. Yates (Farnworth), and Mr. Hudson (Widnes), had finished their task. Their awards were as follow: Manufacturers' double draft horses: 1, Messrs. J. Mns- pratt and Sons; drivers, John Smith and James Mee. 2, Widnes Local Board; drivers, William Howard and Thos. Stanton. Manufacturers' Single Draught Horses: 1, London and North-Western Railway Company, driver Charles Manning; 2, London and North-Western Railway Company, driver John Tanby ; 3, Henry Gordon and Co., driver Frederick Lowe. _ _

Several of the animals were fine specimens, and bore evidence of careful grooming, while all were more or less decorated with ribbons and roses.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

The first of May was not so highly honoured this year at St. Helens as it has been on some former occasions. The procession of horses and vehicles, which is generally the most prominent feature of the day, was only a somewhat desultory affair 3n the present occasion, there seeming to have been no committee or other body foamed to make the necessary arrangements, and consequently there were no such inducements as prizes offered to teamsters to turn out in their most creditable manner. It is certainly to be regretted that this should have been so, as although an exhibition for prizes may be one of the least poetical ways of celebrating the advent of the " merrie month, ' it is undoubtedly one of the most practical and useful, not the least of its advantages being that it is an apt way of engendering a pride in the good condition of their horses in the minds of drivers, and, as a consequence, an increased care and humanity in their treatment. The fineness of the weather, however, on Tues- day, and a vague anticipation that the day would not be allowed to pass without a spectacle of some sort, drew a large number of people into the principal streets, who, if they were not treated to a very splendid pageant, were yet not altogether disappointed. Shortly after noon a short procession, chiefly composed of Corpora- tion horses and vehicles, paraded the streets, but although few in number it must be allowed that they made a very creditable display, and tended to make people think that a very fine procession might be organised in St. Helens. The horses, seven of which were unusually large and powerful looking animals, were evidently in the pink of condition, and their glossy coats were set off by brightly burnished har- nesses, and various coloured ribbons. Tne drivers, of the Corporation carts at least, were dressed in white suits, and had their caps and whips ornamented with ribbons. The following are the names of tho Corporation drivers in the order of procession, the three first-named being in charge of three water carts, and the fourth of a tip waggon, viz. James Houghton, Thomas Thorpe, William Brassing, John McHugh, William Bailey, Daniel Lamb, William Green, Peter Finnigan, Henry .euzark, George Pruce, William Webb, Hugh Finnigan, Christopher Finney, and George Pye ; James Critchley was the driver in charge of a fine horse and cart containing flags belonging to Mr. John Heaton, paviour, and a cart full of coals and drawn by a powerful black horse, belonging to Mr. T. B ilnaer, carter, were in the charge of Adam Grundy. A horse and cart containing bricks be- longing to Mr. R. Davies, in charge of Rabert Tetlock, and an advertising van belonging to Mrs. (Thorley, brought up the rear of the procession. Later on in the afternoon six lurries, drawn by as many splendid and pewerful horses, and laden with a miscellaneous collection of goods, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company also paraded the streets, under the charge of the following drivers :—Lawrence Lee, Joseph Yates, Joseph Kerwin, Jas. Hayes, Joseph Lepp, and James Ormrod. These horses, like those in the former procession, were in first-rate condition, and were bedecked with ribbons and other ornaments. In addition to these the horses and vehicles of various private firms, although not forming part of any procession, were noticeable by reason of their decorations and the general merit of their turnout, notably *hose belonging to Messrs. J. Cammack and Co., mineral water manufacturers; Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., brewers; and Mr. J. Donnelly, furniture remover, whose two huge vans were very con- spicuous objects.

div.head: PHCENIX PARK MURDERS. TRIAL OF FIIZRARRIS.
div.p: THE PHCENIX PARK MURDERS. TRIAL OF FIIZRARRIS.

Another and important member of the " Invincible " brotherhood was placed upon his trial at the Dublin Com- mission on Monday, before Mr. Justice O'Brien, James Fitz- harris, alias 'Skin-the-Gat," being indicted for the murder of Mr. Burke. It was not set forth by the prozecu- tioa that the prisoner was one of the actual murderers, but an equal measure of legal responsibility was imputed to him as an accessory betore the crime. The Crown was repre- sented by the Attorney-General. M.P., Mr. James Murphy, Q.C., and Mr. Peter O'Brien, QC. ; and the counsel for the prisoner were Mr. John Ouseley Byrne, 8.L., and Mr. C. Minerney, who were in- structed in the case by Mr. Gerald Byrne, prisoner's solicitor. The Attorney-General, in stating the case for the Crown, detailed the connection which had existed between the prisoner and the " Invincibles " Fitzharris, who was the owner of a horse and car, was in the habit of driving different members of the conspiracy about the city, and was instrumental in conveying some of them to the places where they lay in wait on several occasions for Mr. Forster. He it was who induced the informer Smith to join the Society, selecting him apparently for the reason that he was familiar, from his occupation at the Castle, with Mr. Forster's appear- ance and movements. On the sth and 6th of May the p isoner drove James Carey and other " Invincibles" into , the Phcenix Park, and on the latter day actually witnessed the I murders, afterwards driving off at top speed with the assassins to the further side of the city. Smith in his evidence spoke to the prisoner as being the man who persuaded him to enter the conspiracy. He was subjected to a severe cross- examination, but his evidence was not materially affected. In reply to Prisoner's counsel, Smith said he expected no pecuniary reward from the Government, lou.t merely wished to be sent out of the country adding significantly that "he knew what he would get if he stopped ia it." James Carey also repeated his story of the formation and doings of the "Invincible,," and identified Fitzharris as the driver of the car upon which the murderers entered and left the Phcenix Park. The same evening Carey paid him " under a sove- reign" for his services. In cross—examination Carey said the prisoner was not enrolled as an " Invincible." Peter Carey stated that Fitzharris had admitted that he saw the murders committed. Other independent witnesses proved that he was in the park with his car immediately before the crime was discovered. The trial was adjourned until Tues- day, the case for the Crown having closed.

The trial of Fitzharris came to a—close on Tuesday. There was no attempt to set up an alibi as in the previous trials, his counsel merely urging that the prisoner in driving the miscreants about Dublin was simply following his occupa- tion, and was innocent of the atrocious objects of the con- spiracy. Mr. Murphy, coumel for the Crown, made an ex- ceedingly strong appeal to the jury not to accept the argu- ment put forward for the defence. In his summing up, Mr. Justice O'Brien told the jury that if they believed that what Peter Carey said was true that would not establish the charge of murder against the prisoner, nor would his bare concealment alone of an intention to commit the crime be sufficient unless he actively in sotoe way assented to it, and was there with a view of assisting in the escape of the per- sons engaged in the affair. His bare concealment of the crime would not make him guilty; a silent acquiescence in it would not make him guilty; he must have gone to the park with the knowledge of the intention to commit the crime, and also with the design in his mind to give some form of support and assistance to the commission of the crime.—The Jury were in consultation for half an hour, and they returned into court with a verdict of not guilty. It was intimated on behalf of the Crown that there were "other charges," and the prisoner was detained in custody.

div.head: PLEAS OF GUILTY.
div.p: PLEAS OF GUILTY.

Patrick Delaney and Thomas Caffrey, two of the Phcenix Park assassins, on Wednesday pleaded guilty, and were sentenced to death. They were two of the men who fled from the scene of the murders on Kavanagh's car. While admitting being in the company of the murderers, both denied having had any actinl hand in the crime, and they pleaded that they were present under cmpulsicn and that their absence would have cost them their lives. Delaney said that Kavanagh and Carey had told the truth, and that it was Brady and Kelly—and no other person—who com- mitted the murders. Delaney, who is under sentence of penal servitude for the attempt on the life of Mr. Justice Lawson, claimed that he was the cause of the Judge's life being saved. He was, he said, put on to shoot his Lordship by Mullett and Brady, but he drew the attention of one of the Judge's body-guard to the intended attack, and this brought about its failure. The solicitor for the two prisoners informed the Judge that he had in vain endeavoured to dissuade the me u from pleading guilty, telling them that the result would be the same as though they were convicted—sentence of death—. and that he could not hold out any hope whatever that any- thing would be done for them—an explanation which caused the Judge to remark, "It is quite right that you should make that statement." A Dublin correspondent nays tbat Delaney, who has given very important evidence

to the Crown, is not to be '.aanged ; but there is no reason to believe that Caffrey wir...l receive any consideration. The execution of Delaney and Caffrey was appointed to take place on the 2nd :rdn'oe. Ivr..ORE PLEAS OF GUILTY. • The Pr"r4dings at the Dublin Commission on Thursday will tend to revive public interest in the protracted trials arisin from the murder revelations. Early in the day the c's.,anty and city grand juries were called together, and new bills of indictment against some of the men now in custody, in respect of the Park murders and the attack on Mr. D. J. Field, were laid before them. The action of the authorities against the reputed chiefs of this organisation was made clear by the preferring of indictments for murder and conspiracy against P. J. Tynan (the notorious "No. 1"), P. J. Sheridan (the "organiser "), and John Walsh. Against these persons true bills were found for participa- tion in the asaassinations of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke, and for conspiring to murder Mr. Field. On the latter charge the grand jury arrived at a similar result in the cases of James Mullett, Joseph Mullett, Laurence Hanlon Edward M'Caffrey, Ed- ward O'Brien, Peter Doyle, George Smith, Thomas Doyle, William Moroney, Daniel Delaney, and James Fitz- harris. The county grand jury found true hills for the Phoenix Park murders against Edward O'Brien and M'Caffrey, and against Fitzharris as an accessory after the fact. James Mullett and William Moroney were then arraigned on the charge of conspiracy, and both pleaded guilty. Sentence was deferred. The young man Laurence Hanlon was next indicted for wounding Mr. Field with in- tent to murder him. Evidence—chiefly that of informers— was adduced to show that the prisoner on the night of the outrage rode on Kavanagh's car with Brady, Daniel Delaney, and Timothy Kelly, and that ke jumped off and stabbed the unfortunate special juror at his own door. Kelly, it was also said, had been present at the flinging of the knives used into Ringsend Basin. Mr. Field, in his testimony, failed to identify any of his assailants, the night being dark and the attack wholly unexpected.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill came before a select committee of the House of Commons on Tuesday. Sir Joseph Bailey is chairman of the committee, and the other members are Mr. Reginald Yorke, Mr. Arthur Vivian, and Mr. Stafford Howard. The bill was the occasion of great interest, and the committee room was crowded during the day. That portion of the bill which refers to the construe- Lion of a low-water channel in the Mersey by means of training walls has been struck out in conseqaence of plans and sections of the contemplated work not having been de- posited, and the promoters obtained a suspension of the standing orders of both Houses on condition that the por- tion of the billr elating to the canal proper only should be pro- ceeded with. The original petitioners agaiust the bill were the company and proprietors of the Mersey and 'mall Naviga• Lion and the Bridgewater Navigation Company, the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners, the trustees of the River Weaver Naviga- tion, the Shropshire Union and Canal Company, the Corporation of Liverpool, the Corporation of Birken- head, the company and proprietors of the Rochdale Canal, owners of property, manufactures, and trades in Widnes, the Widnes Local Board, owners, merchants, and manufac- turers in and near Warrington, the South Lancashire and Cheshire Coal Association, the Trustees of the Duke of Bridgewater, Sir R. S. Brooke. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Wigg Brothers and Steele (Runcorn), Greenall, Whitley, and Co., Limited; Edward Spencer Hargreaves, the Manchester Racecourse Company, Limited; Sir Humphry de Trafford, the Corporations of Manchester Salford, and Warrington; elle Trustees of the Peace of the County of Lancaster, the Warrington Highway Board, the Barton, Eccles, Winton, and Menton Local Boards; the Flixton, Urmston, and South Barton Highway Board • the Guardians of the Poor of Bar- ton and Irwell, the London and North-Western Railway Company, the Great Western Railway Company and the Cheshire _Lines Committee, and the Midland Railway Company. Che counsel engaged were : For the Bill: Mr. Pember, Q.C., Mr. Michael, Q.C., Mr. Pembroke Stevens, Q.C., Mr. Balfour Brown, and Mr. Cripps; Mr. Littler, Q.C., the Hon. E. Chandos Leigh, and Mr. Worsley Taylor for the Cheshire Lines Committee; Mr. Shriegwill and Mr. Hargreaves for Mr. E. S. Har- greaves; Mr. Aspivall, Q.C., Mr. Pope, Q.C., and Mr. Led- gard for thp Liverpool Corporation; Mr. Pope, Q.C., Mr. Littler, Q C., Mr. Sutton Mr. Moon, and Mr. Polloak for the London and North-Western Railway Company ' • Mr. Addison, Q.C., for the Manchester Corporation; Mr. Edge for the Manchester Racecourse Company; Mr. Saunders, Q.C., and Mr. Faber for the Mersey and Irwell and Bridge- water Navigation Company; Mr. Rodwell, Q C., Mr. Littler, Q.C., Mr. Ledgard, and Mr. Squarey for the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board; Mr. Bidder, Q.C., Mr. Saunders. Q.C., and Mr. Noble for the Midland Railway Company; Mr. Saunders, Q.C.. and Mr. F. Clifford for owners, merchan's, and others in and near Warrington; Mr. Littler, Q.C., and Mr. M'lntyre for Sir Humphrey de Trafford ; and Mr. Littler' Q.C., and Mr. Rigg for the Corporation of Warring- ton. The proceedings attracted the attention of several members of Parliament in addition to those forming the , committee.

Mr. Pember, the leading counsel for the promoters, stated the case in favour of the bill with great ability. He ad- vanced the familiar arguments in its favour, and declared that Lancashire was alive with expectation and anxiety with regard to the scheme. Go where one might in this county and ask what questions one pleased, and the answer would be the same—strone,dy in favour of the bill. With regard to Manchester the learned counsel said that "the men who had spent a million upon a Town Hall—a kind of costly toy—would not hesitate to put down ten times that amount in order to provide an artery to the heart's blood of their commerce and to provide for the develop- ment of their trade." Mr. MdisOn, QC., as representing the Manchester Council,gave a "strong and hearty support" to the scheme. At the conclusion of the preliminary speeches, the committee interposed in a manner which took the pro- moters of the bill by surprise. It appeared that the Standing Orders Committee had communicated with the Select Committee in regard to the famous 26th clause, that referring to the low water canal in the Mersey, which has been amended by striking out the part relating to the works in the Mersey river. The Chair- man (Sir J. Bailey) asked Mr. Pember to proceed at once with the evidence of the engineers on this, "the crucial point in the case." The Committee wished to save expense, and it was useless to eit and listen to evidence as to the commercial value of the Canal unless the promoters were able to show that the scheme was practicable. Mr. Pember said that the course taken by the Standing Orders Commit- tee was a very extraordinary one. It was usual to take the engineering evidence last. The Chairman hereepon asked : "Are we to suppose you have come with this bill before a Parliamentary Committee without knowing how you are to make the canal to the sea?" Mr. Pember replied that the promoters knew perfectly well how to make it, and had not the slightest hesitation in facing the difficulty. After some further conversation, in which the Committee still pressed for the engineering evidence, the proceedings were adjourned until Wednesday. The Committee re-assembled on Wednesday, and after some explanations had passed as to the communication which had been received from the Standing Orders Corn- witte, Mr. Pember proceeded with his address ',on behalf of the promoters of the Bill. The learned counsel com- municated to the Committee the arrangement proposed by the Commissioners of the Mersey Conservancy in refer- ence to the deepening of the low-water channel of the river. The Commissioners stated that they saw no ob- jection in principle to the proposed deepening of the channel, providing the proposed specified works could be carried out without injury to the navigation, the anchor- age, or the moorage grounds, or interfering with the ar- proaches to the docks, or inducing a permanent silting up of any part of the channel. The views of the Com- missioners were embodied in a clause, and they reserved to themselves the right to take all necessary steps to se- cure the adoption of their suggestions. Mr. Pember thought the provisions suggested would be extremely valuable in the interests of the public, and he stated that he should advise the promoters of the scheme to adopt them without hesitation.

The committee met again on Thnrsday, when Mr. E. Leader Williams, the engineer of the company, was under examination all day. He said he had an intimate know- ledge of the river Mersey, both in the c,nstrnction of docks at Runcorn and sea walls at Weston. For seventeen years he had been employed as an engineer by the River Weaver Navigation, and for seven years by the Bridgewater Naviga- tion. In the course of his examination he explained the depth of the proposed channel in the estuary and the height and velocity of the tides in the Mersey, the channel of which was continually shifting owing to the nature of the bed and other causes. The scheme of the company, he said, had been designed on the plans adopted in the improvement of the river Tees.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIN. AT SANKEY BRIDGES.
div.p: THE ATTEMPTED SUICIN. AT SANKEY BRIDGES.

The particulars of a dettperate attempt to commit suicide, were brought out before 'l'. Comber, 'l'. J. Gillespie, C. Pil- kington, and A. C. MeCorquodale Esql. at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, when a middle-aged man named James Heath was charged with attempting to com- mit suicide.—Superintendent Jackson said: I mty just 1 state that on Tuesday afternoon last, this man was ram- bling about in Great Sankey near Warrington, in a semi- muddled state and he told several people that he was going to commit suicide. He went along the canal hank and , threw himself into the water, and I believe after be was pulled out that he jumped in again. A man pulled him out twice if T mistake not.—James Prince then d eposed that he saw the prisoner on the previous evening as he was walking along the road near the canal. The prisoner came to him and said "I am going to make a mess of myself, " but did not say in what way or what he meant by it. At last he said" lam going to put an end to myself "and wit- ness replied " You are a fool for that." The prisoner told him his name and address, adding that "If lam picked .up 1 in the course of a day or two, you will know 1 who I am." He did not say anything else, and witness did not think be was going to carry out his threat. He ultimately saw the prisoner jump into the canal, and saw him pulled out, when he appeared to be dead.—James Dickenson, a young man employed at the Whitecross Iron Works, Warrington, stated that on the previous Tuesday night he saw the defendant walking on the canal bank. The prima asked him if he knew his mother or brother, and witness replied that he did not. The prisoner said if Le would inquire at Widnes he would find them, adding that he was about to make away with himself. Witness tcld

him he would be foolish for so doing, but the prisoner agaili threatened to carry out his threat, and refused to go bait Witness then seized him by the collar and threw him to ground. He was overpowered, however, and the prison_t again attempted to jump in. Witness seized him once and again threw him down. He succeeded iR holding 1111 down for sometime, until he promised "before God 1' that he would let him go he would not get into the canal but home to Widnes. Upon that witness allowed hinlatra get up. He then ran about 200 Yards biat jumped into the canal. Witness Ind nothing to rescue with, but a train was passing, and he called out to the IwIP in charge of the engine and the latter threw down alt He tried three or four times to get the rope round the 1311,4 head, but was unsuccessful until just as he was sinking 1 the last time the rope wrapped round his head, and will, v—of managed to get him to tho side.
