div.head: *RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS
div.p: *RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. T. Norman presided, and there were present Dr. MacDonell, Messrs. W. Rhodes, J. Wil- liams, F. A. Lake, J. Pritchare, W. Whittaker, J. W. Light- burn, W. Fisher, P. Briscoe, J.Meadowcroft, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), Dr. Mouritz (.nedical officer), and W. Barker (surveyor.) 41 RATIFYING INTELLIGENCE. The MEMCM, OFFICER read his monthly report, which stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn dining the past month amounted to 24, repretenting a death rate of 19 per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths 11 were due to chest affections, 4 to diseases of the nervous Tystem, 4 to abdominal diseases, 2 to maraemus, 2to diseases of the throat, anal to cancer. Eleven deaths oc- curred-among children 3 years old and under, and 8 below 1 year. Four inquests were held, making the total deaths 213.-a4n reply to the Chairman, Mr. BARKER said there were-27 deaths during the same period last year.—Dr. ItotErrz observed that scarlet fever and measles had been theroughly eradicated, and he hoped the disease would not be imported again. THE HOARD O'N THE PRESS AND PRIVILEGE. Mr. BROOKES said two paragraphs, based upon informa- tion given in the agenda, had appeared in a contemporary, and as it would be setting a precedent for the publication of the peoceedings of committees before sanctioned by the Board, he should like an expression of opinion on the matter.—lne CHAIRMAN thought it wrom, to publish anything until it had passed the Board, but Mr. Brookes pointed out that in Liverpool, Warrington, and other places the proceedings of committees were often published in the newspapers before submitted to the Council meetings.—Dr. nitcDoucaLt. did not see much harm in what had been done. It was a question of privilege, inasmuch as it was usual to have these matters discussed by the Board, and un- usual for committees to take upon themselves the responsi- bility of giving information on subjects not yet decided by the Board. They had an instance where a committee had given information recently, and he said it was that unfortu- nate example which had been followed. Perhaps the re- porters, now their attention bad been called to the matter, would consider it a question of privilege, and exercise discretion in the future.—Mr. PRITCHARD called attention to a paragraph which appeared in the newspapers with reference to a conference at Manchester on the Ship Canal, and he desired an explanation how a privileged report of that ,nature should have got Into the public prints, even before the matter had would be well to .press the matter any further. There was Coate before the Board.—Dr. MACDOUGALL did not think it un 'doubt the Press had shown the Board great indulgence on more than one occasion, and he did not think that the Press having erred in discretion on this occasion that the Board should go too far with the matter. It was the duty of a newspaper representative to do what he could to convey early intelligence to the public.—Mr. 0. LIGHTBURN, refer- ing to the remark about the conference, said he was quite willing to take the responsibility of his position and to justify any course he took in the matter.—The CHAIRMAN : think what has been said will cause the reporters to use their discretion.—Mr. LAKE observed that it was to the benefit of the representatives of the Press to treat that Board and every other public body with consideration, as news• papers were simply business speculations. He also stated that the fact that reporters received an agenda at the same time as the members easily explained a few things that the Board had been puzzled about before. After some further conversation the subject dropped. MITE AUDIT. The Law CLERK stated that the auditor had fixed the .24th inst. as the time of the audit.

THE SCHOOLS AND INFECTIOUS DISEASES.—SUGGESTED POSTAL FACILITIES.—COMPLAINTS AEATNST THE CONTRACTOR'S WORK. The minutes of the Highway Committee for the 12th ult., stated that instructions had been given to the sur- veyor to serve Mr. Roberts with a notice to remove obstruc- Cousin front of his premises, near the Town Hall, and at a meeting on the 26th ult., it was resolved that 'no proceedings be taken at present against Mr. -R. Roberts, Bridge-street, for obstruction. A letter was read from the clerk to the Runcorn School Board stating that instructions had been given to the mis- 'tress of the'Board School in consonance with the request of the Commissioners with reference to scarlatina. The sec- retary having written to Mr. Footner with reference to the completion of the bridge slope, a reply was received stet- -ing that the office to be placed at the •foot of the bridge slope would be completed in about a fortnight, and when placed in position the approach would be opened.--Mr. G. L. Wide} complained of the nuisance arising from the Mougbland-road sewer, and the surveyor was instructed to prepare a plan and estimate of the cost of providing and fix- ing a self-flushing apparatus to the sewer. It was resolved that the law clerk call the attention of Mr. Cliff to the complaints of the surveyor that the streets were not suffi- -ciently watered, or properly swept and cleansed. It was also resolved that placards be issued warning persons against putting refuse into the streets. Recommendation that the foot- way in front of Stanley-villas be paved with Buckley bricks. It was also recommended that Mr. Henry Linaker, of Frod- sham, be asked to report as to the most suitable place for a junction with the Liverpool water main, and that Messrs. P. Speakmen and W.'Fisher be appointed to confer with him on the subject. Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. Lake and Whittaker were appointed a committee to consider the circu- lars from the Home Office with reference to the Explosives •-Acts, and to report on the beat way to carry out the instruc- tions. It was recommended that the postal authorities be requested to make arrangements near to the Top Locks where stamps could be purchased for the convenience of the shipping and commercial interests and residents of the dis- trict, and that the present letter box be removed from the foot of Waterloo Bridge to the 'said office; and also that the receiving office for letters, and the distribution of stamps be provided near Delph Bridge for the convenience of the residents of that district.—Dr. MACDOTVALL moved the confirmation of the the minutes. He asked whether similar notices to that served on the School Board with reference to starlatina had been forwarded to other schools in the town, and whether similar letters bad been received from thern.—Mr. BROOKE'S said petters were sent to all schools both public and private at the same time as the one was sent to the School Board. The latter body had only replied.—Dr. MacDou- CULL said it might be questioned whether they had a right to expect a reply to a circular of that kind ; but although the School Board, with their usual courtesy, had replied, he sincerely trusted that the other authorities would recogrise in the same open way the efforts the Board were making to stamp out scarlet fever. -The Board had been somewhat unfortunately circumstanced with regard to this infectious disease, but they had it on the authority of the medical officer, and to far as his experience went he (the speaker) -would confirm the statement that scarlet fever, measles, and the other disagreeable infections diseases in the district had been reduced to a small nurni.ier of cases indeed. That must be very satisfactory. Referring to Mr. Cliff, Dr. MacDougall said the public interest was of more im- ,cortanee than any private interest, and it would be the duty --of the Board to take such steps as they might be legally advised to do, to see that the contract was carried out ac- cording to the agreement. (Hear, hear.) Grave complaints - had been made from time to time that Mr. Cliff's contract was not carried out, but that matter would no doubt be dis- cussed if the committee found it necessary to take any ex- treme step beyond warning the contractor.—Mr. PRITCHARD ceconded the motion. He observed that if the proposed alterations to Waterloo Bridge were carried out, it would be necessary to move the letter box at present there, and he thought it an opportune moment to endeavour to obtain a little extra postal facility at that end of the town. He was Lure it would be appreciated by the residents of the district, and also by those interested in the shipping trade. (Hear, hear.) It was not an unusual thing to see sailors, after their arrival at the port, come into the town with a letter in their band, and finding the pillar boxnre unable to post the letter because they cannot procuse a stamp in the dis- trict. They had in consequence to inquire their way until they reached the general post office. Postal facilities were also wanted near Delph Bridge. At the general post office all the business had to be done at one counter, and the place was frequently so crowded that , people. although every attention was paid to them, were not able to get them wants attended to with that facility which a community might naturally expect. They had to consider too that at the pre- sent time there was included in that one small place the postal, the telegraph, the banking, and the inland revenue businesses zo that really the inhabitants of Runcorn were not overdone w;th postal facilities. in addition they bad the pcospect of having in a few months another department added in tbe shape of the parcels post, which would require a great amount of accommodation, and when sixpenny tele- grams were allowed, a great increase of -business might be expected inahatelirection. He therefore thought that if some conveniences such as those suggested mere given to the community it would relieve the [block which .soine- times teak place at the general post office. and be bad no dcubt that having the support of the Cornseissionen, the postal authorities would grant them.—Mr. MF.ADOWCROFT inquired whether Mr. Cliffs was *unposed to water Duke'sield—(hear, bear)—as well as Other parts of the town. It seemed to be entirely neglected. —Mr. BA.RIERS: He should.water all streets that require it. Of course I would not send him into streets that are not made.—The Cwassasare said -there were great complaints ovith regard to Duire's,Field.—Mr. BARKER: He cannot do eit with one cart. It would take two carts all their time.— The CHAIRMAN: He is bound to do it.—Dr. MacDo-soar,r, eeaiel be had seen the contractor since the committee meet- ing, and be ventured to tell him that the feeling of the .Boasd about the way is which he Was executing his duty was getting very strong. Mr. eliffe promised to reform con- siderabi y; he thought his health would be better soon, and /bat-be would be able to attend to-hieduty bmer. He (the Apeaker) sold him that if he did not consider it necessary to have his health improve the Commissioners would think it necessary to improve it for him in a .ilrection which he Wouti4l nottlihe—The minutes were then pazAed.

THE HosnrAtt. The minutes of the Canal Saats and Hospital Committee contained a recommendation that the penalty against Mr. W. Statham under the hospital contract be redwed to £1; that a caretaker of tto hospital premises be engeged, and in consideration therea live rent free in the cottage, be provided with coal and csater, and enter into an agreement ;to be prepared bv the law clerk; that Mr. W. Statham be Paid £8 on account of the hospital fence contract.—Ur. Yjbalta moved, and Mr. P. SFYAHMAN seconded, the adop, 1101:Lot the minates.--A discnssi4n took place with regard f 9 :41.psopointment of a egetaker,—.Dr.MAcDoneeLL spoke

satirically of the "fancifully-built cottage," which he alleged had cost more than the hospital itself; and sug- gested that person should be engaged as caretaker who could alto perform the daties of nurse when required. I —Eventually, the minute 170:5 referred back for further con. I sideration, and the advice ct the medical officer.
TRE GAS COMPANt AND PUBLIC LIGHTING.-TEE I'IIENADE CONCERTS.

The General Pe'rposes Committee, at their meeting= the 25th ultimo, resolved that the Runcorn brass sands be allowed to play in the Market-place during the summer months. The Runcorn Gas Company wrote asking whether the Commissioners were willingto purchasethe Cargo lamps erected by the company, and to bear the cost of the gas con- sumed therein. The secretary was instructed to reply thereto.—Mr. Brascon moved, and Mr. Leest seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. MEADOWCROFY speaking of the caution given to the brass bands, asked whether if such a-course should lead to a serious obstruction, the Commie-, Isioners would be liable for such obstruction. He thought it was an unwise step for the Board to take, and very im- proper to give the bands power to -stop in the streets.—he CHAIRMAN remarked that it was mot suggested that they should play in the street, but at the top of the market.—Mr. Mnenowonr said there was net room there for a body of people to stand and listen to the music.—Mr. Bemoan observedtbat this recommendation was made jest as a trial. Before tk3 committee came to that decision, they anertained the feeling of the shopkeepers in the neighbourhood. They said thev had no objection to the concerts, which could only ha held on ona evening in the week.—Mr. FISHER was afraid the people in the neighbourhood would soon tire of the music.—The Calannex: Let us try it for one month. —Dr. MACDOUGALL scarcely expected to hear such an illiberal speech from 'Mr. Meadowcroft, who, he should think, knew the value of music as a source of intelligence. The speaker adverted to the elevating influence of music, and said if Mr. Meadow-croft had been at the first concert which took place on the previous night, when there was a large .slumber of people present, he would have seen that it was thoroughly enjoyed and that there was no obstruction. The Board ought to do all they could to cultivate a taste of music in the people, and he hoped the question would be discussed from a musical point of view. It was very kind of the bands to come forward and make an effort of this nature without reward in any way whatever beyond the hope that they might do something for their day and generation —Mr. MEADOWCROFT explained that he had no objection to the band of music, and his re- mks had simply reference to the question whether an ob- struction would be made.—Dr. MACDouGLLL : Hear, hear; glad to hear RyloDEs asked what was the nature of the reply sent to the Gas Company.—Mr. FISHER: I have always been under the itnpression that these lamps were supplied free of cost by the Gas Company. Is that se The CHAIRMAN: Hitherto they have. Mr. FISHER: Well, then, what is the object of this letter. Are they withdrawing their generosity ? The CHAIRMAN : We cannot tell you that. We have asked for an explanation.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN : I should like to have that letter read.—The SECRETARY: There is no com- munication drawn up.—Mr. FISHER said it was rather a pily the Board had got into the bad graces of the company. These lamps were a great boon in the places where they were fixed. (Hear. bear.) He was very sorry the Gas Company were about to withdraw their generosity.—Mr. RHODES asked if the secretary had received instructions as to the manner in which he had to reply ?—Mr. LAKE ex- plained that in April, 1882, the Board applied fora reduction in the Gas Company's charges for lighting the street. In reply to that the gas company said they were supplying these lamps free of charge, and gave this as a reason for not reducing the price of gas. The Board was now drawing the company's attention to their application and the reply there- to.—The minutes were confirmed. I FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The estimates of this 'committee, which were paestd, showed that the receipts for the past month amounted to £79 19s 2d, and accounts amounting to £lB9 143 2d were recommended for paymen:.—The seal of the Board was• affixed to the district rate, and the Board then resolved it- self into committee.

div.head: CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.
div.p: CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.
WIDNES
BRANCH.

The second anniversary of' the establishment of this so- ciety was celebrated on Saturday by a procession, a tea party, and a public meeting. Rain descanded heavily in the morn- ing, and it did not seem improbable that the first part of the day's programme would have to be abandoned. As two o'clock approached, however' the rain ceased, aud although dark clouds hovered over bead, and the roads were very ' wet and very muddy, about 1,000 of the members put in an appearance at the National Schools. Here they were formed in processional order, and paraded the main streets. Heading the procession was a new and handsome banner, having on the front a representation of Moses striking the rock, with the words "Church of England Temperance Society, Widnes branch." On the reverse was a representation of Daniel in the lions' den, with the temperance text "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging." Next came the Star of Temperance Brass Band, followed by the members of the adutt section of the society, Runcorn Parish Church Brass Band, Simms Cross section of the society, Mersey Mission Band, and the juvenile members brought up the rear. A stoppage was made at Anderson's Corner' on the site of the proposed new church, where Mr. E. J. Parr and Mr. Carr delivered appropriate addresses to the assemblage. The Vicar (the Rev. J. Wright Williams) read a telegram from the architect of the new -Church, stat- ing his intention to commence building operations next week. The announcement was received with loud cheers. Afterwards the procession wended its way to the Parish Church, where service was held. The Rev. W. H. Duggan read the service, and the lesson was read by the Rev. Geo. Bond, the vicar of Farnworth. The Vicar of Widnes preached a sermon, after which a collection was made on behalf of the funds. At five o'clock tea was provided in the National school. About 620 persons were present, and their wants were attended to by the following ladies :—Mesdames Duggan, Cave, Thomas, Faulkner, Fairclough, Richards, James, Shaw, Atherton, Cleaver, Davies, Tushington, Moss, Hunt, Pemberton, Jones, Bruce, Pervin, Kenyon, Misses Hedley, Purvin, Woods, Lea, Whitley, the Misses Edwards, Fairley, and Mallin. Subsequently a public meeting was held, under the presidency of the Rev. J. Wright Williams, the vicar. There was a large audience, amongst those pre- sent being the Revs. S. A. Spooner, W. H. Duggan, J. Hirst (organising district secretary), Messrs. E. J. Parr, Carr, Bruce, Atherton, Kilcross, tire.

The Cliainnfax, in a short address, said he felt very much gratified that although the day opened so unfavourably their hearts did not fail. He adverted to the great increase in the membership during the past year ; and, after observ- ing that the manufacturers of the town were not in ignor- ance of their movement, but unfortunately through residing away from Widnes could not be present that night, read a letter from Mr. H. W. Deacon who thanked tae vicar for his invitation. He understood that the vicar was thinking of starting a reading-room in connection with the society. He thought the idea a very good one, and hoped that he would be able to carry it out; and as a small contribution, he begged to enclose a cheque for £5, which be asked the vicar to please accept and use as he thought best. (Ap- plause.) _

The 'Rev. S A. SPOONER made a few remarks, and the SECRETARY (Mr. F. Cave) read the report, from which we take the following extracts :—Two years to-day, • that is on the 28th day of April, 1881, the society in Widnes was in its infancy; to-day we might say it had grown to man's estate, and although the committee do not wish to claim all the credit from the entire amount of good wh!ch has re- sulted from the efforts put forth for the spread of the tem- perance cause in Widnes; still it has not been achieved without a great deal of prayerful thought and sacrifice of time on ,their part. It is but just that special mention should be made in reference to the efforts of the committee at the great national festivities of Christmas time, while there were and always are extra inducements held out for the indulgence of excess, the committee hit upon a plan to counteract in some measures those inducements. That plan the committee very happily called "fine nights with the Church of England Temperance Society," and they are happy to EIX7 that under the blessing of God their efforts to provide counter attractions proved a marked success. For although the season did not pass without some of our mem- bers falling wietims to the arch enemy drink, still the I number thus lost to us were few in comparison to thtenum- I her who declared for total abstinence during the same season. Our loss in the month of December, IgB2, and January, 1883, being 13, whilst n the same two w..onths there were no fewer than 146 per- sons signed ourtetal abstinence pledge, thus proving beyond the shadow of a doubt that temperance principles are taking a great hold on tbn,pablic mind in Widnes. With regard to our work, it entaits a great amount of visiting on your com- mittee, and with Wormed numbers increased help is needed, and your committee earnestly ask all and everyone who have an aptitude ,for visiting, and have a few hours' time in each week that they could devote to that purpose to, give their names to the secretary, so that they may be en- rolled on the visiting list and put into harness. With regard to our membership,, last September:there were on the ,books :—general section, 80; total abstinence, 492; Water- loo-road senior boys and girls, 102; juveniles, 172; Simnfg fGross juvenile branch, 2.54; making a total of 1,050. After deducting 15 who had not -been able to keep their pledge of abstinence, the number left good on the books was 1.035. The numbers now are :—general section, 30; tote( abetin- enceezection, 679; Waterloo-road 2nd division, boys 104, gii Ls 78, total 182; juveniles, girls 157, boys 176; Simm's Cross Juvenile Branch, girls 129, boys 104; making a total of 1,457. From .this must be deducted 16 who have not been able to,keep their pledge, 2 from death, and one has left the town, thus leaving good on the books 1,438. In addition to these there are also 297 persons who have signed the society's total abstinence pledge. This makes the entire number of total abstainers 1,735. The Tontine Society in connection withthe Widnes branch is making rapid progress. The num- ber et members last September was 85, and at the end of the Year a bonus return of X 1 3s. was paid to each full member. This b Wog in addition to the benefits derived from the society y. those who were compelled to have recourse to medical skill. Thla year the number in the society is 150, and the amount available for etividend is, for the first einarter. Is. 6d. to each member. Another project is on foot. It is to Provide medical attendance at the lowest possible rate for those mem- bers of .the C.E.T.S and those families who are not already so provided. It wip be callad the Family dispencar7 Club, and will be started ir.nmediately.” Various pas9agez m the report were cheered.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAT 5, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAT 5, 1883.

Addresses were delivered by Mr. E. J. Parr and the Rev. I J. Hirst. A vote of thanks wa,. accorded to the speakers, on the motion of the Rev. W. H. DIIGGIN, in a near speech, se- conded by Mr. F. V.I:AVE.—Mr. WATsoN moved, and Mr. BRUCE seconded a Vote of thanks to the managers of the school for the use of the building during the past year, and it was carried rananimeusly. Votes of thanks to the secretaries (Mr. Cave, Mr. Farrant, and Mr. 'Thomas), the Chairman, the Star of Temperance B ind, and the Mersey Mission Band, Runcorn, concluded le proceedings.
WARRINGTON NEWS,
In the HodSe of Commons, on Tnesclay night, the re- port of the Select Committee on the Cheshire Lines Committee Bill was considered and agreed to, and the Bill was ordered to be read a third time.

WARRINGTON OVERSEERS.—A meeting of overseers was held on Thursday evening under the presidency of Mr. Al- derman Kean. There were also present Messrs. Mackie, Harrison and Tunstall (deputy assistant overseer), but there was no business of public importance. ST. JOHN'S rRESBYTERIA.N CHURCH.—The anniversary sermons in connection with this church were preached on Sunday last by the Rev. Wm. McCaw, D.D., of Manchester, l moderator of the Presbyterian Church of England. The collections, in aid of the church fund, amounted to about £B.

TIIE SALVATION ARMY AT WARRINGTON.—The services held this week in the Salvation Army Barracks, Academy- street, have been very largely attended, and large numbers of persons have been unable to gain admission each even- ing. No disorderly scenes have occurred, nor has there been any marked obstruction in the street. I wonder why Mr. Peter Rylands does not turn his at- tention to the salary and appointments of the Irish Chancellor? That functionary receives £B,OOO a year, and a retiring pension of half that amount. As he changes with the Government, it sometimes happens that we have three or four ex-Chancellors, as well as one Chancellor in esse, upon the Irish establishment. The office in this way rarely costs the country less than £16,000, and often £20,000, a year.— Vanity Fair. ANNUAL TREAT TO THE RIFLE, VOLUNTEERS.—The annual treat to the Warrington Rifle Volunteers and their wives and children took place on Monday at the Drill Shed. About 400 persons assembled and partook of tea, after which the usual quadrille party was held, a number of the sergeants and their wives from Orford Barracks joining the party. Dancing was kept up till after twelve o'clock, at w'tich time the party broke up, having spent a very pleasant evening. Captain liepherd was present a short time during the evening. SALE OF MR. FILDES' PICTURES.—At the sale of the col- lection of modern pictures belonging to Mr. Thomas Taylor, the well-known cotton manufacturer of Wigan at Messrs. Christie and Co's., on Saturday last, "The Widower," by Mr. Luke Fildes, A.R A, was sold with the copyright for £2.100. The picture was exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1876. The second picture by the same artist, namely, "Applicants for admission to the casual ward," exhibited in 1874, which brought Mr. Fildes into repute, was sold with the copyright for £2.100, to Mr. Martin for Professor Holloway's noble institution for the higher education of women.
WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY. —House-

surgeon's report for the week ending 'Thursday, May 4. Patients admitted and discharged: Home patients, 18; out patients, 42; accidents, 9; total, 69. Cured, 0; dead, 0; discharged, 0; total,,O. Present number of home patients, —. In-patients: Admitted, 4; discharged, 3; remaining in hospital, 11. Hon. treasurer, J. R. Buckton, Esq.; hon. secretary. Joseph Davies, Esq.; house-surgeon, Mr. C. E. Richmond. The House Surgeon will feel obliged for con- tributions of old linen, Jzc. Honorary surgeon for the ensuing week, Mr. Joseph.

DRUNK AT THE SALVATION ARMY BARRACKS.—MichaeI Millett, cabinetmaker, 17, Bennett-street, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with being drunk in Academy-street on the 22nd April.—From the evidence of P.S.Cox it seemed the prisoner went to the Salvation Army Barrack, in Academy-street, drunk, and was refused admit- tance. He then became very disorderly, and had to be taken away.—The Chief Constable remarked that if any- body annoyed the Salvation Army when they were conduct- ing themselves in an orderly manner the police would ask the magistrates to deal severely with the offenders. He had heard that on the previous day people went to the barracks with bottles of drink, and he thought there would be a case or two for hearing on Monday next.—Defendant was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment in default. WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—Mr. J. Greening presided at the meeting of the Board on Wednesday. The other members present were the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Blackhurst, Cooper, Darbyshare, Harri- son, Brown, Mackie, Caldwell, Forster, Greenall, Siddeley, Hunt, Walmsley, W. Houghton, Grange, J. Houghton, Forster, Swinton, Humphries, Kilshall, Gibson, Bonnell, Worthington, Roberts, and Jolley, with Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk.)—The Clerk, in answer to Mr. Harrison, said the children would be removed to the new schools immediately after the inspection this week.—At the conclusion of the business, which was furely formal, several members rose to leave when-the Chairman said he thought the relief busi- ness of the Board was of sufficient importance to attract the attention of gentlemen who sometimes spoke very strongly about the rates, and the amount of money that was collected and expended in relief. (Hear, hear.) He thought there- fore those gentlemen should see that the money that was collected was properly administered, so that he should be very much pleased if those members who could stay would do-so as often as possible. (Hear, hear.)

STREET ACCIDENT IN LATCHFORD.—OD Wednesday evening, near the Norton Arms Hotel, Wilderspool cause- way, a trap and bicycle came into violent collision, and considerable damage was done to both. Mr. W. Fletcher; draper, Bridge-street, was in charge of the trap, and was driving in the dection of Wilderspool, while a young man named Jesse Howson, of Lymm, was coming in the opposite direction on a bicycle. Two carts were proceeding towards Warrington Bridge immediately in front of the bicyclist, and in order to pass them he turned his machine on to the wrong side of the road, apparently not seeing the trap coming in the opposite direction until it was too late to avoid a collision. The bicyclist ran into Mr. Fletcher's horse, and was thrown to the ground. The accident ap- pears to have frightened one of the horses in the carts men- tioned, as it commenced to plunge, and caused some dam- age to Mr. Fletcher's trap. The bicyclist, however, seemed to have been little hurt by his fall, for he bad in the mean- time recovered his feet and pushed his disabled machine as far as Warrington Bridge when Mr. Fletcher came up with him, and, in the presence of a policeman, obtained his name and address.

GOOD TEMPLARS' QUARTERLY MEETING AT WARRING- TON. —The quarterly session of the Walter Bonehill Lodge of Good Tempters was held on Tuesday evening last, in the lodge-room connected with Mr. W. Gallop's Coffee Tavern, Buttermarket-street, when there was a very good attend- ance of members. After the usual opening and routine business had been gone through, three candidates were ad- mitted to membership, after which theireports of the vat ious officers for previous quarter were tendered. That of the W. Secretary shewed a arand work done during the quarter, the members, along with others, being actively engaged in carrying on weekly public meetings, whicle, it was stated, could not fail to do good, the net result of a quarter's work being an increase of 19 members on the previous quarter, which was very gratifying. The financial report showed a fair balance to the credit of the lodge after all expenses had been paid. The reports being adopted, Brother Sergeant J. Jackson was recommended to the G.W C.T. as the Lodge Deputy for the ensuing term (twelve months), after which Brother Sergeant Jackson, assisted by Brother Parkes, of the Temperance Mission Lodge, installed the officers for the ensuing quarter as foilows :—W.C.T., Tro her Stockton; W.V.T.. Sister Bibby, jun.; W. Secreta-y, Brother Hender- son; W.F. Secretary, Brother Corpo. a Howard; W. Treasurer, Brother Tynan; W. Chap. Brother Gilbert; W.M.. Brother W. Gallop; W.l.G.,,Brother White; W.A. Secretary, Sister Greatorix ; W.D.M., Sister Forshaw ; P.W.C.T , Brother T. Fairbrother. After installation, the Sick and Absentee 'Visiting and Finance Committees were appointed, the Enter- tainment Committee being the lodge officers. Brother Sergeant Jackson notified to the members that the next session of the District Lodge was being held at St. Helens on May 12th. A very pleasant session was closed in the usual form by the W.C.T. at 9-45 p.m. AN EXPENSIVE " LARK " AT WARRINGTON.— Four young men named Joseph Lawton and Charles Lawton, of Penketh, James Tierney and George Lynch, of Warrington, were charged at Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, before the ex-Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), with maliciously injuring door-plates belonging to Dr. Charles White, and Mr. Birch Browne, Sankey Street.—Mr. G-. T. Moore, who appeared for the defence, asked that the summonses might be withdrawn, by permis- sion of the magistrates.—The Chief Constable said he wished to make a few observations.—Mr. Moore asked Mr. Hunt to let the summonses be withdrawn without any remarks, as the defendants had agreed to the publication of an apology in a local paper. Compensation had been paid, and the receipt was in his (Mr. Moore's) office. Taking into con- sideration the position of all the parties concerned, he must ask the Chief Constable, as a gentleman of well-known benevolence, not to enter upon the case.—The Chief Con- stable replied that right was right all the world over, and he could not permit the flattery of Mr. Moore to prevent him discharging what he felt to be a public duty.—Mr. Moore: don't want to softsoap Mr. Hunt. (Laughter.)— The Chief Constable was sure that the ex-Mayor was wish- ful that justice should be done; and what he heel to say to the court that day would not be uttered in a persecuting spirit. He had, however, a public duty to discharge, and must be allowed to make a statement. It appeared that about twenty minutes to twelve on the night of the 19th ult. Dr. White heard someone make a great noise at his gate, ani went out, He found that the sign now produced had been forced from the place which it had occupied for years, and that very great violence had been used for the purpose. Farther inquiry showed that , the sign of Mr. Browne's, hairdresser, had else been removed. Week after week and month after month similar proceedings were going on in various parts of of the borough. The police books were full of such reports, and now that they had trot hold of three or four respect- ably-connected young men, who were doing these sort of tricks as a lark, the matter was treated very lightly. The defendants were only summoned for wilful damage, but they might have been proceeded against for felony; and it was a Question for the magistrate to consider as to whether he i would permit such a serious charge to be settled in such a fashion. Proceedings of this nature were beyond a lark, and it was not the first time the defendants had been guilty of such conduct.—The ex-Mayor said that cases of this , character must certainly be put a stop to. They could not I allow men like defendants to escape through the kind- heartedness of such a gentleman as Dr. White. He would adjourn the bearing of the summons until Friday.—Mr. Moore explained that the amount of damage was to be paid, and the fees of himself and Mr. Davies, and after this had been done what remained out of a sum of £B, which had been paid in by the defendants, would be handed over to the dispensary.—The ex-Mayor said after this explanation iv Waal permit the summonses to be withdrawn.

div.head: EXCITING STRUGGLE IN A BEDROOII.
div.p: EXCITING STRUGGLE IN A BEDROOII.

Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, a young man, Emmanuel Carter, seaman, was brought up on remand charged with havi4ig, on the 2nd inst., unlawfully and maliciously wounded James Chambers. —The prosecutor said he was a butcher, and lived at 67, Wellington-street, Runcorn. The prisoner, who was his stepson, was in the habit of going to his house when he had had any drink, and on Wednesday night, about half-past eleven, after he (witness) had gone to bed the prisoner , broke open the front door, and entered the bedroom where! the prcsecutor's sons were sleeping. He asked, "Where's the -- Chambers?" and then entered prosecutor's bed- room. The prosecutor could see that the prisoner was "in drink." The prisoner rushed to the bedside, and with his fist struck the prosecutor on the side of the head. The latter was in the act of getting up, when the prisoner pushed him down on the bed again, and a struggle took place. While it was proceeding, the prisoner bit the prosecutor's ear, which bled a great deal. The prisoner's mother said, "Oh, • leave go of him, man; don't do that, or you will get your- self into trouble." Releasing himself from the prisoner's grasp the prosecutor ran downstairs, and although only wearing his shirt and flannel, ran to Savage's Bridge, where he informed two policemen of what had taken place. .The shirt worn by the prosecutor was produced. It was alltit covered with blood.—Dr. McDougall deposed to examining the prosecutor on 3rd inst. He found that a Piece was missing from the upper portion of the right ear. It might have been removed by a bite. From the injuries he had found, he should think the prosecutor would bleed freely.— P.C. Noden said about half-past eleven ou Wednesday night he went to the prosecutor's house in Wellington-st., where he saw the prisoner making his way through the back door. Witness captured him, and leaving him in charge of P.C. Price, went upstairs. In the front-room he found a pool of blood by the side of the bed, and on looking about he found a small piece of the ear. He afterwards charged the pri- soner, who said I didn't bite it." He received the shirt produced from Chambers, and the stains of blood upon it were then wet.—Prisoner was now formally charged, and in reply said " I am very sorry that it happened, and if is had not been for being drunk it wouldn't have ben done."-For the defence, Ann Chambers, wife of the prosecutor and mother of the prisoner, stated that the house door bad neither lock nor bolt, and was usually fastened with a bit of stick or a spoon, and on the slightest shake it would open. When the prisoner entered the house he went straight uptairs and lay down in his own bed; but her husband making use of several oaths shouted out to him. The prisoner then went to the bedroom door, when Chambers jumped out of bed, picked up his clog, and with it struck the prisoner. He then seized him by the throat,and they wrestled together on the floor. For ten minutes they fought, first one on the top and then the other, and she thought her husband would have throttled the prisoner. The prisoner was very drunk, but he thumped the prosecutor as well as he could. Cham- bers again picked up his clog and struck the prisoner three or four times with it. The prisoner then seized the ugly implement and struck the prosecutor, who was afterwards bleeding. The struggle continued for some time longer, and eventually the police were called in. She did not see the prisoner bite the prosecutor's ear, and she did not think it could be done without her seeing.—The prisoner was com- mitted to take his trial at the Kuutsford Sessions. The ma- gistrates admitted the prisoner to bail, himself in £4O and .one surety in £2O.

div.head: LYADI LOCAL BOALD.
div.p: LYADI LOCAL BOALD.

A meeting of the newly-constituted Board was held in the Board-room en Thursday evening. Mr. H. Cameron pre- sided, and there were also present Messrs. Dawhurst, Rogers, Callender, Foster, Gibbon, Appleton, Thomason, and Ridg- way (clerk).

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEES.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEES.

A special meeting of the Board was held on the 19th ult, when Mr. Cameron was appointed chairman of the Board for the ensuing year. The following committees were also appointed :—Building and Ere engine: Messrs. Appleton, Gibtion, and Taylor. Finance: Messrs. Thomason, Dew- burst, and Rogers, Road: Messrs. Dewhurst, Gibbon, and Foster. Sanitary; Messrs. Callender, Gibbon, and Rogers. Gas : Messrs. Thomason, Callender, and Rogers. School attendance : Messrs. Appleton. Gibbon, and Thoma- -son.—The chairman is a member of all the committees.

div.head: PROGRESS OF THE SEWERAGE WORKS.
div.p: PROGRESS OF THE SEWERAGE WORKS.

Messrs. Wilson and Mu'liner, the Board's engineers presented their monthly report respecting the progress of sewerage works. It stated that there had been a fair amount of work done since the last report in laying the 16- inch main sewer, which was now complete from the outfall to Pool-lane, excepting a short length of iron pipes at the outfall end and a few minor matters. The sewer had been extended from opposite to Oakfield in Whitbarrow- lane, part way into Mr. Warburton's field, to 380 on plan at a depth of from 10 to 14. In this length the contractor had had to contend with a quicksand in which water was flowing very freely. Fortunately there was a bed of clay in the bottom in which the sewer was laid. They ex- pected the quicksand would extend yet for some distance, and would retard the progress of the work. The sewer was also laid through field to 418 belonging to Mr. Ross. The total length of sewer laid to present time was about 1,840 lineal yards. There had been but very little further work done on the outfall land. Altogether the work done was satisfactory. They had instructed the contractor to clear Whitbarrow-lane as quickly as possible that it might be opened for traffic.

div.head: NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT.
div.p: NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

The NUISANCE INSPECTOR reported that there bad not been much difficulty of late in the disposal of the scavenging material owing to its being in greater demand by the farmers in the district. But as the season advanced it was probable this demand would fall off to a considerable ex- tent, and they might be subjected to a bock during the hot weather of summer. It seemed, therefore, desirable to take into consideration the adoption of Fowler's patent closet wherever it was reason- ably practicable to do so, as it promised to be a cheap and efficient remedy for many existing nuisances in connection with privies, especially in confined localities. With refer- ence to the state of scarlet fever, he was not aware of more than twa cases in the district at the present time, and thesa were confined to the same house in which cases of fever had previously existed. In all cases disinfection had taken place after convalesence, and it was to be hoped that the district would soon be entirely free.—Mr. Rocierts explained to Mr. Thomason the principles upon which Fowler's patent closet is worked, and said it would be a valuable acquisi- tion.

div.head: SURVEYOR'S REPORT.
div.p: SURVEYOR'S REPORT.

This report,contained nothing of public interest with the exception of an intimation from the surveyor that the Navi- gation Company propose to enclose the piece of land lying between the roads and adjoining Camsby Bridge, leaving only a width of 24 feet for the main road, and 22 feet for the road leading to Massey Brook. A PETITION.
Tl•e following petition respecting the construction of the sewer was read:—

We, the undersigned, being owners of property through which, according to the original plan. it f was intended to carry the sewer now in course of construction, notice with much satisfaction that an alternative sheme has teen devised by your engineer, by the adoption of which our several properties will be preserved to us intact. Whilst much regreqing to occasion your Board any additional exisense In carrying out the sewage scheme, duty to ourselves and our successors demands that we should take such steps as shall secure to us our present and prospective rights and privileges. We notice, however. that at the last meeting of your Board that this amended schetne was considered, but was not adopted. the Board having separated without having passedany resolution upon it. This leads us to infer that, though the alternative scheme has been prepared and submitted, the original has not been entirely abandoned; and in order to protect our rights and privileges, we beg re- spectfully to give you notice that in the event of the original scheme being adored by your Board, we shall most reluct- antly be compelled taciaim as compensation for damages done , to our respective properties, and the interference with our present and prospective rights and privi- leges, the SIM of not less than £550 for such damage and interference. Thanking your Botrd for the courtesy manliested•by meeting our views by she pro- posed dive, sion of the sewer, and trusting that this amended scheme will be adopted, and that we shall be lel-, in undis- turbed possession of our respective properties, we are yours re- spectfully, (signed). Isaac trouxhton, James Gregsott. Riehd. Whitelegge, John B. Taylor, J. E Rawson. J. W. Evans, Ed- Ain Brown, Benjamin Whitelegge. per R. W.
It was decided that the alternative scheme be adopted, subject to certain conditions.
_TILE GAS kOESTION.

Mr. ROGERS read a report on the condition of the as and moved that it be recorded on the minutes.—Tbe motion having been seconded ace carried, Mr. ROGERS said that it was not the quality of the gas that was bad, but the means of conveying it. The mine were not large enough to admit of a sufficient quantity of gas passing through them, ;and the works were coneiderahly higher than the places to which the gas was distributed, and it required some pressure. The gas, as he had said before, was good enough. if they could only get a sufraeient quantity of it. It seemed to be the general impression of the Board that the mains ought to be taken up and larger ones laid.—Mr. CALLENDER asked where was the money to some from.—Mr. Itotaxas: There is £5OO yet, you know.—The CLERK said if the Board intended to make an alteration it would be better to do it at once as the season was getting ads anced —Mr. DEWEURST thought it would be best to have the place examined by an engineertefore the Board committed them- selves to anything.--Mr. ROGERS said be alteration would increase every gas bill in the town.—The CLERK thought it would be more satisfactory to the ratepayers to have a cm- petent engineer's report on the matter, and they would see why they were paying more money.— After a little further discussion, Mr. ROGERS moved, and Mr. DEWHIIRST seconded, that Mr. Paterson, of Warrington, be requested to come over and inspect the gas works and mains, and report to the Board whether any improvements were necessary.—The motion was carried unanimously. Mere was no other bueincce of importance.

div.head: DIVISION ON THE AFFIRMA-
div.p: THE DIVISION ON THE AFFIRMA-
TION BILL.
itiE INTEREST TAKEN IN THE DIVISION

The keen interest taken in the division upon the Affirma- tion Bill was sheWn not only by .the full attendance of members cla both sides of the House of Commons, but also by 0.0 crowded state of all the galleries. The parliamen- tary lobbies and entrance hall were likewise thronged by ex- pectant or disappointed visitors, for whom there was no space in the legislative chamber. In response to urgency of the summonses issued by the whips of both parties there were present many members who are not often seen at St. Stephen's save on critical occasions, but on the other hand there were many absent, whose absence was the more con- spicuous by reason of their usually regular attendance. Amongst the Irish members who did not attend or take part in the division were Sir P.:O'Brien, Rev. Isaac elson, Dr. Kinnear, Sir Thomas M'Clare, and Messrs. Nolan, Errington, Redmond, Denis O'Connor, P. J. Smyth, Healy, C. Russell, Lea, T. A. Dickson, R. P. Blennerhassett, the Attorney-General for Ireland, Mr. Given and Mr. Findlater. Among the English Liberal absentees, through illness or engagements abroad, were Mr. H. Whalley, Mr. Magniac, and Mr. W. Holms, whilst on the Conservative side the absentees included Mr. Watney, who is in Australia, and Mr. Schieiber, from ill- ness. There was a comparatively small number of pairs, Mr. Muntz paired for the Government with Mr. H. Birley against the Bill. The absent members included Mr. S. Morley, Alderman W. Lawrence, Alderman M'Arthur, Sir George Campbell, and Mr. C. R. N. Talbot. Mr. Gabbett was present during the division, but abstained from voting. The division commenced at a quarter-past one, and, of course, proceeded mainly on party lines; but upon the Liberal side there were a few desertions and numerous ab- stentions. Amongst those who voted against the Govern- ment were the two members for the City of Dublin, Dr. Lyons and Mr. M. Brooks, the Hon. C. W. Fitzwilliam, Hon. W. H. Fitzwilliam, Hon. W. J. Fitzwilliam, Messrs. Torrens, Jerningham, O'Shea, and Fay, Sir G. Bal- four, Sir E. Watkin, and the Land League mem- bers. No Conservative voted with the Government. When the House was cleared there was an influx of noble

lords in the peers' gallery, a sight seldom witnessed, and the Ministerial bench was crowded. The Prime Minister, Lord Hartington, and Sir Charles Dilke were observed in close consultation. There were about six members, three Liberals and three Homo Rulers, on whose decision depended the whole issue. The nominal Liberals were Sir E. Watkin, and two of the lion Messrs. Fitzwilliam. The Home Rulers were Mr. Fay, Mr. M. Brooks, and the O'Gorman Mahon. The latter would have voted for the Government but for the interposition of Mr. Parnell, who at the last moment pre- vailed upun the veteran member to absent himself from the division. Mr. Fay was nearly taken into the Ministerial lobby by Lord Kensington, one of the Liberal whips, when Mr. Callan appeared on the scene, and was heard all over the House to be persuading his colleague to go with him against the Government, and succeeded in inducing him to take that course. Before it was possible for any official announcement of the result of the division to be made, Mr. Ashmead-Baetlert rushed up the floor of the House and addressed the leaders of the Conservative party in words which, although not precisely heard, were interpreted with great satisfaction by the sup- porters of the Opposition to indicate that the Government had been defeated. Behind the Speaker's chair there was a large concourse of the opponents of the Bill, who seemed rather doubtful of the result of the vote presently to be an- nounced. Lord Richard Grosvenor, the senior whip to the Ministerial party, and Mr. Rowland Winn, the Opposition senior whip, forced their way to the clerks at the table, who wrote down the numbers on the paper. The conversation that a moment before had generally prevailed now ceased, and on the paper being handed Mr. Rowland Winn, who received it witb an apparently gratified smile, there was a most extra- • ordinary outburst of cheering. The Speaker, standing, tried by gesture to restrain the demonstration, but finding his efforts useless his features relaxed into a smile. Mr. Gladstone seemed deeply concerned, and watched every feature of the animated proceedings. At last the numbers were announced by Mr. Rowland Winn, and several honourable members in the front rank of a crowd below the bar literally seemed to dance, whilst other mem- bers behind the front Opposition bench actually threw their hats into the air. The majority of the occupants of the strangers' gallery, forgetting the strict conditions of their presence, rose to their feet and joined in the demon- stration, calling as loudly as the honourable members them- selves—the efforts of the officers to restrain them being of no avail. On the Ministerial side of the House there was a strange contrast of subdued silence. Mr. Bradlaugh, sitting below the peers' gallery, watched with apparent interest the exhibition of feeling on the Opposition side of the House, and shortly afterwards retired. Contrary to general expec- 4ation, the Prime Minister made no announcement as to the views of the Government in regard to the effect of the vote just given. Ten minuses afterwards the House adjourned, for it was obvious that there was no desire for the House to sit after the declaration of the division on the Affirmation Bill. Indeed, the House became rapidly deserted by hon. members, who rushed, as if with One accord, to their respective clubs, where the newly-created political posi- tion was eagerly discussed, especially at the Carlton and Reform.

div.head: _THE CLOSING SCENE.
div.p: _THE CLOSING SCENE.

The Daily Telegraph thus describes the. closing scene of the debate :—lt was exactly five minutes after one o'clock when Lord Hartington concluded. No man presumed to follow him. The Speaker put the question. Those to the right cried "Aye," and those to the left in more stentorian tones shouted" No." The sand-glass was turned and the electric bells rung to summon members from the library. When they bad all assembled the doors were shut and the division took place, Mr. Bradlaugh remaining the while in his seat below the bar. As members crowded back from the lobbies the excitement grew, and when it was found that the Government lobby was first exhausted the sensation became intense. Mr. Callan had the satisfaction of bringing the first positive news of the result, and he declared it loudly enough for all to hear. The cheering which followed from the occu- pants of the now overflowing benches to the left of the Speaker surpassed anything that has been heard in this Parliament. It was sometime before Mr. Winn, the victo- rious teller, was able to announce the figures—For the se- cond reading, 289; against, 292; majority against, 3. A scene of great excitement, in contrast with the normal de- corum of the House, followed. Members stood up, waved their hats (one gentleman threw his into thej air), clapped hands. and " Hurralf'd" for several minutes. Some of the

Irish members were loud in their ejaculations.—W i-t-hisrr; quarter of an hour, however, all was changed and silence reigned in the deserted camber. Mrs. Gladstone, it may be stated, had, from the ladies' gallery, being a spectator of the proceedings.

div.head: ANALYSIS OF THE DIVISION.
div.p: ANALYSIS OF THE DIVISION.

The division was the closest as well as the most exciting that has taken place on any great party question since that of March 11, 1873, when, upon the question that the Irish University Bill ahould be read a second time, the first Gladstone Administration was defeated as the second now has been, and, a singular coincidence, by exactly the same majority. The numbers then were 287 to 284, a total of 571 as against 581 who in this latest division passed through the lohbies. The number last given is larger than that which took nart in any of the divisions of the Parliament of 1874-80, whtn the two heaviest votes were upon Mr. Glad- stone's motion on the Eastern question, and Lord Harting- ton's on the bringing over of the Indian troops, when the numbers were 572 and 578 respectively. But it is appreciably smaller than it was last year upon the question of the closure, when the numbers were 318 to 279, a total of 597 who voted. It is, however, by far the largest division that has been taken upon this question of Mr. Bradlaugh's ad- mission to the House. On Jane 22nd, 1880, a motion by Mr. Labouchere to the effect that Mr. Bradlaugh should be allowed to affirm was defeated by 275 to 230, a total of 505; on the succeeding July Ist, a motion of Mr. Gladstone allowing Mr. Bradlaugh to affirm subject to his liability under the statute was carried by 274 to 236, a total of 510. On April 26th, 1881, Sir Stafford Northcote's motion to pre- vent ths junior member fc,r Northampton from taking the oath was carried by 208 to 175, 383 members thus taking part in the division. On February 7th, 1882, a motion by the same right hon. gentleman to a similar effect was passed by 286 to 228, a total of 514; and on March 6th of the same year it was re-affirmed (after Mr. Bradlaugh's expulsion and re-election) by 257 to 242, a total of 499. It will,lrom these figures (which practically traces the history of the question. so far as the House is concerned, and leaving out of account the division after various scenes) be seen that previous to this division 274 was the highest number that had voted in favour of Mr. Bradlaugh being allowed to affirm, and 286 the highest that had voted aglinst that course—the former being raised by fifteen and the latter by six on the question of an Affirmation Bill. But although the division was thus heavy, it leaves a great many members unaccounted far, though the list of " pairs " when it is issued, will slightly diminish that total. Ten Liberals—viz. Hon. C. W. Fitzwil- liam, Hon. H. W. Fitzwilliam' Hon. W. J. Fitzwilliam, Mr. Montagu Guest, Mr. Jerningham, Dr. Lyons, Mr. William Nicholson (Petersfield), Mr. M'Cullogh Torrens, Mr. Villiers Stuart, and Sir E. Watkin—vhted against the Government, as did also the followiug Home Rulers:—Messrs. Barry, Bellingham, Biggar, Blake, Brooks, Byrne, Callan, Colthurst, Corbet, Daly, Dawson, Far, Gray, Harrington, Kenny, Lalor, Leahy, Leamy, fever, Macfarlane, M'Carthy, M'Coan, M'Kenna,.slartin, Marum, Mayne, Metge, Molloy, Moore, O'Brien, Arthur O'Connor, T. P. O'Connor, O'Donnell, O'Kelly, O'Skea, O'Sullivan. Parnell, R. Power, Sexton Shaw Shell, Smithwick, Sullivan, and Synan ; a total of 45. NO Conservative voted in the majority, and the following are the names of those absent from the division: though some of them undoubtedly have paired :—Liberals, Messrs. All men, Michael Bass, Blennerhassett, H. A. Brassey, Corbett, J. Dickson, T. Dickson, Earp, Findlater, Givan, Holland, William Holms, Jones Parry, Kinnear, William Lawrence, T. Lea, G. 11. C. Leigh, Magniac, Middleton, Samuel Morley, Muntz, Porter, Pugh, J. N. Richardson, Charles Russell, an Wballey, and Sir R. Blennerhassett, Sir George Campbell, Sir William M'Arthur, Sir T. Maclure, Sir P. O'Brien, Sir Harry Verney, and the Marquis of Staf- ford—a total of thirty-three. Conservatives.: Messrs. Birlev, Close, Eaton, Schreiber, Watney,-and Wyndham—a total of six. Home Rulers: Messrs. Commins, Errington, Gabbett, Healy, Mitchell Henry, Meldon, Nelson, Nolan, D. M. O'Conor, The O'Gorman Mahon, O'Connor Power, and P. J. Smyth—a total of twelve. Only two Home Rulers voted with the Government—viz, The O'Donoghue and Mr. O'Shaughneesr

PINIONS OF THE PRESS. The T,letes points out that the purpose of the Bill could only De carried out by a decision of the House of Commons, te unmistakable as to place the meaning out of the reach of renewed attacks by the Opposition, and to overawe the an- I tipathies of the House of Lords. The difficulties were not lessened, but rather increased by the fact that the normal majority for Ministers was a large one. A party which, under ordinary conditions, is able to carry its measures by a majority of at least 80, is weakened for the special business in hand far more than is represented by the mere reduction I, of numbers when that majority sinks towards a vanishing I point. That the majority should have been turned into a minority does not, in fact, make the result more un- favourable to the Government. It tends to simplify the t situation. It is certain that the moral effect of the division must have been forecasted, and that the Ministry have already made up their minds how the judgment of the House of Commons is to regulate their future course on Oaf:s.l question of the Parliamentary oath. The Daily News observes :—The forces of bigotry and intolerance have triumphed. Strange as it may seem, there appears to be members of Parliament who think that the claims of religion, natural or revealed, upon the allegiance of the human mind and heart are supported by and even based upon the use of legal and constitutional formulae. We can hardly believe that those who employ this sort of ' argument on public occasions, and in the heat of debate, ' would be prepared deliberately to maintain it in their calmer moments. Theconsecpences of it in a particular event would be so momentous, and as we should say, if the subject were not such a solemn one, so absurd, that almost any sane man would shrink from adhering to it. Conservatives, as Mr. Gladstone said the other night, are now defending, with rather ludicrous inopportuneness, the admission of Jews to Parliament. But if the arguments used by the Conserva- tives on this point 30 years ago were well founded, there is no escape from the conclusion that England has ceased for a quarter of a century to be a Christian country. The Parliament of the nation did not cease to be Protestant when Mr. O'Connell was allowed to take his seat, nor Christian when the Jews were admitted into it. It would not become atheistic had Mr. Bradlaugh been allowed to affirm. The House of Commons, however, has not acted on this sound principle. The frantic cheering and excitement with which the numbers were received by the victorious party of honest bigots and the electioneering traffickers in in the name of God were mixed with cries for Mr. Gladstone. But the time had not come then for any Ministerial an- nouncement.

The Standard remarks :—lt is a remarkable, perhaps an ominous, coincidence that it was precisely by the same ma- ion.), of three votes that Mr. Gladstone's last administration was defeated on the Irish University Bill, ten years ago. Although the full significance of this morning's division cannot be measured by the numerical dimensions of the majority, the result is in itself as decisive as it was in a sense unexpected. The question now isnot as to the cause of the Ministerial discomfiture, but as to its consequence. What will the Government do next ? They dare not appeal to the country, and they have no intention of resigning. They must consequently continue in office under the stigma of a defeat such as no Government has tamely endured since Sir Charles Wood had to reconstruct his budget three times in one session.

The result (says the Daily Telegraph) had it occurred at the second or third night of the debate might have caused surprise, but towards the close of the discussion the better informed class of observers were prepared for it. To Minis- ters themselves it seems to have caused little astonishment, and certainly nothing like consternation. The Prime Minister did not even move the adjournment of the House, and Mr. Trevelyan proceeded with the Bill of which he is in charge as if nothing had happened. The truth is, indeed, that although a victory for the Government was at first au- ticipated, the majority which had been reckoned upon a week ago retained no permanent place in expert calculations. The division, after all, only precipitates a re- sult which would have happened later on if the second read- ing had been carried by a small majority. It was not for the Government, nor even for the Liberal party, but for Parliament amid the country to say whether a law which happens to press hardly upon Mr. Bradlaugh should or should not be altered, and Parliament having decided in the negative, the responsibility of Ministers is at an end. We are not so sanguine as to suppose that we have heard the last of Mr. Braiihiegh. He may very possibly cause casual interruptions of public business for some time to come, but there will at least be no more wasting in . long, embittered, and profitless discussion of the time which still remains to Parliament for the fulfilment of the promised programme of legislation. The Daily Chronicle observes :—lf the debate had been conducted in a legitimate manner it would hardly been ne- cessary even to mention Mr. Bradlaugh's name, and in that case the whole question, might have been disposed of in ten minutes. Time has been wasted, prejudice excited, and a really paltry question magnified into Imperial importance. A SHUR]: HISTORY OF THE BRADLAUGH QUESTION.

The following facts will be read with interest at the pre- sent juncture. In 1868 and 1874 Mr. Bradlaugh contested Northampton, but he had not the united support of the Liberals, and was consequently defeated. In March, 1880, he again came forward, and was adopted at head-quarters as a Liberal candidate. In consequence of this he was re- turned by 700 votes. His election was thus directly due to the wire-pullers of the Liberal party. In due course he pre- sented himself at the table of the House of Commons, and requested to be permitted to make an affirmation, instead of taking the oar h. The speaker was not clear as to Mr. Bradlaugh's right to do this, and he appealed to the House for instructions. On the motion of the Government, a com- mittee was appointed to consider and report on the question. The committee gave it as their,opinion&that such persons as Mr. Bradlaugh had not a legal right to affirm. The minority, however, included men so famous for their legal lure as Sir H. James Q C., Sir F. Herschell,Q.C., Mr.Watkin Williams, Q.C., and Mr. Sergeant Simon. On the day the report was issued (May 20th) Mr. Bradlaugh wrote to the newspapers a letter saying that the oath contained words which were to him of " an idle and meaningless character.".on the follow- log day, notwithstanding this, he presented himself to take the oath. Sir H. D. Wolff interposed against this piece of ! public profanation, and a fresh committee was appointed to consider Mr. Bradlaugh's claim to take the oath without question. The report was against Mr. Bradlaugh's right to have the oath administered to him; but the committee (led by an eminent Liberal lawyer) suggested that ! Mr. Bradlaugh should be allowed to affirm at his peril, and so have a legal right of testing the point in a court of law. Mr. Labouchere consequently moved that Mr. Bradlaugh be allowed to affirm, anct was supported by the Government. An amendment of Sir H. Giffard's that Mr. Bradlaugh be neither permitted to take the oath nor make an affirmation was carried by 275 to 230. On the fol- lowing day Mr. Bradlaugh went to the table of the House, and refused to withdraw. As Mr. Gladstone would not act, Sir S. Northcote moved that Mr. Bradlaugh be taken into custody for disobeying the orders of the chair. This was done, and on the following day he was discharged, on the motion of the Conservative leader. A Cabinet Council was held to consider the subject, and on July Ist Mr. Gladstone moved the rescinding of Sir H. Giffard's motion, and the allowing of Mr. Bradlaugh to affirm. An amend- ment proposed by Sir S. Northcote was rejected by 303 votes to 249. Mr. A. M. Sullivan then moved that the new ! resolution should apply only to future members; but was defeated by 274 to 236, the Government all voting against him. On the following day Mr. Bradraugh made an affir- mation. A suit was thereupon commenced by Mr. H. L. Clarke, to recover penalties from Mr. Bradlaugh for having ! sat in the House of Commons without having made the oath required by law. Judgment was given in favour of Mr. Clarke, and on appeal the judgment was confirmed, Lord Justice Bramwell saying, "It is about as plain a case as ever came before a court of justice ; I think it is a perfectly plain case that the defendant was not entitled to affirm." Accordingly on the next day (April Ist 1881), a new writ was issued for Northampton, and Mr. Bradlaugh was again returned. On the 26th of the same mouth Mr.l Bradlaugh presented himself at the table and claimed to take the oath. Sir S. Northcote otjected to Mr. Bradlaugh taking the oath as an idle form, and moved that he be not permitted to do so. Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Bright, and Sir H. James opposed this motion, but it as carried against the Government by 208 to 175. Another scene occurred here, Mr. Bradlaugh refusing to leave the table, and Sir S.North- cote again having to act as leader of the House and order his removal. As he again returned to the table the House adjourned, and on his acting similarly the next day it was understood the Government would bring in a bill on the subject. They could, however, only get a morning sitting to discuss the question by a majority of 20 in a full House, and they let the matter drop on May 9th, 1881. On the following day Mr. Bradlaugh again presented him- self at the table. Mr. Gladstone taking no action, Sir S. Northcote moved that Mr. Bradlaugh should be, and re- main, removed from the House until he undertake not to disturb its proceedings. This was carried. ThG more recent incidepts in the case are too well known to need re- counting here. The expectation that a bill would be pro- mised in the Queen's Speech, delivered two months since ; the demonstration in Trafalgtr-square ; the subsequent; promise of a bill ; the character of that measure—retrospec- tive in the first instance, non-retrospective in the second ; the shoals of petitions and the strenuous Conservative op- position to it throughout, as well as the result of the divi- sion, are all fresh in the public mind. I '

The rejection of the Affirmation Bill has caused great ex- citement in Northampton. The Daily News understands that an inquiry will be made into the composition of the signatures to the petitions against the second reading of the Affirmation Bill presented to the House of Commons, and that possibly a return may follow.

THE PECULIAR PEOPLE.-At the Central Criminal Court on Wednesday, Robert Conaens, a member of the religious sect known a; the Peculiar People, surrendered to answer a charge of the manslaughter of his child Alice by neglecting to provide medical assistance for it when suffering from bronchitis. The Grand Jury had ignored the bill, and no evidence was offered in support of the coroner's rcquisition, and the prisoner was ordered to be discharged. A RECKLESS BONDSMAN.-At Prescot on Tuesday a man applied to the magistrates to be released from a bond into which he had too hastily entered. A man named Eastham having about six weeks ago been held to bail for a breach of the peace the applicant, though he knew nothing about him, had become one of his sureties, and now East- ham having" begun lighting again" he wished to with- draw from the responsibility—The magistrates told the ap- prcant they could not help him.in.the matter.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that a MEETING of the Owners and Ratepayers of the borough of Warrington, in the counties of Lancaster and Chester. will be held on TUESDAY. the EIGHTH DAY of MAY 1883. at Seven o'clock in the Evening, in the PUBLIC HALL, In RYLANDS-STREET. in WARRINGTON. in pursuance of the provisions of an Act of the 3bth and 36th Victoria, cap. 91, intituled, "An Act to authorise the applica- tion of Funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies in sertai u cases," for the purpose of considering a resolution passed by the Council of the Borough of Warrington, at a meet- ing held by the Council on the Seventeenth day of April. 1883, and, if thought desirable, of passing a further resolution con- firming the said resolution of the touncil. and authorizing the Council to take such steps as they shall think, or be advised. may be necessary for opposing a Bill in Parliament, in the present Session thereof, to authorize the construction of a Ship Canal to Manchester and for other purposes; and also to sanction the payment of the coats. charges, and expenses in- curred, and to be incurred, in such opposition, upon the Borough Fund, Borough Rate, or other fund, or rate, or account of the said Council applicable thereto.—Dated this Third day of May, 1883. LEWIS'S N LIVERPOOL, AND THE PROVIDING OF THE BEST Tx A TO FAMILIZS, HOTELS, AND PUBLIC AND PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS THROUGH- OUT THE UNITED KINGDOM. Who are Lewis's? Well, Lewis's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Bank of England is known le London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago. and Lewis's have at this present time one,of the very largest businesses in Eng- land. Lewis's have not always sold Tea, but having a very large number of employes to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's were struck with the difficulty of pr i curing a good drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly abominable. Tired of the constant and not unreasonable complaints and of the perpetual changing of their Tea Dealers, Lewis's at last resolved to buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from the shippers, and to en- gage a qualified person to make the purchase. Lewis's cou'd hardly believe there could be ouch a ehange for the better in the cost and quality of the tea so bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's thought what was good enough for the use of all their establishments, public and private, would sorely be good enough for the general public. I ewis's then began to sell Teas to their friends, and at last were induced to make the sale public in Lancashire, where they sell 20,000 pounds of Tea per week. Lewis's now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future to make their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a pound. Lewis a have no other price Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. Two shil- lings is a favourite cries with tewies, they having been able to supply the public with many excellent things at the price. Not till after much hard work did Lewis's succeed in blending a splendid and most deliciously-flavoured Tea, which they are giving to the public for 2s a pound. Many tea dealers charge the public Os and Is 6d for a similar quality. Lewis's desire to be the universal suppliers of Tea. Tea is drunk in every house- hold in the United Kingdom; it should therefore be sold at a less profit than any other article of consumption, except bread. Lewis's wish particularly to direct the attention of every family and every househo:der to the great advantage there lain buying Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The flavour is so good and the strength so very great, that one pound goes further than 18 ounces of most other Teas providing always the water boils thoroughly. The proof dial Lewis's do not exaggerate the appreciation in which their Two Shilling Tea Is held lies in the fact that they receive thousands of orders every day from all parts of the United Kingdom. Lewis's would like members of the Press all over the United Kingdom to write for a pound of Lawis's Two Shilling Tta; they are sure to be satisfied Red astonished with the result. Every hotel-keeper, and every public and private institution throughout the country, should write to Lewis's in Liverpool for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The risk is not great; It is only to send 2s in stamps to Lewis's in Liverpool, and in return they will receive a sound of splendid Tea, packed neatly in a box. carriage paid, to any address in the United Kingdom. —Address Lewis's in Liverpool.
